docs.text: What happens if stock is incorrect? ¤ When physical inventory doesn't match system records, you need to investigate and correct it. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Common causes of stock discrepancies ¤ Common cause What to check Transaction errors Parts issued but not recorded, returns not processed Physical issues Items misplaced, wrong bin locations , damaged items System issues Data entry mistakes, incomplete transactions Figure 1 outlines the sequential six-step inventory correction process: Verify the count : recount the item to confirm physical quantities. Review transactions : look at recent activity for missed entries. Check related records : inspect work orders and receipts. Get approval if needed : obtain supervisor sign-off for large adjustments. Adjust the balance : update records by using Inventory Adjustments. Follow up : resolve underlying causes to prevent recurrence. Figure 1: The inventory correction process 💡 Tips: Best practices for inventory accuracy ¤ Daily habits: Record transactions immediately Verify before confirming Return items promptly Keep storeroom organized Report issues quickly Weekly tasks: Review high-value items Check reorder items Spot check locations Investigate variances Update procedures Monthly activities: Analyze error patterns Review adjustment reports Conduct cycle counts Train as needed Improve processes Why fix inventory errors quickly? ¤ Inventory discrepancies can cause stockouts, excess inventory , and inaccurate costs. Fixing errors quickly ensures: Accurate records No work delays Reliable stock levels Correct cost tracking Regular counting and prompt adjustments keep your inventory data trustworthy. What causes inventory errors? ¤ Transaction errors ¤ Parts issued but not recorded Returns not processed Wrong quantities entered Duplicate transactions Missing receipts Physical issues ¤ Items misplaced in storeroom Wrong bin locations Damaged or lost items Theft or shrinkage Items in wrong storeroom System issues ¤ Data entry mistakes Timing differences Incomplete transactions System errors Integration problems Figure 2 shows how three distinct sources of error result in a stock discrepancy: Transaction errors : parts issued but not recorded, returns not processed, or wrong quantities entered. Physical issues : items misplaced in the storeroom, wrong bin locations , or damaged and lost items . System issues : data entry mistakes, timing differences, or incomplete transactions. Figure 2: Common sources of inventory errors How do I identify discrepancies? ¤ During work ¤ You might notice: Item shows in stock but can't find it Physical count doesn't match system Bin is empty but system shows quantity Wrong item in labeled bin Unexpected items in storeroom Through cycle counts ¤ Regular counting reveals: Quantity differences Location errors Missing items Extra items Condition issues From reports ¤ System reports show: Negative balances, which are physically impossible Unusually high balances No movement for long periods Frequent adjustments Cost variances TODO: Add visual content A screenshot showing an inventory discrepancy report would be useful here. How do I investigate discrepancies? ¤ Step 1: Verify the physical count ¤ Before adjusting the system: Recount the item : Check all bins for this item Look in nearby locations Verify item number matches Check for similar items Check for reserved items : Items in pick lists Parts allocated to work orders Items being transferred Staged materials Look for recent transactions: Issues not yet processed Returns in progress Receipts being entered Transfers pending TODO: Add visual content A checklist for investigating discrepancies would be useful here. Step 2: Review transaction history ¤ Check recent activity: Issue transactions : Were parts recorded? Receipts : Did everything get entered? Returns : Were returns processed? Transfers : Did transfers complete? Adjustments : Previous corrections made? Look for patterns: Repeated errors with same item Specific user or storeroom Particular transaction type Time of day issues occur Step 3: Check related records ¤ Verify: Work orders : Materials recorded correctly? Receipts : All delivered stock entered? Inventory transfers : Transfers completed properly? Issues : Items picked and issued from storeroom? Figure 3 maps the four related records to check when a stock discrepancy is identified: Work orders : verify whether materials were recorded correctly against work tasks. Receipts : confirm whether all delivered stock was entered into the system. Inventory transfers : check whether transfers completed properly across locations . Issues : verify whether items were picked and issued from the storeroom. Figure 3: Related records to check when stock is incorrect How do I correct inventory ? ¤ Make adjustments ¤ Once you've verified the error: What to do: Open the Inventory application. Find the item . Go to the storeroom with error. Use Inventory Adjustments . Enter correct physical quantity. System calculates difference. Add reason for adjustment. Include detailed notes. The system updates balance, adjusts cost, records transaction, and creates audit trail. TODO: Add visual content A video showing how to adjust inventory would be useful here. Adjustment best practices ¤ Always document: What you found What you expected Why the error occurred Who discovered it When it was found Corrective action taken Get approval if needed: Large adjustments High-value items Frequent corrections Unusual circumstances Follow up: Prevent recurrence Train if needed Improve processes Monitor for patterns Types of adjustments ¤ Quantity adjustments ¤ Increase balance: Found items not recorded Receipt was missed Return not processed Transfer not completed Decrease balance: Items issued but not recorded Damaged or lost items Theft or shrinkage Items moved to another location Location adjustments ¤ Moving items : Wrong bin recorded Reorganizing storeroom Consolidating locations Correcting bin assignments Cost adjustments ¤ Correcting costs: Wrong price entered Cost method changed Vendor price correction Currency adjustments TODO: Add visual content A table comparing adjustment types would be useful here. How do I prevent inventory errors? ¤ Good practices ¤ At issue time: Record transactions immediately Verify quantities Check item numbers Confirm locations Complete transactions fully At receipt time: Count carefully Match to purchase order Verify item numbers Put in correct location Record promptly During returns: Process immediately Verify condition Return to correct bin Update system Note any issues Regular cycle counting ¤ Count frequently: High-value items weekly Fast-moving items monthly All items quarterly Random spot checks Count systematically: Follow schedule Use count books Verify before adjusting Document findings Analyze patterns TODO: Add visual content A sample cycle count schedule would be useful here. Storeroom organization ¤ Keep organized: Clear bin labels Logical layout Similar items separated Regular housekeeping Defined locations Control access: Authorized personnel only Proper training Clear procedures Accountability Security measures Handling specific scenarios ¤ Negative balance ¤ If system shows negative quantity: This shouldn't happen physically. Indicates transaction error. Review recent issues. Check for duplicate transactions. Correct immediately. Investigate cause. Large discrepancy ¤ For significant differences: Don't adjust immediately. Investigate thoroughly. Get supervisor approval. Document extensively. Implement prevention. Monitor closely. Recurring errors ¤ If same item has frequent issues: Analyze error pattern. Identify root cause. Fix process problem. Retrain if needed. Consider item changes. Monitor improvement. Figure 4 outlines the decision paths and corrective actions for three inventory discrepancy situations: Negative balance : when the system shows a negative quantity, correct it immediately by reviewing recent issues and looking for duplicate entries, then investigate the root cause. Large discrepancy : when the difference is significant, do not adjust immediately; investigate thoroughly, obtain supervisor approval, and document the findings. Recurring errors : when the same item has frequent issues, fix the process by analyzing the error pattern, identifying the root cause, and retraining staff if needed. Figure 4: How to handle different types of inventory error What's the impact of inventory errors? ¤ On operations ¤ Stockouts: Work delays Emergency orders Higher costs Service issues Excess inventory : Wasted space Tied-up cash Obsolescence risk Carrying costs On costs ¤ Direct costs: Incorrect work order costs Wrong inventory valuation Budget variances Financial reporting errors Indirect costs: Time investigating Emergency purchases Lost productivity Customer dissatisfaction On planning ¤ Poor decisions: Wrong reorder quantities Incorrect stock levels Bad purchasing decisions Inefficient operations TODO: Add visual content An infographic showing error impacts would be useful here. When should I perform physical inventory ? ¤ Full physical count ¤ Do complete inventory when: Annual audit required Major discrepancies found System implementation Storeroom reorganization Change in responsibility Cycle counting ¤ Regular partial counts: Less disruptive Continuous accuracy Catches errors early Maintains reliability Spreads workload How do I use count books? ¤ Count books help organize counting: Group items logically Schedule counts Assign counters Track completion Record results Analyze variances The system can: Generate count books Assign to users Track progress Record counts Calculate differences Create adjustments You create count books in the Count Books application. You count items in the Inventory Counting app on the desktop or in IBM Maximo Mobile. In Inventory Counting, you can: Count the items in a count book. Count items that are not in a count book. Count items and rotating assets . Set tolerances that allow for small differences between the system balance and the physical count. See alerts for differences that need a recount. Count in batches as part of a cycle count. After you count, the Reconciled? checkbox on the inventory balance shows whether the count is reconciled. [SME confirmation required: Confirm that you can open Inventory Counting in a desktop browser in Select as well as in IBM Maximo Mobile, and confirm where counts are reconciled.] TODO: Add visual content A screenshot showing a count book would be useful here. docs.text: How do I track stock levels? ¤ Monitor what's in your storerooms so you know what's available, what needs reordering, and where items are located. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Stock balance types ¤ Balance type What it means Current balance Total quantity in storeroom (includes reserved items ) Available balance What you can actually use (current minus reserved) Reserved quantity Parts allocated to work orders Reorder point Minimum level before reordering 💡 Tips for success ¤ Regular monitoring: Check stock levels daily Review reorder needs weekly Analyze usage monthly Audit inventory quarterly Maintain accuracy: Issue parts promptly Return unused items Perform cycle counts Investigate discrepancies Optimize levels: Adjust reorder points based on usage Reduce slow-moving inventory Increase stock of critical items Balance cost versus availability Use reports: Stock status reports Reorder reports Usage analysis Cost reports ABC analysis: prioritize high-value items Why track stock levels? ¤ Good inventory tracking prevents stockouts and ensures parts are available when you need them. When you track stock levels, you can: Know what's available right now See what needs reordering Find where items are located Control costs Optimize storeroom space The system tracks quantities, costs, and locations automatically as items move in and out. What can I track? ¤ The Inventory application shows: Current balance How many items are in stock. Location Which storeroom and bin. Cost Current value of inventory . Reorder status Items below minimum levels. Reserved items Parts allocated to work orders . Usage history How items are being consumed. How do I view inventory levels? ¤ Check a specific item ¤ What to do: Open the Inventory application. Search by item number or description. Select the item . View the information you need: Current quantity on hand Available balance: not reserved Cost information Reorder point and minimum stock level If the item is in multiple storerooms, you can view all locations on one screen and compare quantities across sites . Check storeroom contents ¤ What to do: Open the Storerooms application. Select your storeroom. View all items stocked there: Current quantities Items below reorder point Reserved quantities Items in pick lists View by bin or lot ¤ For detailed tracking: Bin level : See exactly where items are stored Lot level : Track specific batches Condition : Monitor item condition changes Rotating assets : Track individual asset items Figure 1 illustrates the storeroom inventory hierarchy across three connected columns representing physical location , item tracking levels, and real-time balance calculations: Physical location : Navigates from Main storeroom as the primary inventory site , down through aisle and shelf coordinates such as Row A, Shelf 03, to a specific storage compartment, BIN-04. Item tracking level : From the physical bin, items branch into three tracking modes: standard inventory items tracked by item number, lot and batch tracking recording batch numbers and expiration dates, and rotating serialized assets tracking unique serial numbers. Balance calculation : Tracks inventory availability across records, where a current physical balance of 25 items minus a reserved quantity of 5 items allocated to work orders yields an available balance of 20 items ready for issue. Figure 1: Storeroom hierarchy for bin, lot, and rotating asset tracking How do I understand inventory balances? ¤ Key balance types ¤ Current balance Total quantity in storeroom Includes reserved items Shows what you physically have Available balance Current balance minus reserved What you can actually use Updates as items are reserved Reserved quantity Parts allocated to work orders Not available for other use Released when work order closes Reservations are either hard or soft. A hard reservation immediately reduces available balance and requires sufficient stock to exist. If stock is insufficient, the reservation cannot be created and work order approval may fail. A soft reservation records demand without locking stock. If your storeroom uses hard reservations and a critical spare such as a nozzle seal for Filler FL-02 runs out, technicians will not be able to reserve it at approval time, causing delays. Check which reservation type is configured for critical items . Picked quantity Items in active pick lists Being prepared for issue Not yet issued to work order How do I monitor reorder needs? ¤ Reorder point system ¤ The system tracks: Table 2: Reorder settings and when each is required ¤ Setting Required when Reorder point You want the system to flag items for reordering automatically Lead time The reorder calculation should account for procurement time. Without it, items may be flagged too late Order quantity (EOQ) You want the system to recommend how much to order, not just flag that an order is needed Safety stock Only when demand is unpredictable and you need a buffer above the reorder point When balance drops below reorder point, the system flags the item so you can replenish stock. How the reorder calculation works ¤ The system uses this formula: Order quantity = Reorder point + 1, minus quantity on order, minus available balance. The +1 means a reorder point of 0 still triggers an order when balance hits zero. Setting your reorder point equal to your minimum-on-hand target is a common misconfiguration that causes reorders to trigger one unit too early and leads to excess stock over time. Check items to reorder ¤ What to do: Filter for items below reorder point. See recommended order quantities. Check vendor information. Review lead times. Take action: Order parts from supplier or request replenishment Transfer from another storeroom Adjust reorder settings if needed How do I track item costs? ¤ Cost information available ¤ For each item , see: Average cost : Current average unit cost Last cost : Most recent purchase price Standard cost : Planned or budgeted cost Total value : Quantity × cost How costs are calculated ¤ Average cost method Weighted average of all purchases Updates with each receipt Smooths price fluctuations Most common method If a high-value emergency purchase is received, it raises the average cost for all future issues of that item until the balance normalises. This can distort maintenance cost reports for that period. For frequently used spare parts such as nozzle seals for Filler FL-02, average cost is usually appropriate. For low-volume, high-value items , consider whether standard cost gives you more predictable reporting. Standard cost method Fixed cost set in advance Doesn't change with purchases Variances tracked separately Used for budgeting How do I monitor inventory usage? ¤ Usage tracking ¤ The system records: When parts are used, from issue transactions What jobs used items , from work orders How often items are needed Usage patterns over time Analyze usage ¤ Use this information to: Identify fast-moving items Spot slow-moving inventory Adjust stock levels Improve reorder quantities Reduce excess inventory Special inventory types ¤ Rotating items ¤ For serialized assets : Track individual items Monitor asset condition See installation history Manage asset rotation Item kits ¤ For grouped items : Issue multiple items together Track kit components Maintain kit integrity Simplify common issues Table 3: Special item types comparison ¤ Item type How it works Typical example Rotating items Rebuildable units tracked by inventory balance and individual asset serial number 50 HP slurry pumps, electric drive motors, and gearboxes Item kits Pre-assembled collections of items issued together under a single kit identifier PM overhaul seal kits, filter replacement bundles Condition-enabled items Items tracked and valued by distinct physical condition rates Reconditioned spare valves, refurbished circuit breakers Lotted items Batches tracked by unique lot identifiers for expiration and manufacturer traceability Food-grade lubricants, chemical sanitizers, and specialty adhesives Common scenarios ¤ Item running low ¤ When stock is getting low: Check reorder settings. Verify lead time. Order replacement stock or transfer from another storeroom. Update reorder point if needed. Excess inventory ¤ If you have too much: Review usage history. Check for obsolete items . Transfer to other locations . Adjust reorder quantities. Consider disposal if appropriate. Can't find item ¤ If item shows in stock but you can't find it: Check bin location . Verify storeroom. Look for reserved quantity. Check pick lists. Perform physical count. Adjust if necessary. Figure 2 illustrates the diagnostic workflow when an item shows a positive stock balance in the system but cannot be found on the storeroom shelf: Diagnostic trigger : Starts when the system balance shows stock on hand, but the item is missing from its primary shelf location . Step 1 (Verify bin locations ) : Check primary, secondary, and staging bins. If found in an alternate bin, pick the item and update the bin assignment in the system. If still missing, proceed to Step 2. Step 2 (Check transfers and receipts) : Verify in-transit transfers between storerooms and recent receiving staging areas. If located in receiving or transit, complete the pending transaction. If still missing, proceed to Step 3. Step 3 (Check reservations and kits) : Inspect active work orders and staged item kits. If the item was allocated to an active work order , it is already staged for maintenance. If still missing, proceed to Step 4. Step 4 (Conduct physical count) : Count physical shelf stock across the storeroom. If a true variance is confirmed, enter an inventory adjustment in the Inventory application to reconcile the balance. Figure 2: Missing inventory item troubleshooting workflow Why accurate tracking matters ¤ Prevents stockouts: Parts available when needed No work delays Better service levels Fewer emergency orders Controls costs: Reduces excess inventory Optimizes stock levels Improves cash flow Lowers carrying costs Improves planning: Better reorder decisions Accurate budgeting Informed purchasing Efficient operations Good stock visibility means fewer surprises when jobs need parts and fewer delays when it matters most. docs.text: Why can't I issue materials to a work order ? ¤ Material issues fail when required fields or relationships are missing. Looking to troubleshoot material issues right away? Skip to material issue troubleshooting checklist ↓ What to check first ¤ Storeroom, item , and quantity are valid ¤ The system needs to know: Which storeroom the part is coming from Which item you're issuing, using the correct item number How many you're issuing, as a valid quantity What to do : Verify all three pieces of information are correct and the item exists in that storeroom. Work order exists and is chargeable ¤ You can only issue materials to work orders that: Exist in the system Are in a status that allows charging Haven't been closed or completed What to do : Check the work order status . If it's closed or in a non-chargeable status , you'll need to reopen it or change the status first. Required fields are populated ¤ Some organizations require additional information: Bin location : Where in the storeroom the part is stored Unit of measure : The unit you're issuing, such as each, box, or meter GL account : For cost tracking What to do : Fill in all required fields. If you're not sure what's required, check with your supervisor or system administrator. Why didn't inventory update after issuing? ¤ Material issues should trigger inventory and cost updates simultaneously. If they didn't, something went wrong. Figure 1 illustrates the parts issue validation and update workflow: 1. Issue entry methods : Work begins from an active work order , at the storeroom counter, or via the mobile app. 2. Validation checks : The system checks four conditions: valid storeroom and item number, chargeable work order status , sufficient available storeroom balance, and populated required fields. 3. Simultaneous updates : When all validation checks pass, the system performs three actions at the same time: deducts the physical balance from the storeroom, records actual material costs on the work order , and evaluates whether remaining stock breaches the reorder point. If any validation check fails, none of these updates occur. Figure 1: Parts issue and material transaction workflow Transaction didn't complete ¤ The issue might have failed partway through. What to check : Look for error messages you might have missed Verify the transaction appears in the work order 's materials list Check if inventory balance changed What to do : If the transaction didn't complete, try issuing again. If it appears to have worked but inventory didn't update, contact your system administrator. Wrong storeroom or item used ¤ If you issued from the wrong storeroom or selected the wrong item , the inventory update happened in the wrong place. What to do : Return the incorrectly issued material Issue the correct item from the correct storeroom Add notes explaining the correction Issue not confirmed ¤ Some systems require confirmation after issuing. What to do : Check if there's a confirmation step you need to complete, or verify the issue was saved properly. Why do users issue parts incorrectly? ¤ Common causes of issuing errors: Confusion between planned vs unplanned materials ¤ Planned materials : Already listed on the work order , just need to be issued Unplanned materials : Need to be added and issued What to do : Check if the material is already planned on the work order . If so, issue it directly. If not, add it first, then issue. Multiple ways to issue ¤ You can issue materials from: The work order , which is the most common The inventory application Mobile apps Each method works slightly differently. What to do : Use the method your organization prefers, typically issuing directly from the work order . Missing understanding of cost tracking ¤ When you issue materials, costs are automatically recorded against the work order . Why it matters : Incorrect issues lead to: Wrong costs on work orders Inaccurate inventory balances Poor cost reporting What to do : Always issue materials to the correct work order and verify quantities are accurate. Why are costs or usage incorrect? ¤ Issues are often caused by: Issuing to the wrong work order ¤ If you issue materials to the wrong work order , costs are charged incorrectly. What to do : Return the material from the wrong work order Issue it to the correct work order Add notes explaining the correction Using incorrect quantities or units ¤ Issuing the wrong quantity or using the wrong unit of measure causes cost and inventory errors. What to do : Double-check quantities before issuing Verify the unit of measure is correct Return excess materials if you issued too much Skipping planned reservations ¤ If materials were reserved for a work order , issuing different materials can cause confusion. What to do : Issue the reserved materials when possible, or update the reservation if you need to use different materials. Material issue troubleshooting checklist ¤ Use this checklist to identify why a material transaction failed to record: Table 1: Material issue troubleshooting checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Chargeable work order status Work order is in an approved or in-progress status (APPR, WSCHED, or INPRG), not WAPPR, CAN, or CLOSE [ ] Active storeroom Selected storeroom record exists and is set to ACTIVE status [ ] Inventory item record Item is linked to the storeroom with an established inventory record [ ] Bin balance availability Storeroom bin has sufficient quantity on hand, or the storeroom allows negative balance [ ] Unit of measure alignment Issue unit on the transaction matches the inventory issue unit defined for the item [ ] Storeroom user authorization User account has security authorization to issue materials from the selected storeroom Continue building your skills ¤ Know what you have before you issue ¤ Monitor stock levels so you can see what's available in each storeroom before you start a job. docs.text: Planned materials : Already listed on the work order , just need to be issued Unplanned materials : Need to be added and issued What to do : Check if the material is already planned on the work order . If so, issue it directly. If not, add it first, then issue.

docs.text: You can issue materials from: The work order , which is the most common The inventory application Mobile apps Each method works slightly differently. What to do : Use the method your organization prefers, typically issuing directly from the work order .

Why it matters : Incorrect issues lead to: Wrong costs on work orders Inaccurate inventory balances Poor cost reporting What to do : Always issue materials to the correct work order and verify quantities are accurate.

docs.text: If you issue materials to the wrong work order , costs are charged incorrectly. What to do : Return the material from the wrong work order Issue it to the correct work order Add notes explaining the correction

docs.text: Issuing the wrong quantity or using the wrong unit of measure causes cost and inventory errors. What to do : Double-check quantities before issuing Verify the unit of measure is correct Return excess materials if you issued too much

docs.text: How do I act on alerts? ¤ Operational dashboards in Maximo Application Suite Select consolidate critical operational signals into a single view. When a key performance indicator breaches an alert threshold, or when urgent maintenance enters a work queue, supervisors and administrators can review the situation and take immediate corrective action directly from the dashboard. Acting on alerts promptly prevents small anomalies, such as an overdue preventive maintenance inspection or a rising emergency backlog, from escalating into unplanned production downtime . Looking to verify your alert response workflow right away? Skip to alert and work queue checklist ↓ When you first sign in, Select shows the Operational Dashboard that matches your security group . Your administrator assigns the group. Select includes some dashboard content, and an administrator can edit the dashboard to add cards such as KPIs and work queues. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Check your Operational Dashboard at the start of each shift. Review red threshold breaches first, followed by yellow caution indicators. Use work queue cards to take direct action. You can assign labor , update work order status , or open the full record without navigating through the main menu. Ensure newly created work queues are activated. In Work Queue Manager, new queues default to inactive until an administrator explicitly sets their status to active. Customize work queue queries so they capture only actionable records. Queues containing thousands of general records dilute focus and cause alert fatigue. Where alerts appear on your dashboard ¤ Your Operational Dashboard organizes alerts and work items into distinct visual cards. Table 1: Alert indicators on the Operational Dashboard ¤ Card type What it displays Alert condition Immediate action KPI trend cards Single performance indicator with historical trend line Card turns red when value breaches the alert threshold; turns yellow at caution level Use the card menu to open the KPI in KPI Viewer and analyze the underlying historical records Work queues card Table of urgent work categories, such as overdue work or emergency requests Badge count increases when new records match the queue query Select a queue to inspect records, assign technicians, or update status directly Condition monitoring alerts Assets exceeding measurement action limits Corrective work orders appear in unassigned or emergency work queues Review the asset condition history and dispatch qualified personnel Responding to KPI threshold breaches ¤ When a KPI card changes to yellow or red, investigate the underlying cause before adjusting operational priorities. Table 2: Common KPI alert triggers and corrective responses ¤ KPI alert What the breach indicates Immediate corrective response PM compliance below 85% Routine inspections and servicing are falling behind schedule Open the Overdue PMs work queue and reschedule delayed maintenance to available shifts Emergency work order spike Unplanned equipment breakdowns are consuming maintenance capacity Review recent failure codes in the Work Orders application to identify repeat defect patterns Overdue work order accumulation Team capacity is mismatched with incoming work demand Reassign low priority backlog work and focus available crafts on critical production assets Stock-out frequency increase Essential spare parts were unavailable when requested Coordinate with the inventory clerk to expedite reorders and adjust reorder points in the Storeroom Processing work items from a work queue card ¤ The Work queues card on the supervisor dashboard allows you to triage and process work without opening multiple menu screens. Table 3: Actions available within the work queue card ¤ Action How to perform it Operational outcome Assign labor Select the work order row, click Assign, and select a qualified technician Assigns the work order and sends it directly to the technician mobile work list Update status Select the record and choose a new status , such as Approved or Canceled Advances the work order lifecycle and removes it from unapproved queues Open record Click the work order number link Launches the full Work Orders application for detailed planning and job plan adjustments Filter table Enter criteria in the column filter boxes Narrows the active queue to specific assets , locations , or priority levels Real-world example: Responding to a packaging line alert ¤ Consider how a supervisor at the ice cream main plant responds to morning dashboard alerts. Scenario: Morning shift review ¤ The supervisor opens Operational Dashboard : Supervisor . KPI Card 1, PM Compliance: Displays 78%, highlighted in red alert status because the threshold is 85%. Work Queues Card: Displays Overdue PMs (Count: 4) and Emergency Work Orders (Count: 1) . The supervisor clicks Emergency Work Orders . The table displays work order WO-10492 for asset Drive motor on filling line filler FL-02, generated by a condition monitoring high vibration action limit. Direct action: The supervisor clicks Assign , selects a mechanical technician certified in drive alignments, and updates the status to Approved, APPR . Next, the supervisor clicks Overdue PMs , reviews the four routine filter changes, and allocates them to the afternoon shift schedule. How to configure work queues in Work Queue Manager ¤ Select includes some work queues. Administrators can use them as they are, or create and manage their own for the operational dashboards. Step 1: Create the work queue definition ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Work Queue Manager and open it. Click New Work Queue . In the Work Queue field, enter a unique name, such as WQ-OVERDUE-PM . In the Description field, enter a descriptive label, such as Overdue Preventive Maintenance . In the Object Structure field, select the target object structure , such as MXAPIWODETAIL . In the Launch Application field, select WOTRACK or Work Orders . Step 2: Define the query and person group access ¤ In the Query field, select the saved public query that filters the records, such as OVERDUE_PMS . To restrict the queue to specific roles, add the target group in the Person Groups table, such as SUP_MAINT . If left blank, the queue is available across all dashboards with work queue cards. In the Status field, change the value to ACTIVE . Step 3: Add the work queue card to the operational dashboard ¤ Go to the target dashboard, such as Operational Dashboard : Supervisor . Click Edit Dashboard . Add the Work queues card, and select your work queue from the list. Verify that your active work queue is selected. Click Save Dashboard . If you added a person group to the work queue, the queue does not show on the Work queues card by default. People in that group can select the Work queues card, edit the dashboard, and select the queue on the Advanced tab of the card gallery. docs.text: How do I detect issues early? ¤ Equipment rarely breaks down without warning. Before a motor bearing seizes or a refrigeration compressor fails, assets show physical symptoms, such as elevated vibration, rising operating temperature, pressure drops, or degraded lubricant color. Condition monitoring allows you to track these physical indicators systematically. By defining acceptable limits for meter readings, Maximo Application Suite Select helps you identify developing defects and generate corrective maintenance before an unexpected breakdown halts operations. Looking to verify your condition monitoring setup right away? Skip to condition monitoring checklist ↓ In Maximo Application Suite Select, you enter meter readings manually. Select does not receive a continuous stream of readings from sensors or IoT devices. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Select the correct meter type before creating records. Gauge meters track numeric values that fluctuate; characteristic meters track qualitative observations; continuous meters track cumulative run hours. Remember that warning limits are informational only. The system does not automatically create work orders when a reading crosses a warning limit. Automated work order generation requires an action limit linked to an active job plan . Avoid setting action limits too close to normal operating variance. Tight thresholds trigger unnecessary work orders and cause alert fatigue for supervisors. Group related meters into meter groups when multiple assets share the same monitoring profile, such as standard drive motors. Choosing the correct meter type ¤ Every condition monitoring strategy begins in the Meters application. The system supports three distinct meter types, each designed for a specific maintenance purpose. Table 1: Meter types and maintenance applications ¤ Meter type How measurements behave Maintenance purpose Typical examples Where configured Gauge Numeric values that fluctuate up and down over time Track operating condition against acceptable upper and lower limits Operating temperature, vibration velocity, line pressure, oil level Condition Monitoring application Characteristic Qualitative observations chosen from a predefined list of values Record visual inspections and trigger work for specific degraded states Oil color, belt condition, leakage severity, corrosion level Condition Monitoring application Continuous Numeric values that accumulate and increase indefinitely Track usage intervals to trigger routine scheduled servicing Operating run hours, odometer mileage, production cycles Preventive Maintenance application Continuous meters track usage intervals, such as running a service every 500 hours, and do not use condition monitoring measurement points. Condition monitoring relies on gauge meters and characteristic meters . How measurement points work ¤ In the Condition Monitoring application, you create a point record that connects a specific meter to an asset or a location . Each point record applies to a single asset or a single location at your site . Table 2: Measurement points versus observation points ¤ Point type Meter type used Limit structure Work generation trigger Measurement point Gauge meter Upper and lower warning limits; upper and lower action limits Reading exceeds an upper action limit or falls below a lower action limit Observation point Characteristic meter Specific observation values mapped from a domain Reading matches an observation value that has an attached job plan or preventive maintenance record Understanding warning limits versus action limits ¤ A frequent point of confusion is the difference between warning limits and action limits on gauge measurement points. Table 3: Limit types on gauge measurement points ¤ Limit type Purpose System behavior Recommended use Warning limit Highlights that an asset is trending away from optimal condition Informational only; recorded in history and visible in reports, but generates no automated work Early warning for inspectors and supervisors during routine rounds Action limit Identifies that an asset has reached an unacceptable condition requiring intervention Triggers work order generation when combined with an active job plan or preventive maintenance record Immediate corrective maintenance to prevent equipment failure Every action limit must include an active job plan or a preventive maintenance record. If an action limit is populated without a job plan or preventive maintenance record, the system generates an error during work order processing. Real-world example: Ice cream plant monitoring ¤ Consider how condition monitoring applies across equipment and areas at the ice cream main plant. Example 1: Drive motor vibration on Filler FL-02 ¤ The drive motor on filling line filler FL-02 operates in the filling line room. Excessive vibration indicates bearing wear or misalignment: Application: Condition Monitoring Asset : Drive motor Meter : VIB-VEL with gauge type, measured in millimeters per second Normal operating range: 0 to 2.5 mm/s Upper warning limit: 2.8 mm/s, signaling early wear during inspection reviews Upper action limit: 4.2 mm/s, mapped to job plan JP-MTR-ALIGN to dispatch a technician for precision alignment and bearing inspection Example 2: Cold storage room ambient temperature ¤ The cold storage room must maintain strict sub-zero temperatures to protect finished product: Application: Condition Monitoring Location : Cold storage room Meter : ROOM-TEMP with gauge type, measured in degrees Celsius Normal operating range: -22°C to -18°C Lower action limit: -26°C, mapped to job plan JP-REF-LOW to check expansion valve settings Upper action limit: -14°C, mapped to job plan JP-REF-HIGH to inspect refrigeration compressors immediately Example 3: Gearbox lubricant inspection ¤ Technicians inspect gearbox oil condition during monthly rounds: Application: Condition Monitoring Asset : Drive motor gearbox Meter : OIL-COND with characteristic type, using values CLEAR , CLOUDY , DARK , and CONTAMINATED Normal values: CLEAR requires no follow-up action Trigger value: CONTAMINATED is mapped to job plan JP-OIL-FLUSH to schedule an immediate oil replacement and seal inspection Common setup mistakes to avoid ¤ Review these four common pitfalls when designing condition monitoring points: Table 4: Common condition monitoring mistakes and solutions ¤ Mistake Why it causes problems Recommended solution Using continuous meters in Condition Monitoring Continuous meters accumulate indefinitely and cannot evaluate upper or lower thresholds Use continuous meters in the Preventive Maintenance application to trigger usage-based maintenance Expecting warning limits to create work orders Warning limits carry no automated workflow triggers in the system Define action limits with attached job plans for conditions that require maintenance work Leaving job plan fields blank on action limits The system cannot determine what tasks or resources are needed when limits are breached Always assign an active job plan or preventive maintenance record to every populated action limit Setting limits without historical baselines Setting action thresholds too tight creates dozens of duplicate work orders for minor temperature spikes Establish baseline readings during normal operating conditions before defining action limits How to set up condition monitoring in desktop applications ¤ Setting up early issue detection follows four sequential steps across the desktop applications. Step 1: Create the meter ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Meter and open it. Click New Meter . In the Meter field, enter a unique identifier, such as VIB-VEL . In the Meter Type field, select GAUGE for variable numeric values or CHARACTERISTIC for qualitative observations. In the Reading Type field, select ACTUAL for raw values or DELTA for change increments. Click Save Meter . Step 2: Associate the meter with the asset or location ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Assets or Location and open it. Open the asset or location record, such as asset Drive motor . Open the Meters tab and click New Row . In the Meter field, select the meter you created in Step 1. Click Save Asset or Save Location . Step 3: Create the measurement point record ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Condition Monitoring and open it. Click New Measure Point . In the Point field, enter a unique point number or accept the system-generated value. Specify the Asset or Location to monitor. In the Meter field, select the associated gauge or characteristic meter . For gauge meters , enter your Upper Warning Limit , Upper Action Limit , Lower Warning Limit , or Lower Action Limit . In the Job Plan or PM field next to each action limit, select the active maintenance plan to execute when the limit is breached. Click Save Measure Point . Step 4: Generate work orders from condition breaches ¤ When technicians record meter readings during inspections, work orders can be generated in two ways: Manual generation: Open the Condition Monitoring record and select Generate Work Order from More Actions . Automated generation: Administrators configure background processing so that work orders generate automatically whenever a qualifying measurement is entered. Condition monitoring checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm that your condition monitoring point is properly configured and ready to protect equipment. Table 5: Condition monitoring verification checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Meter type alignment Gauge meter is used for fluctuating numbers; characteristic meter is used for observational codes [ ] Asset or location link The meter is added to the Meters tab of the target asset or location record [ ] Action limit job plans Every populated action limit has an active job plan or preventive maintenance record assigned [ ] Realistic thresholds Limits reflect true operational boundaries and avoid nuisance triggering during normal startup [ ] Work order priority The work order priority field on the point record is set to reflect the urgency of the condition Continue building your skills ¤ Respond to system alerts and work queues ¤ Once condition monitoring points detect abnormal readings, alerts appear on operational dashboards. docs.text: In the Find navigation item field, search for Meter and open it. Click New Meter . In the Meter field, enter a unique identifier, such as VIB-VEL . In the Meter Type field, select GAUGE for variable numeric values or CHARACTERISTIC for qualitative observations. In the Reading Type field, select ACTUAL for raw values or DELTA for change increments. Click Save Meter .
docs.title: Step 1: Create the meter

docs.text: In the Find navigation item field, search for Assets or Location and open it. Open the asset or location record, such as asset Drive motor . Open the Meters tab and click New Row . In the Meter field, select the meter you created in Step 1. Click Save Asset or Save Location .
docs.title: Step 2: Associate the meter with the asset or location

docs.text: In the Find navigation item field, search for Condition Monitoring and open it. Click New Measure Point . In the Point field, enter a unique point number or accept the system-generated value. Specify the Asset or Location to monitor. In the Meter field, select the associated gauge or characteristic meter . For gauge meters , enter your Upper Warning Limit , Upper Action Limit , Lower Warning Limit , or Lower Action Limit . In the Job Plan or PM field next to each action limit, select the active maintenance plan to execute when the limit is breached. Click Save Measure Point .
docs.title: Step 3: Create the measurement point record

docs.text: When technicians record meter readings during inspections, work orders can be generated in two ways: Manual generation: Open the Condition Monitoring record and select Generate Work Order from More Actions . Automated generation: Administrators configure background processing so that work orders generate automatically whenever a qualifying measurement is entered.
docs.title: Step 4: Generate work orders from condition breaches

docs.text: Use this checklist to confirm that your condition monitoring point is properly configured and ready to protect equipment.
docs.title: Condition monitoring checklist

docs.text: Check Item What to verify [ ] Meter type alignment Gauge meter is used for fluctuating numbers; characteristic meter is used for observational codes [ ] Asset or location link The meter is added to the Meters tab of the target asset or location record [ ] Action limit job plans Every populated action limit has an active job plan or preventive maintenance record assigned [ ] Realistic thresholds Limits reflect true operational boundaries and avoid nuisance triggering during normal startup [ ] Work order priority The work order priority field on the point record is set to reflect the urgency of the condition
docs.title: Table 5: Condition monitoring verification checklist

docs.text: What metrics matter? ¤ Maximo Application Suite Select tracks maintenance performance through key performance indicators (KPIs). A KPI measures one specific variable over time, such as how many work orders were completed on schedule, or how long equipment typically runs before failing. Some KPIs are available when you first sign in. You can also create your own. The metrics that matter most depend on your role. A supervisor needs to know whether today's work is on track. An administrator needs to know whether the overall maintenance program is healthy. An inventory clerk needs to know whether parts are available when work demands them. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Start with three to five KPIs, not twenty. Too many metrics dilute focus and make it harder to act. Set thresholds for every KPI: a green target, a yellow caution level, and a red alert level. Without thresholds, a KPI is just a number. Review KPIs on a regular cadence that matches your role: daily for supervisors, weekly or monthly for managers and administrators. A KPI is only as reliable as the data behind it. If technicians are not closing work orders accurately, completion rate and MTTR figures will be wrong. What metrics matter to supervisors? ¤ Supervisors use KPIs to monitor daily work progress and respond to problems before they escalate. The Operational Dashboard for supervisors gives you a role-based view of the metrics most relevant to your team. Table 1: Supervisor metrics ¤ Metric What it tells you Where to find it Work order completion rate How many work orders were completed vs. scheduled in a given period. A low rate signals resource or planning problems. Operational Dashboard, Supervisor Overdue work orders Work that has passed its required finish date. Growing overdue counts mean scheduling or capacity issues. Operational Dashboard, Work Queues PM compliance The percentage of preventive maintenance work orders completed on schedule. Target is 85% or higher. Operational Dashboard, Supervisor Emergency work orders The count of unplanned, reactive work orders . High numbers indicate equipment is failing unexpectedly instead of being maintained proactively. Operational Dashboard, Supervisor Maintenance backlog The volume of outstanding work. A healthy backlog is 2 to 4 weeks of work. Above 6 weeks signals a resource problem. Work Queues Schedule compliance How often planned work is completed when it was scheduled. Targets above 90% indicate a well-run maintenance program. Operational Dashboard, Supervisor How supervisors use these metrics ¤ Review completion rate and overdue work orders daily. Use the Work Queues card on your Operational Dashboard to act on items directly. You can change status , assign work, or escalate without leaving the dashboard. What metrics matter to administrators? ¤ Administrators use KPIs to assess the health of the overall maintenance program and configure the system to support it. KPI Manager is where administrators create, configure, and manage KPIs for the organization. Table 2: Administrator metrics ¤ Metric What it tells you Where to find it Planned maintenance percentage (PMP) The ratio of planned maintenance hours to total hours. Above 80% means your program is proactive, not reactive. KPI Manager, KPI Viewer Mean time between failures (MTBF) The average time equipment runs before failing. Rising MTBF means reliability is improving. KPI Manager, KPI Viewer Mean time to repair (MTTR) The average time to repair an asset after failure. High MTTR indicates slow response or complex failures. KPI Manager, KPI Viewer Asset availability The percentage of time an asset is operational. Critical for production equipment. KPI Manager, KPI Viewer Reactive maintenance ratio Emergency work orders as a percentage of total work. World-class programs keep this below 10%. KPI Manager, KPI Viewer KPI threshold breaches KPIs that have crossed caution or alert thresholds. These require investigation or program adjustments. KPI Manager How administrators use these metrics ¤ Use KPI Manager to create KPIs with defined targets, caution levels, and alert thresholds. Make frequently reviewed KPIs public so they appear on role-specific Operational Dashboards. Review program-level metrics monthly and adjust PM schedules or resource allocation based on trends. Three configuration points that are easy to miss: Set thresholds on every KPI. A KPI without a green target, yellow caution, and red alert level is just a number. The traffic-light colour coding on the Operational Dashboard only activates when thresholds are configured. Without them, supervisors see data but no signal. Make KPIs public. A KPI configured in KPI Manager is private by default. It will not appear on anyone's Operational Dashboard until you explicitly make it public or assign it to a security group . Activate new work queues. In Maximo Application Suite Select, a newly created work queue defaults to inactive. If a work queue shows no results on the Operational Dashboard, check that it has been activated in Work Queue Manager. What metrics matter to inventory clerks? ¤ Inventory clerks use metrics to ensure parts are available when work demands them. Stock-related KPIs help prevent delays caused by missing parts. Table 3: Inventory clerk metrics ¤ Metric What it tells you Where to find it Stock-outs How often a required part was unavailable when needed. Frequent stock-outs delay work and increase downtime . Operational Dashboard, Inventory Clerk Inventory turnover How quickly stock is consumed and replenished. Low turnover may mean overstocking; high turnover may indicate understocking. Operational Dashboard, Inventory Clerk Parts requested vs. available The gap between what technicians need and what is in stock. Helps prioritize reordering. Operational Dashboard, Inventory Clerk Where to find KPIs in the product ¤ Table 4: KPI applications ¤ Application Who uses it What it does KPI Manager Administrators Create, configure, and manage KPIs. Set targets, thresholds, and security group access. KPI Viewer All roles View individual KPI values and trends. Read-only access to configured KPIs. KPI Templates Administrators Create reusable templates to generate multiple related KPIs efficiently. Operational Dashboard All roles Role-based dashboard showing KPI trend cards, work queue cards, and alert summaries. Work Queue Manager Administrators Create and manage work queues that surface actionable items on the Operational Dashboard. Learn how to respond directly from the dashboard without leaving the view. How do I act on alerts? Catch problems before they become failures ¤ Condition monitoring feeds asset health data into your metrics. Set it up so your KPIs reflect equipment state, not just work order counts. docs.text: How do I assign the correct people? ¤ Match the right technician or crew to a work order so the job goes to someone with the correct skills, availability, and access. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Set up crafts and labor records before assigning work. A labor record without a craft won't appear when you filter by skill. See How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? if your workforce isn't configured yet. Check availability before assigning. The system shows scheduled hours and availability based on the labor record's calendar and shift. Use crews when multiple people need to work on the same job at the same time. Assigning a crew takes one step instead of adding each person individually. Set a scheduled start date on every assignment. Without a date, the assignment won't surface in scheduling views at the correct time for planning or dispatch. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Assignment methods ¤ Method Best for Work orders , Plans section Assigning an individual to a work order Crew assignment Assigning a whole team to a job in one step How to assign an individual to a work order ¤ What to do: Open the Work orders application. Search for and open the work order . Go to the Plans section. Under Assignment , click Edit assignments . In the Labor field, enter or select the person to assign. Enter the estimated hours in Time to complete . This is how the system calculates whether a person is over-allocated. Without it, the system shows unlimited availability for that slot and supervisors can unknowingly double-book people. Save the work order . Note Assignments filter by the default craft on the labor record. A person with the correct skill set as a secondary craft will not appear. If the list is empty or missing expected people, check that the correct craft is set as their default in the Labor application. How to assign a crew ¤ Use a crew when a group of people need to work together on the same job. What to do: Open the Work orders application. Search for and open the work order . Go to the Plans section. Under Assignment , click Edit assignments . In the Crew field, enter or select the crew name. The system adds all active crew members as individual assignments. Save the work order . Why isn't someone showing up as available? ¤ The most common reasons a technician doesn't appear in the Available Labor list: No craft assigned ¤ Available Labor filters by default craft only . A person with the correct skill as a secondary craft is excluded from the results. They exist in the system but the filter doesn't find them. What to do : Open the Labor application, find the person's record, and confirm the correct craft is set as their default, not just listed as a secondary craft . Calendar or shift mismatch ¤ Available Labor uses the calendar and shift on the labor record. If the scheduled start date falls outside the person's working hours, they may not appear or show as unavailable. What to do : Check that the calendar and shift on the labor record match the crew 's working schedule. Work order status doesn't allow assignment ¤ You can only assign labor to work orders in an approvable or approved status . Work orders in Waiting for Approval or Approved status accept assignments. What to do : Check the work order status and change it to APPR before assigning. Assigning the correct people consistently means work gets done faster and teams stop stepping on each other. Continue building your skills ¤ Understand why a technician can't see their assigned work ¤ After assigning work, verify it's visible to the correct people. Why can't technicians see their assigned work? Set up the workforce records behind assignments ¤ If assignments aren't working correctly, the issue is often in how crafts , calendars, and labor records are set up. How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? Related topics ¤ How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? Why can't technicians see their assigned work? How do I schedule work? docs.text: How do I customize dropdown values? ¤ Domains control the values users can pick from in dropdown lists and status fields across the application. As an administrator, you can add your own labels to existing status dropdowns to match your organization's terminology. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Domain terminology ¤ Term What it means Domain A list of valid values attached to a field, such as the values available in a work order status dropdown Synonym domain A domain used for status fields. Lets you add your own labels that map to built-in system statuses Internal value The system status that drives business logic, such as WAPPR (Waiting for Approval) or COMP (Complete) Synonym value A custom label you add that maps to an internal value, such as "Needs sign-off" mapping to WAPPR What you can do in IBM Maximo Application Suite Select ¤ Table 2: Domain customization tasks ¤ Task How Add a custom label to a status field Add a synonym value to an existing domain Use different terminology across your organization Set a synonym value at the organization level Find which domain controls a field Use Alt+F1 on the field, then look up the domain in Domains Why add synonym values? ¤ Synonym values let you use your organization's terminology without affecting how the system works underneath. For example, your team might call a work order status "Needs sign-off" rather than "Waiting for Approval." You can add "Needs sign-off" as a synonym that maps to the built-in WAPPR status . Users see your label. The system still processes work orders using the standard internal status . Common uses: Rename work order or asset statuses to match your organization's language Add organization-specific labels for a status Localize terminology for your team What you cannot change ¤ You can add synonym values, but you cannot add new internal values. The system's business logic, meaning what happens when a work order reaches APPR, COMP, or CLOSE, is hardwired to those internal values and cannot be modified. If you need a status that behaves differently from any existing internal value, that is not possible through domain configuration. How to add a synonym value ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Domains and open it. Search for the domain you want to update. For example, search for WOSTATUS to find the work order status domain . Open the domain record. In the Values table, click Add Row , the + button above the values list. Leave the Internal Value field set to the existing system status you want to map to. Enter your custom label in the Value field. Add a description to explain the value. If this value applies to a specific organization only, set the Organization field. An organization-level synonym is visible across all sites in that organization. A value with no organization set applies system-wide. Choosing the wrong scope can expose values to users who should not see them, or hide them from users who need them. To make this the default value for the field, select Default . Click OK . Save the domain record. Before you add synonym values after go-live ¤ Adding synonym values at the organization level after your system is live can cause issues with existing records. If you add synonyms with an organization specified, records that were created before the change may no longer match valid values. If you need to add organization-scoped synonyms after go-live, add a synonym for every existing internal value at the same scope before saving. If you are unsure about the impact, test the change in a non-production environment first, or contact IBM support. How to find the correct domain for a field ¤ To identify which domain controls a specific field: Place your cursor in the field. Press Alt+F1 to open field help. The field name and domain name appear in the field help panel. In the Find navigation item field, search for Domains and open it. Then search for that domain name. Set up a map after your dropdown values are in place. How do I set up maps? Automate your notifications ¤ Keep your team informed automatically. Set up email and push notifications so people know when work is assigned or updated. How do I automate communication? docs.text: Why don't technicians see their assigned work? ¤ This is one of the most common issues. Work is assigned, but the technician can't see it in their queue. Looking to troubleshoot assignment visibility right away? Skip to work assignment visibility checklist ↓ Likely causes ¤ User permissions were updated but sessions weren't refreshed ¤ When permissions change, active sessions might not pick up the new access rights immediately. What to do : Have the technician log out of all sessions completely, then log back in. This forces the system to reload their current permissions. Clear all sessions Logging out of all sessions (including mobile devices and any open browser tabs) often resolves visibility issues immediately. Missing site or data access ¤ The technician might not have access to the site where the work order exists, or their data restrictions might prevent them from seeing certain work orders . What to check : Verify the technician has access to the correct site Check if data restrictions are limiting what they can see Confirm their security group includes the necessary permissions What to do : Contact your system administrator to review and update site access or data restrictions. Cached sessions not picking up new permissions ¤ Even after permissions are updated, cached session data might prevent the changes from taking effect. What to do : Have the technician: Log out completely from all devices Clear browser cache if using a web browser Close and reopen mobile apps Log back in Why can't I update assignment status ? ¤ You might see validation errors or the status doesn't save when you try to move from Assigned → Started → Complete. Status sequence skipped ¤ Some organizations require work orders to progress through specific statuses in order. You can't skip steps. Example : You can't go directly from "Assigned" to "Complete" without going through "In Progress" first. What to do : Follow the required status sequence for your organization. Date validation errors ¤ The system validates that dates make sense. Common issues: Finish date must be after start date Scheduled date must be after creation date Actual dates must align with planned dates What to do : Check all dates on the work order and correct any that are out of sequence. Updates not committing to the database ¤ Sometimes changes appear to save but don't actually commit to the database. What to do : Verify the change was saved by refreshing the screen Check for error messages that might have been missed Try the update again Contact your system administrator if the problem persists Why is it hard to track who is doing what? ¤ Supervisors often struggle with visibility into team workload and assignments. Known limitations ¤ Out-of-the-box views : Standard views don't easily show workload per technician Reporting complexity : Reports can include incorrect or excessive data Filtering behavior : Filters might not work as expected for assignment tracking What to do : Use custom queries or reports designed for your organization Ask your system administrator about available workload views Consider using dashboards that show team assignments Why do assignments disappear after work order completion? ¤ Assignments are typically removed when the work order is closed or completed. Impact ¤ No historical assignment tracking unless configured separately Reporting needs to rely on work order history instead of active assignments What to do : If you need historical assignment data, work with your system administrator to set up: Assignment history tracking Custom reports that capture assignment data before completion Archive processes that preserve assignment information Work assignment visibility checklist ¤ Use this checklist to diagnose and resolve missing work order assignments: Table 1: Work assignment visibility checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Active labor record Technician username is linked to an active Labor record in the Labor application [ ] Craft and skill match Labor record craft matches the craft required on the work order assignment [ ] Shift calendar active Calendar and shift assigned to the labor record cover the scheduled work date [ ] Assignment dates valid Labor assignment has an effective start date and no expired end date [ ] Work order status Work order is in APPR, WSCHED, or INPRG status , not WAPPR or CLOSE [ ] Site security access User security group grants permission to view records for the specific site [ ] Session refreshed Technician has signed out and signed back in after recent permission updates Continue building your skills ¤ Know what work matters ¤ Create job plans that standardize tasks, parts, and time estimates so every technician does the work the same way. How do I decide what work should be done? Plan recurring maintenance ¤ With your team seeing their work correctly, set up schedules that generate work orders automatically so you're not creating them one at a time. docs.text: How do I decide what work should be done? ¤ Create job plans that list the steps, parts, and tools for common maintenance tasks. Job plans work like templates. They keep work consistent every time. You plan the work once. Then you reuse the plan. This saves time and reduces mistakes. Looking to validate a job plan right away? Skip to job plan verification checklist ↓ Figure 1 illustrates how a job plan template flows into an approved work order : Job plan template : defines sequential task steps, estimated labor and craft hours, required materials and quantities, special tools, and default work order priority. Application paths : attached to a recurring preventive maintenance schedule or applied directly to an on-demand corrective work order . Approved work order outcome : upon approval, the system automatically populates task checklists, schedules labor assignments, generates storeroom material reservations, and applies priority ratings. Figure 1: How job plans flow into work orders 💡 Tips: Best practices for job plans ¤ Start with common tasks Create plans for work you do most often. Keep it simple Use clear, short instructions. Add safety notes Include warnings for dangerous work. Update regularly Change plans based on worker feedback. Use for all scheduled work Every maintenance schedule should have a job plan . When to use job plans ¤ Use job plans for: Tasks you do regularly, such as monthly inspections Work with multiple steps Jobs that need specific parts or tools Tasks where safety matters Scheduled maintenance What goes in a job plan ¤ Include these items : Work description What you need to do and why. Task list Step-by-step instructions. Labor estimates How many people and hours you need. When this job plan is applied to a work order and the work order is approved, the system automatically creates assignment records for each labor entry. Without labor estimates, no assignments are created, so planners must add them manually every time. Required materials Parts and supplies you need. When a work order with planned materials is approved, the system automatically creates storeroom reservations. Without materials on the job plan , no reservations are made and parts may not be available when the technician arrives on site . Tools Special equipment or tools. Safety information Hazards and safety steps. How to create and use job plans ¤ Create the job plan ¤ Open the Job Plans application Add a clear name and description List all work tasks in order Add labor , materials, and tools Set the WO Priority field. This pre-fills priority on every work order generated from this plan. Without it, work orders default to null priority and sort to the bottom of every scheduling and assignment view, and urgent work becomes invisible to planners. Use with scheduled maintenance ¤ Attach job plans to your maintenance schedules. Work orders include the job plan automatically. Use with work orders ¤ Add job plans to individual work orders . Technicians see all steps and materials. Keep plans current ¤ Review completed work. Update job plans based on what actually happened. Add missing steps or materials. To change a job plan that is already active, select Revise Job Plan from More Actions first. BMXAA0024E JOBTASK action ADD is not allowed TODO: Add visual content A video showing how to create a simple job plan would be useful here. Job plan verification checklist ¤ Before activating a job plan or attaching it to preventive maintenance schedules, verify that all core planning fields, tasks, and resource estimates are complete. Check Item What to verify [ ] Task sequence All work steps are listed in sequential order with clear instructions and estimated durations. [ ] Labor estimates and crafts Craft , skill level, and estimated hours are specified for each task so automatic assignment records are generated upon work order approval. [ ] Material reservations Required item numbers, direct issue items , and quantities are entered with designated storerooms so inventory reservations generate automatically. [ ] Tool requirements Required tools and operational hour estimates are attached to tasks. [ ] Work order priority The WO Priority field is set so work orders generated from this plan sort correctly in dispatch and scheduling queues. [ ] Safety precautions and hazards Necessary safety steps, lockout or tagout precautions, and hazard warnings are documented on tasks. [ ] Status activation The job plan status is changed to Active so it is available for selection on work orders , preventive maintenance records, and routes. Why job plans help ¤ Everyone does the work the same way No confusion about steps or procedures. Work goes faster No time spent figuring out what to do. You get the correct parts All materials are listed upfront. Reservations are created automatically at approval, so no manual follow-up is needed. Training is easier New workers have clear instructions. Costs are predictable You know time and materials in advance. Assignments are created for you Labor entries on the job plan generate assignment records when the work order is approved. The correct people appear in the assignment queue without a planner having to add them manually. Continue building your skills ¤ Plan recurring maintenance ¤ With job plans in place, set up schedules that generate work orders automatically instead of creating them one at a time. How do I plan recurring maintenance? Schedule your team ¤ Set up calendars and routes so work is assigned when people are available and inspections run in sequence. How do I schedule work? Monitor performance ¤ Track whether work is being completed on time, how much backlog your team carries, and where to intervene. What metrics matter?
