docs.text: How do I plan recurring maintenance? ¤ Create a schedule that automatically generates work orders . The system creates work orders for you based on time, such as every 30 days, or equipment use, such as every 500 hours. This helps you maintain equipment before it breaks. You set up the schedule once. The system does the rest. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Start with a small number of critical assets , such as 5 to 10, then expand once the process works reliably Always create job plans before setting up schedules. They ensure consistent work. Set lead times based on your actual parts procurement time plus a buffer, typically 7 to 14 days Review completed work orders monthly and adjust schedules based on actual equipment performance Activate schedules gradually to avoid overwhelming your team with work orders When to use this ¤ Use recurring maintenance when you need to: Inspect or service equipment regularly Maintain equipment based on how much it runs Follow manufacturer maintenance schedules Prevent equipment breakdowns Keep consistent maintenance records How to set it up ¤ Step 1: Create a job plan (recommended) ¤ A job plan lists the work steps, parts needed, and time required. It keeps the work consistent every time. You can skip this step, but job plans make maintenance easier. Table 1: Job plan contents and when each is required ¤ Include in job plan Required when Task list The work has multiple steps that technicians must follow in order Labor entries You want assignment records created automatically at work order approval Material entries You want storeroom reservations created automatically at work order approval WO Priority This work must appear correctly sorted in scheduling views Step 2: Create the maintenance record ¤ Open the Preventive Maintenance application Choose the equipment or location Describe the maintenance work clearly Step 3: Set the schedule ¤ Choose how often to do the work: Time-based schedule Every 30 days Every 2 weeks Every 6 months Usage-based schedule Every 500 operating hours Every 1000 cycles Every 200 miles Combined schedule Every 6 months OR 300 hours, whichever comes first Every year OR 1000 hours, whichever comes first Fixed vs. floating: choose carefully ¤ This setting controls when the next work order is generated. Fixed schedule : The next work order is created on the calendar interval regardless of whether the previous one was completed. A monthly PM generates every 30 days, every time. Floating schedule : The next work order is not created until the previous one reaches a completed, closed, or cancelled status . If a work order is never closed, the PM stops generating entirely, with no warning. One missed closure can silently halt maintenance on an asset indefinitely. Use a fixed schedule for most time-based PMs. Use floating only when the next maintenance interval should genuinely depend on when the last job was finished, such as usage-based or condition-driven work. Step 4: Set lead time (optional but recommended) ¤ Lead time tells the system when to create the work order before it's due. Example: Set 7 days lead time. The system creates the work order a week early. This gives you time to get parts and schedule workers. If lead time is too short, parts and labor won't be ready when the work order is generated. If it's left at zero, the work order appears on its due date, leaving no time to prepare. A lead time shorter than your parts procurement time virtually guarantees a delayed job. Step 5: Add the job plan ¤ Link your job plan to the schedule. Each work order will include the same steps and parts list. To change a job plan that is already active, select Revise Job Plan first. For details, see Keep plans current . In practice Organizations often create overly complex schedules at the start, which are hard to maintain Schedules are frequently set up but never activated, so no work orders are generated Lead times are often too short, causing parts shortages and rushed work Teams sometimes create schedules without job plans , leading to inconsistent maintenance What happens next ¤ After you activate the schedule: The system creates work orders automatically Each work order includes your job plan steps Technicians complete the work The system calculates the next due date The system creates the next work order The cycle repeats until you stop it. Common mistakes ¤ Creating too many schedules at once instead of starting with critical equipment Setting unrealistic frequencies, either too often or not often enough Not linking job plans , so technicians don't know what to do Forgetting to activate schedules after creating them Setting lead times that are too short for parts procurement What good looks like ¤ Poor setup Create 50 Preventive Maintenance (PM) schedules for all equipment at once. No job plans . Activate all immediately. Good setup Start with 5-10 critical assets . Create detailed job plans first. Test one schedule. Adjust based on results. Gradually add more equipment. Decision support: Choosing schedule type ¤ Use time-based when: Equipment runs continuously or predictably Manufacturer recommends calendar-based maintenance You need simple, easy-to-manage schedules Use usage-based when: Equipment usage varies significantly Meters are reliable and regularly updated Maintenance depends on actual wear, measured in hours, cycles, or miles Use combined when: You want maintenance to happen even if equipment sits idle Usage is unpredictable You need a safety net for both scenarios Why proper planning matters ¤ If schedules are not set up correctly, equipment fails unexpectedly instead of being maintained proactively If lead times are too short, technicians wait for parts and work gets delayed If job plans are missing, maintenance quality varies and problems are missed Poor scheduling leads to either too much work, which overwhelms teams, or too little, which causes equipment failures If a floating schedule is used and a work order is never closed, no further work orders are generated for that asset , so maintenance stops without any alert A schedule left inactive after setup generates no work orders , ever. The first sign is typically an unexpected equipment failure Once your PMs are running, the system takes care of the scheduling. You focus on the work, not the calendar. Continue building your skills ¤ Know what work matters ¤ Create job plans that standardize tasks, parts, and time estimates, then link them to your schedules so technicians always know what to do. How do I decide what work should be done? Schedule your team ¤ Set up calendars and routes so work is assigned when people are available and inspections are grouped efficiently. docs.text: How do I schedule work? ¤ Use calendars to set working hours. Use routes to group inspection points. This helps you plan when work happens and organize inspections efficiently. Calendars track when your team works. Routes let you create inspection work orders for multiple items at once. Looking to verify your work schedule right away? Skip to work scheduling and calendar readiness checklist ↓ 💡 Tips: Best practices for calendars and routes ¤ For calendars: Start simple. Match your standard work week. Add holidays as you go. Update calendars when shifts change. For routes: Group equipment that is close together. Keep routes focused. Do not mix unrelated items . Update routes when equipment changes. Use clear names. Calendars: Set working time ¤ Calendars show when work can happen. They include: Working days and hours Shifts, such as 7 AM to 3 PM and 3 PM to 11 PM Holidays and shutdowns Days off Figure 1 shows how calendars connect to labor , equipment, and work scheduling across three areas: Calendar definition : establishes shift patterns for working hours, standard work weeks for working days, and non-working time for holidays and shutdowns. Assigned records : attaches calendars to labor records for individual worker availability, crew records for crew group availability, and locations or assets for shutdown windows. Work scheduling : validates worker availability against open shifts to assign target start and finish dates. docs.text: Why isn't my PM generating work orders ? ¤ You set up a preventive maintenance record, called a PM, but the work order you expected is not there. Or you try to generate a work order and see a message such as "is not due yet". Looking to troubleshoot right away? Skip to the PM generation checklist ↓ Common causes ¤ The PM is not active ¤ A PM generates work orders only when its status is Active. A PM that is still a draft, or one that was set to inactive, is skipped. What to do : Open the PM and check its status . If it is not Active, activate it. The asset or location is not operating ¤ The asset or location on the PM must have a status of Operating. If it has a different status , such as Not Ready, the system does not generate the work order . You might see a message such as "The asset or location associated with PM 1038 has a status of NOT READY. Change the status to an Active status to generate work orders ." What to do : Check the status of the asset or location on the PM. Change it to Operating if the equipment is in service. A floating schedule is waiting for the last work order ¤ A floating schedule does not create the next work order until the previous one is completed, closed, or cancelled. While the previous work order is still open, you might see a message such as "PM IC-11460 is not due yet, or it does not fall within the active season." What to do : Find the open work order from the previous cycle and finish or close it. If the next work order should not depend on the last one, change the PM to a fixed schedule. For the difference, see Fixed vs. floating: choose carefully . The PM is not due yet ¤ By default, the system checks the frequency of each PM and generates work orders only for PMs that are due. If you generate work orders by hand before the due date, nothing is created. What to do : Check the next due date on the PM. If you need the work order now, clear Use Frequency Criteria in the Generate Work Orders dialog. The system then generates a work order for the selected parent PM regardless of its due date. You tried to generate from a child PM ¤ Work orders can be generated only from the top level PM in a PM hierarchy. If you try it from a child PM, you might see a message such as "PM 1039 is not a top-level PM and cannot generate work orders ." What to do : Open the PM Hierarchy tab, find the parent PM, and generate from there. Why did only some work orders generate? ¤ A parent PM can trigger work orders for its whole PM hierarchy. If one PM in the hierarchy has an asset or location that is not Operating, the system skips that PM and the PMs below it. The rest of the hierarchy can still generate. What to do : Check the asset or location status for every PM in the hierarchy. When you change the status of a parent location or asset , you can roll the status down the hierarchy so the children stay consistent. Why hasn't the work order appeared yet, even though the PM is active? ¤ The system does not create work orders the moment you activate a PM. Generation runs on a schedule in the background. [SME confirmation required: Confirm how often work order generation runs in Select, and whether it runs overnight. The source describing a once a day, overnight run is a video transcript for Maximo Manage.] What to do : Check again after the next generation run. If you need the work order now, generate it by hand with the Generate Work Orders action. PM generation checklist ¤ Use this checklist to find out why a PM is not creating work orders : Table 1: PM generation checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] PM status The PM status is Active, not draft or inactive [ ] Asset or location status The asset or location on the PM has a status of Operating [ ] Schedule type If the schedule is floating, the previous work order is completed, closed, or cancelled [ ] Due date The PM is due, or Use Frequency Criteria is cleared for a manual generate [ ] PM hierarchy You generate from the top level PM, and every asset or location in the hierarchy is Operating [ ] Generation timing Enough time has passed for the next background generation run 💡 Tip: Close work orders promptly on floating schedules ¤ A floating schedule stops generating when one work order is left open. Close or cancel finished work orders so the next one can generate. Related topics ¤ How do I plan recurring maintenance? How do I plan my preventive maintenance strategy? How do I decide what work should be done? How do I schedule work? docs.text: How do I add users? ¤ Before people can work in IBM Maximo Application Suite Select, they need a user account with the correct security group assigned. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Use consistent naming conventions for user IDs Follow principle of least privilege, that is, minimum access needed Keep security group assignments organized What to do ¤ Add a user ¤ Open the Users application. Click Create user . Specify a login email . Specify a user ID . Optionally, add a note in the memo . Example: Temporary access for contractor at ice cream plant A Provide a display name . This is the full name of the user or a recognizable preferred name. Click Select groups and add the user to at least one security group . An email is sent to the login email address. Table 1: Security groups ¤ A security group is a collection of users who share the same access. Security group permissions determine which applications, actions, and data they can access. A role determines what a person can see and do in Maximo Application Suite Select. Assign each user to the security group that matches their role: Security group What they can do System admin Manages system configuration and user access. System administrators can configure domains , communication templates , AI settings, create users, and set up security groups , but typically do not perform day-to-day operational work. Example tasks: Set up notification templates, manage user roles, set up security groups , configure system settings, and maintain data structures. Supervisor Oversees operations and team activities. Supervisors can plan and approve work, review technician work, monitor assets and performance, and access analytics to track progress. Example tasks: Assign and approve work orders , review KPIs, review inspection results, manage job plans , and monitor asset condition and maintenance schedules. Technician Performs maintenance and operational work. Technicians can view and update assigned work, complete inspections, record labor hours, report materials used, and record asset data such as meter readings and condition details. Example tasks: Complete work orders , enter inspection results, update asset condition, record labor hours, report materials used, and report meter readings. Requester Submits and tracks service requests. Requesters have limited access and cannot perform operational or administrative tasks. This role is focused on initiating and monitoring work requests. Example tasks: Create a service request for a broken asset and track its status until it is resolved. Inventory clerk Manages inventory and storeroom operations. Inventory clerks can maintain stock, process item movements, adjust inventory balances, and ensure accurate inventory records. Example tasks: Receive items into inventory , issue materials to work orders , perform inventory counts, adjust inventory balances, and manage storerooms. Note You must assign at least one security group . The user cannot access applications until a security group is assigned. User preferences ¤ Users update their preferences in their profile. They open the profile menu from the top right of the header and can select preferences, such as a default application , storeroom, locale, and language. docs.text: How do I automate communication? ¤ Communication templates let you send automatic emails when things happen in the system, such as when a work order changes status or a task is assigned. Push notifications send real-time alerts to mobile devices so field technicians know about new or updated work without having to check the app. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Set the status of a communication template to Active before trying to use it. Inactive templates will not send. Do not edit the built-in system templates. Duplicate an existing template and modify the copy instead. Use roles as recipients rather than hardcoding individual email addresses. Roles resolve dynamically, so notifications reach the correct person even when team membership changes. Test your template by triggering the relevant action on a test record before rolling it out. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Communication terminology ¤ Term What it means Communication template A reusable email template that can be triggered automatically or manually from a record Accessible from Controls where the template can be used: Applications or All Role A dynamic recipient definition that resolves to a person or group at the time the email is sent Substitution variable A placeholder in the template body that pulls live data from the record, such as the work order number Push notification A real-time alert sent to the IBM Maximo Mobile app on a user's mobile device Communication templates ¤ Communication templates automate outbound email for work order assignments, status changes, approvals, and other events. You create a template once, then attach it to an escalation , a workflow, or trigger it manually from a record. How to create a communication template ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Communication Templates and open it. Click New Communication Template . Enter a unique Template ID and a clear description. Set Accessible From to the context where this template will be used, such as APPS or ALL . Enter a Send From email address. This is the address recipients will see as the sender. Enter a Subject line. Use substitution variables to include record data, for example: Work order :wonum has been assigned to you Enter the message body. You can use substitution variables here too, for example :description to include the work order description. Go to the Recipients tab. Add recipients using one or more of the following: Roles : recommended. The role resolves to the correct person at send time. Person groups : sends to group members based on availability. Persons : sends to a specific named person. Email addresses : sends to a fixed address. For each recipient, select To , cc , or bcc . Save the template. Use Change Status to set the template status to Active . Send an email about a KPI ¤ When a KPI reaches its caution or alert level, you can email the people who need to act. From the KPI, use the Create Communication action and choose a communication template to fill in the subject and message. The email is recorded in the KPI's log. [SME confirmation required: Confirm that the Create Communication action is available for KPIs in Select, and whether an administrator can set up these emails to send automatically when a KPI reaches a threshold.] Push notifications ¤ Push notifications send real-time alerts to the IBM Maximo Mobile app on iOS and Android devices. Users receive a notification on their device when an event occurs, such as a work order being assigned to them, without needing to have the app open. Setting up push notifications is a two-step process: generate an API key from the IBM push notification portal, then configure it in MAS. Step 1: Generate an API key ¤ Open https://pushnotification.suite.maximo.com in a browser. Sign in with your IBMid. Enter a meaningful name for the API key, for example MAS-PROD-PushNotif . Click Generate API Key . Copy the API key immediately. It will not be shown again once you leave the page. Store it securely. Step 2: Configure push notifications in MAS ¤ In MAS, click the Administration icon and go to Configurations . In the Users and Identity section, click Push Notifications . In the Bundle Identifier field, enter: com.ibm.iot.maximo.mobile In the URL field, enter: https://pushnotification.suite.maximo.com/pushnotification/sendMessage In the API Key field, paste the key you generated in Step 1. Save the configuration. To confirm the setup is working, ask a user to log in via the IBM Maximo Mobile app and trigger a relevant event such as a workflow assignment. The notification should arrive on their device within a few seconds. When users receive push notifications ¤ A user receives push notifications only when all of the following are true: The user has an active session in IBM Maximo Mobile. The user has not signed out of the app. The app has not been reset. If a user's session expires, notifications stop until the user signs in again. The network on the device must also allow connections to the Apple and Google push notification services. Continue building your skills ¤ Configure Maximo Mobile for field teams ¤ Let technicians, supervisors, and inventory clerks use a mobile app to access their work from anywhere. How do I configure IBM Maximo Mobile for my team? Load your existing data ¤ Now that your configuration is in place, bring in your locations , assets , and inventory from existing records. You can use substitution variables here too, for example :description to include the work order description. Go to the Recipients tab. Add recipients using one or more of the following: Roles : recommended. The role resolves to the correct person at send time. Person groups : sends to group members based on availability. Persons : sends to a specific named person. Email addresses : sends to a fixed address. For each recipient, select To , cc , or bcc . Save the template. Use Change Status to set the template status to Active .
docs.title: How to create a communication template

docs.text: When a KPI reaches its caution or alert level, you can email the people who need to act. From the KPI, use the Create Communication action and choose a communication template to fill in the subject and message. The email is recorded in the KPI's log. docs.text: Push notifications send real-time alerts to the IBM Maximo Mobile app on iOS and Android devices. Users receive a notification on their device when an event occurs, such as a work order being assigned to them, without needing to have the app open. Setting up push notifications is a two-step process: generate an API key from the IBM push notification portal, then configure it in MAS.
docs.title: Push notifications

docs.text: Open https://pushnotification.suite.maximo.com in a browser. Sign in with your IBMid. Enter a meaningful name for the API key, for example MAS-PROD-PushNotif . Click Generate API Key . Copy the API key immediately. It will not be shown again once you leave the page. Store it securely.
docs.title: Step 1: Generate an API key

docs.text: In MAS, click the Administration icon and go to Configurations . In the Users and Identity section, click Push Notifications . In the Bundle Identifier field, enter: com.ibm.iot.maximo.mobile In the URL field, enter: https://pushnotification.suite.maximo.com/pushnotification/sendMessage In the API Key field, paste the key you generated in Step 1. Save the configuration. To confirm the setup is working, ask a user to log in via the IBM Maximo Mobile app and trigger a relevant event such as a workflow assignment. The notification should arrive on their device within a few seconds.
docs.title: Step 2: Configure push notifications in MAS

docs.text: A user receives push notifications only when all of the following are true: The user has an active session in IBM Maximo Mobile. The user has not signed out of the app. The app has not been reset. If a user's session expires, notifications stop until the user signs in again. The network on the device must also allow connections to the Apple and Google push notification services.
docs.title: When users receive push notifications

docs.text: How do I configure IBM Maximo Mobile for my team? ¤ IBM Maximo Mobile lets technicians, supervisors, and inventory clerks view and complete work, manage inventory , and update records from their mobile device. As an administrator, you configure the defaults that control how mobile devices sync data, which map app your team uses for navigation, and how service requests and work orders behave in the app. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Configure mobile settings before your team downloads and signs in to IBM Maximo Mobile. Changes to defaults apply to all users. Set up Map Manager before configuring mobile map settings. The map app you choose here opens the map that Map Manager provides. Start with the defaults and adjust after your team has used the app in the field. Most settings can be changed at any time. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Data sync options ¤ Each data category offers the same three options. Choose the option that balances data freshness against bandwidth and device storage for your team. Option What it does Reload all data Downloads the full data set each time a sync runs. Use when you need your team to have complete, current data regardless of what changed. Update recent changes Downloads only data that changed since the last sync. Faster and lighter on bandwidth. Suitable for most teams. Do not download data Skips this data category during sync. Use when the data is not needed on the device. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the option labels and where you set them in Select. The Maximo Manage documentation calls the options "Complete", "Only delta", and "Do not download", and lists them under "Worklist data" and "Supporting data" in the Mobile administration app. This page uses "Record data" and "Supporting data".] Before you start ¤ Confirm that your role has permission to update mobile configuration settings in Maximo Application Suite Select. Confirm that Map Manager is configured if you plan to use map navigation. See How do I set up maps? . Confirm that labor records and security groups are set up so technicians can be assigned work. See How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? . [SME confirmation required: Identify which Maximo Application Suite Select roles can update mobile configuration settings.] Open the mobile configuration ¤ Open the Mobile properties application. Choose how mobile data is synchronized ¤ The Default data sync settings section controls what data mobile devices download when a user syncs the app. Configure each category separately. Record data ¤ Record data controls how work orders and service requests are synced to the device. Select one of the three options described in Table 1 . Supporting data ¤ Supporting data controls how lookup data, such as asset records and location lists, is synced to the device. Select one of the three options described in Table 1 . Map data ¤ Map data controls whether map data is downloaded to the device. Select Update recent changes or Reload all data to download map data to devices. Select Do not download data to skip map data during sync. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the exact option labels for map data in the Maximo Application Suite Select design. The Maximo Manage equivalent is a single "Download map data" toggle rather than the three-option model.] Choose the map app ¤ The Map settings section controls which map application IBM Maximo Mobile opens when a user navigates to a location . The available options are: Apple Maps Google Maps Waze Select the map app that your team uses. [SME confirmation required: Confirm whether map app options are platform-specific (for example, Apple Maps on iOS only) or available on all supported platforms. Confirm whether a browser fallback option appears in the final Maximo Application Suite Select design.] Configure service request behavior ¤ The SR mobile settings section controls how the service request experience works in IBM Maximo Mobile. Enable follow similar requests ¤ Enable follow similar requests allows technicians to see service requests that are similar to the one they are creating or viewing. Turn this setting on or off depending on whether your team uses this feature. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the exact effect of enabling or disabling this setting, and whether "similar requests" is defined by a matching location, asset, description, or another criterion.] Service address priority ¤ Service address priority determines which address IBM Maximo Mobile uses when a service request has more than one address associated with it. Select the priority value that reflects how your organization resolves address conflicts. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the available priority values and their order of precedence in the final Maximo Application Suite Select design.] Enable show all systems ¤ A system is a hierarchy of locations . Enable show all systems controls whether users can select locations outside their primary system when they create service requests. For more about systems, see Can I organize the same locations more than one way? Turn this setting on if your team reports problems at locations outside their own primary system. Configure work order behavior ¤ Two sections control how work orders behave in IBM Maximo Mobile: Work order status and Miscellaneous settings . Work order status ¤ Work order status controls which status values are available to technicians when they update a work order in the app. Complete status sets the status value that IBM Maximo Mobile applies when a technician marks a work order as complete. [SME confirmation required: Confirm whether COMP is the default complete status value in the Maximo Application Suite Select design, and whether technicians see the status code or a plain-language label.] Allow go to report work ¤ Allow go to report work controls whether technicians see an option to navigate to the report work view from the work order . Turn this on if your team records labor , materials, or other actuals directly against work orders in the mobile app. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the exact label used in the Maximo Application Suite Select interface for the report work view. Do not use "Report Works" or "Actuals" unless those terms appear in the final product interface.] Date attributes ¤ The Miscellaneous settings section includes settings that control which date attributes are visible in the app. [SME confirmation required: Confirm which date attributes are exposed in the Maximo Application Suite Select design (for example, scheduled start, scheduled finish, target start) and whether the SCHEDULE default selection is confirmed in the final design.] Configure travel guidance ¤ The Travel settings section includes Enable travel prompt and Travel radius . Use these settings if your team tracks travel time to a work location . What to do next ¤ After you configure IBM Maximo Mobile, prepare your team to use it: How do I automate communication? : Set up real-time push notifications so field technicians receive alerts on their mobile devices when work is assigned. How do I complete a work order ? : Understand what technicians experience when completing work in the app. How do I find my work? : See how technicians and supervisors access their work queue in IBM Maximo Mobile. Share with your team ¤ Send technicians, supervisors, and inventory clerks to How do I get IBM Maximo Mobile? for download and sign-in instructions. Continue building your skills ¤ Load your existing data ¤ With your system configured, bring in your locations , assets , and inventory records. How do I prepare data for import? docs.text: What is the correct load order? ¤ Import order matters. Referenced records must exist before records that use them, and parent records must exist before child records. Figure 1 outlines the five sequential steps of the data onboarding pathway: Understand the correct load order : review dependency rules so supporting data and parent records load first. Plan your location and asset hierarchies : design physical places and equipment breakdown structures top-down. Prepare data for import : download CSV templates from Data Management, format columns as text, and validate fields. Get data into the system : upload files, run preview validation, and commit the import. Fix import errors : diagnose rejected records in error logs and re-import corrected rows. Figure 1: The five-step data onboarding pathway Why does load order matter? ¤ Child records reference parent records. If the parent does not exist yet, the child import fails. Similarly, if a record references supporting data that does not exist, the import fails. Example : You cannot create Ice cream main plant > Production building > Filling line room if Ice cream main plant and Production building do not exist. Recommended import order ¤ 1. Reference data used by locations and assets ¤ Import supporting records before importing locations or assets that reference them. What to import first : GL accounts Service addresses Calendars and shifts Failure classes Vendors and manufacturers Asset type values Classifications and specifications Addresses, including bill-to and ship-to addresses Why this matters : Locations and assets reference these records. If the referenced data does not exist, the import fails. 2. Locations in hierarchy order ¤ Import locations from top to bottom of the hierarchy: Top-level locations first , such as Ice cream main plant Second-level locations next , such as Production building Lowest-level locations last , such as Filling line room What to check : Verify the location hierarchy before importing Import parent locations before child locations Confirm that system location references use valid values Confirm that each child location references the correct parent Import hierarchies sequentially Hierarchies require sequential loading from the top down. Import parent locations first, then their children. 3. Assets and asset relationships ¤ Import assets after their locations exist. What to check : Location references are valid Parent assets exist, if you use asset hierarchies. Learn how to structure equipment packages in How do I plan my asset hierarchy? . For asset hierarchies : Import parent assets before child assets or subassemblies Verify that each child asset references the correct parent asset Verify that the parent asset exists and is at the expected location 4. Other records that reference locations or assets ¤ Import other records that depend on locations and assets : Work orders , which reference assets and locations Inventory and storerooms, which reference locations Common hierarchy patterns ¤ Location hierarchies ¤ Correct order : Top-level location , such as Ice cream main plant Second-level location , such as Production building Lower-level location , such as Filling line room Further sub- locations , if applicable What happens if you import in the wrong order : Child locations fail because their parent does not exist. What to do : Sort your import file so parent records come before child records. Asset hierarchies ¤ If you use parent-child asset relationships: Correct order : Parent assets Child assets or subassemblies What to check : Parent asset IDs are correct Each child asset references the correct parent Parent assets exist at the expected location Parent-child relationships ¤ General rule : Always import parents before children. What to check : Parent location IDs are correct Hierarchy levels are properly defined System location references are valid What to do : Verify all parent records exist before importing child records. Data onboarding roadmap ¤ Follow these five steps in sequence to load your facility data: Table 1: The five steps of data onboarding and the guide for each ¤ Step Action Guide 1 Understand load order Review dependencies and ensure referenced records and parent locations exist first. What is the correct load order? 2 Plan your location and asset hierarchies Map your locations and equipment top-down on paper before creating records. How do I plan my location hierarchy? How do I plan my asset hierarchy? 3 Prepare data for import Download CSV templates from Data Management, format ID columns as text, and clean fields. How do I prepare data for import? 4 Get data into the system Upload CSV files in Data Management, validate rows in preview mode, and commit the import. How do I get data into the system? 5 Fix import errors Diagnose preview errors, correct source CSV rows, and re-import failed records. How do I fix import errors? Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Plan your hierarchies ¤ Before preparing spreadsheet files, sketch your locations and equipment top-down to avoid orphan records and grouping errors. How do I plan my location hierarchy? How do I plan my asset hierarchy? Related skills ¤ How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? : Classify every facility entity, machine, and consumable wear item accurately. How do I plan my asset hierarchy? : Structure equipment packages, subassemblies, and maintainable components. How do I prepare data for import? : Format and clean your CSV files and prevent spreadsheet corruption. How do I get data into the system? : Upload and preview your records in the Data Management application. How do I fix import errors? : Troubleshoot missing parents and referenced record failures. docs.text: How do I create inspection forms? ¤ Digital inspection forms replace paper clipboards with structured, interactive checklists on mobile devices. Technicians and inspectors use inspection forms to execute safety audits, hygiene checklists, equipment condition assessments, and routine operator rounds. In Maximo Application Suite Select, you design forms in the Inspection Forms application. Technicians and inspectors complete them in the Inspections role-based app or directly within mobile work orders . Looking to verify your inspection form setup right away? Skip to inspection form verification checklist ↓ What you can capture on an inspection form ¤ The Inspection Forms application gives you flexible ways to capture exact field observations. You can create questions such as: A pass or fail check, for example, whether the sanitary seal on Filler FL-02 is intact. A choice from a standard list of values, for example, lubricant condition rated as clear, cloudy, or dark. A meter reading that updates the asset meter , for example, discharge pressure on the cold storage compressor. A number that you track without updating a meter , for example, ambient warehouse temperature. A photo or file, for example, a photo of a scored drive shaft. A signature, for example, sanitation supervisor sign-off after a clean-in-place flush. The application offers more ways to capture answers than these examples. Use them as a starting point, and explore the options when you design a question. Figure 1 illustrates the inspection form lifecycle from initial authoring to field execution: Step 1 (Design) : build the form using three core question types: Single or domain choice : pass or fail checks and domain picklist selections. Meter or numeric entry : readings that update asset meters or track standalone values. Media or signature : photo attachments and digital sign-offs. Step 2 (Activate and link) : activate the draft template and attach it to PM schedules, route stops, or work orders . Step 3 (Field execution) : technicians complete the interactive checklist in the Inspections role-based app or on mobile work orders . Figure 1: Inspection form design, configuration, and field execution lifecycle Step 1: Create a form template ¤ You create and revise inspection forms in the Inspection Forms application. To open it, use the Find navigation item field and search for Inspection Forms. When you design a form, you can: Give the form a clear, descriptive name, such as Filler FL-02 Daily Sanitation & Mechanical Inspection . Choose the purpose of the form, such as an inspection, an audit, or a round. Add instructions, such as safety lockout procedures or required personal protective equipment. Add the questions that make up your checklist. Mark critical questions as required, so that technicians cannot complete the form without answering them. For a meter reading question, you also choose the meter that the answer updates, such as DISCH_PSI . 💡 Tip: Use conditional logic for failed steps ¤ Configure conditional questions so that when a technician marks an item as a failure, the form reveals follow-up questions. For example, require a photo and an explanatory note. This guarantees complete failure documentation. Step 2: Configure conditional response logic ¤ Conditional rules keep inspection checklists compact while capturing detailed evidence when problems occur. For example, you can set up a pass or fail question so that a failed answer asks the technician to take a photo of the defect and describe the observed damage. Step 3: Activate the form template ¤ Inspection forms start in draft status . Activate a form before you assign it to work orders or preventive maintenance schedules. When updates are needed later, create a revision of the active form. The existing version remains active for in-progress work until you activate the new revision. Step 4: Link inspection forms to maintenance workflows ¤ Once a form is active, you can attach it to automate field checklists: PM schedules: Attach the form to a PM so that every generated work order includes the digital checklist. Route stops: Attach specific forms to individual route stops to guide technicians through multi-room plant rounds. Work orders : Add a form to a work order or to a specific task on the work order . Inspection form verification checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm your inspection forms are configured for reliable field execution. Table 1: Inspection form setup checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Clear title and instructions Form specifies safety precautions and required tools in the header [ ] Mandatory flags configured Critical regulatory and safety questions are marked as required [ ] Meter bindings verified Meter reading questions connect to valid continuous or gauge meters [ ] Conditional logic tested Marking failure options reveals required photo and description prompts [ ] Status set to Active Form is promoted from draft to active for work order selection [ ] PM or Route associations Recurring maintenance schedules have the approved form template attached Related topics ¤ How inspections work How do I plan recurring maintenance? How do I set up meters and meter groups? How do I standardize across teams?

A meter reading that updates the asset meter , for example, discharge pressure on the cold storage compressor. A number that you track without updating a meter , for example, ambient warehouse temperature. A photo or file, for example, a photo of a scored drive shaft. A signature, for example, sanitation supervisor sign-off after a clean-in-place flush. The application offers more ways to capture answers than these examples. Use them as a starting point, and explore the options when you design a question. Meter or numeric entry : readings that update asset meters or track standalone values. Media or signature : photo attachments and digital sign-offs. Step 2 (Activate and link) : activate the draft template and attach it to PM schedules, route stops, or work orders . Step 3 (Field execution) : technicians complete the interactive checklist in the Inspections role-based app or on mobile work orders . docs.text: You create and revise inspection forms in the Inspection Forms application. To open it, use the Find navigation item field and search for Inspection Forms. When you design a form, you can: Give the form a clear, descriptive name, such as Filler FL-02 Daily Sanitation & Mechanical Inspection . Choose the purpose of the form, such as an inspection, an audit, or a round. Add instructions, such as safety lockout procedures or required personal protective equipment. Add the questions that make up your checklist. Mark critical questions as required, so that technicians cannot complete the form without answering them. For a meter reading question, you also choose the meter that the answer updates, such as DISCH_PSI .

docs.text: Conditional rules keep inspection checklists compact while capturing detailed evidence when problems occur. For example, you can set up a pass or fail question so that a failed answer asks the technician to take a photo of the defect and describe the observed damage.

docs.text: How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? ¤ When setting up Maximo Application Suite Select, every physical entity in your plant or facility must be classified as one of three primary record types: a location , an asset , or a spare part. Making the right classification before importing data ensures accurate maintenance history, simplified storeroom operations, and clean drilldown navigation in Maximo Mobile and desktop applications. Misclassifying entities leads to cluttered asset registers and duplicate data entry. For more about planning equipment structures, see How do I plan my asset hierarchy? Looking to verify your record classification right away? Skip to classification decision checklist ↓ As outlined in What is the correct load order? , locations and items are loaded before maintainable assets are established. Video 1: Deciding between locations, assets, and spare parts (about 2 minutes). [Video in production, placeholder preview for design review] The three-way classification model ¤ Maximo Application Suite Select uses three distinct record types to track facilities, machinery, and replacement materials. Figure 1 illustrates the three-tier classification hierarchy: Location : a physical place where work happens, such as Filling line room , which stays in place and retains room-level history. Asset : maintainable equipment operating within the location , such as Filler FL-02 , including serialized child subassemblies such as drive motor MTR-DRV-01 . Spare part : consumable replacement items cataloged in Item Master and referenced on the asset 's Spare Parts tab, such as flange gaskets, o-rings, mechanical seals, and fuses. Figure 1: The three-way classification model in Maximo Application Suite Select 1. Location : A place where work happens ¤ A location represents a place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired. A location can be a building or room, but it can also be a section of a map grid or a telephone pole: Primary purpose : Tracks the place, accumulates its maintenance history, and provides the structure for your plant. Key characteristic : A location stays in place when the machinery in it is replaced or moved, so its history stays with the location . Examples : Production building , Filling line room , Mixing room , Main storeroom . Application : Locations application. 2. Asset : Maintainable equipment ¤ An asset represents a specific piece of serialized equipment or subassembly that operates at a location : Primary purpose : Tracks the lifecycle, maintenance costs, runtime meters , failure history, and work orders for a specific machine. Key characteristic : Assets can move between locations , go into a storeroom for repair, or transfer to another line while retaining their complete work history. Examples : Filler FL-02 , Syrup Pump P-101 , Drive motor MTR-01 . Application : Assets application. 3. Spare part: Consumable replacement item ¤ A spare part represents a stocked or non-stocked replacement material cataloged in the Item Master: Primary purpose : Manages inventory balances in storerooms and allows parts to be issued and charged directly to work orders . Key characteristic : Spare parts are consumed or discarded during maintenance. They do not track individual serial numbers, separate runtime meters , or independent work histories. Examples : Flange gaskets, o-rings, mechanical seals, replacement filters, fuses, drive belts. Applications : Item Master, Storerooms, and the Spare Parts tab on asset records. The four-question decision framework ¤ To classify any physical item or facility entity, follow these four sequential decision questions: Figure 2 outlines the decision pathway through the four classification questions: Question 1 (Place) : if the entity is a place where work happens, create a location in the Locations application. Otherwise, proceed to Question 2. Question 2 (Maintainable equipment) : if it is maintainable equipment with a serial number or nameplate, create an asset in the Assets application anchored to its location . Otherwise, proceed to Question 3. Question 3 (Rebuildable storeroom unit) : if it is a rebuildable unit cycling through storeroom inventory , create a rotating asset using Item Master and Assets . Otherwise, proceed to Question 4. Question 4 (Consumable wear part) : if it is a consumable wear part replaced during repairs, catalog it as a spare part in Item Master and link it to the asset 's Spare Parts tab. Figure 2: The four-question classification decision framework Question 1: Is it a place where work happens? ¤ Ask: "Does this record represent a room, building, bay, outdoor area, or other place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired?" If yes , create a location . If no , proceed to Question 2. Question 2: Is it maintainable equipment that retains its own history? ¤ Ask: "Does this equipment carry a unique serial number or manufacturer nameplate, undergo regular overhauls or preventive maintenance , track runtime meters , or move between locations ?" If yes , create an asset and anchor it to its operating location . If no , proceed to Question 3. Question 3: Is it a rebuildable unit that moves through storeroom inventory ? ¤ Ask: "Is this a standard motor, pump, or gearbox that is stocked in the storeroom as inventory , issued to a machine, pulled for overhaul when it fails, and returned to stock?" If yes , create a rotating item in Item Master and track the serialized unit as an asset . If no , proceed to Question 4. Question 4: Is it a consumable part replaced and discarded during servicing? ¤ Ask: "When this item fails, is it thrown away and replaced with a new one from the storeroom without tracking individual overhaul history?" If yes , catalog the spare part in Item Master and link it to the parent asset 's Spare Parts tab. Boundary cases: How to classify tricky items ¤ Some physical items sit on the boundary between locations , assets , and spare parts. Use these real-world examples from the ice cream plant to guide your decisions. Table 1: Boundary cases for classifying tricky items ¤ Equipment or item Correct record type Why it is classified this way Conveyor line routing Location The path through the building is a place that stays the same when the conveyor equipment changes. Conveyor drive package Asset The motorized mechanical drive has a nameplate, PM schedule, and runtime meter . Conveyor belt and rollers Spare part Consumable wear components issued from storerooms and replaced during repairs. 50 HP rebuildable drive motor Asset Serialized rotating equipment that undergoes shop overhauls and bearing replacements. Fractional throwaway fan motor Spare part Inexpensive non-rebuildable unit; replaced and scrapped upon failure. Calibrated safety relief valve Asset Requires mandatory inspection certification, calibration records, and test history. Manual isolation ball valve Spare part Standard pipe fitting; replaced and discarded upon failure without dedicated history. Main electrical switchgear cabinet Asset High-voltage distribution cabinet installed in an electrical room location . Cabinet power circuit breaker Child asset Maintainable subassembly with its own trip testing and maintenance history. Cabinet fuses and terminal blocks Spare part Consumables cataloged in Item Master and issued to electrical repair work orders . Figure 3: Boundary classification example for a conveyor system In Figure 3, a conveyor line illustrates how to divide complex equipment across the three classification tiers: Location : Packaging zone provides the route where the conveyor operates. Parent asset : Conveyor CV-01 is the main maintainable equipment package with its own operating history and PM schedule. Child asset : Drive motor MTR-DRV-02 is a serialized rotating subassembly tracked for shop overhauls and rewinds. Spare parts : Wear items like modular belt sections, drive rollers, and guide bearings live on the Spare Parts tab and are issued directly to repair work orders . 💡 Tip: Using the Spare Parts tab for consumable parts ¤ Never create asset records for wear parts like gaskets, o-rings, bearings, or filters. Instead, add these stocked items to the Spare Parts tab of the parent asset in the Assets application. Technicians can view the approved bill of materials directly on active work orders and reserve parts from storeroom inventory with one click. Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your understanding before building your records. Problem 1: The 1:1 Location -to- Asset trap ¤ A maintenance planner creates a separate location record for every pump, motor, and machine in the plant, such as creating Filler FL-02 Operating Location to hold Filler FL-02 . Figure 4 illustrates the anti-pattern where artificial location records are created for individual machines, showing Filling line room divided into duplicate locations Filler FL-02 Operating Location for asset Filler FL-02 and Syrup Pump P-101 Operating Location for asset Syrup Pump P-101 . Figure 4: Problem 1: The 1:1 location-to-asset anti-pattern What goes wrong when equipment is replaced or when technicians navigate in Maximo Mobile? Show the answer Creating a 1:1 location for every asset doubles data entry, clutters navigation trees, and destroys asset mobility. When Filler FL-02 is moved or overhauled, planners must rename or reconfigure the location record. Technicians also lose the ability to see all equipment operating inside a single room. What to do instead: Create one location for the room, such as Filling line room , and place multiple assets directly inside that room location . Figure 5 shows the correct structure where the single room location Filling line room contains three independent assets : Filler FL-02 , Syrup Pump P-101 , and Feed Conveyor CV-01 . Figure 5: Solution 1: One location containing multiple assets Problem 2: The over-assetization trap ¤ To help technicians find every part during repairs, a team creates asset records for all internal o-rings, flange bolts, and fuses under Filler FL-02 . What happens to storeroom operations and asset drilldown trees? Show the answer The database becomes flooded with thousands of static records that never receive individual work orders . Asset searches become cluttered, and storeroom clerks cannot issue replacement parts through normal inventory stock balances because the items were modeled as assets instead of inventory materials. What to do instead: Catalog replacement materials in the Item Master and link them to Filler FL-02 through the Spare Parts tab. When work is performed, technicians select items from the spare parts list and charge them directly to the work order . Problem 3: Modeling a building or room as an asset ¤ A data team imports Production building and Cold storage as asset records so they can attach equipment as child assets . What happens when supervisors look for work across a facility? Show the answer Buildings and rooms are places, not maintainable equipment. Modeling places as assets breaks filtering by location in Maximo Mobile and prevents accurate tracking of room and building maintenance. What to do instead: Model buildings, floors, and rooms in the location hierarchy under the Locations application. Anchor equipment records into their respective operating location records. Follow the layout guidelines in How do I plan my location hierarchy? . Problem 4: Throwaway vs rebuildable motors ¤ The ice cream plant uses two types of motors: large 50 HP homogenizer drive motors that cost thousands of dollars to rewind and rebuild, and small fractional horsepower exhaust fan motors that cost fifty dollars and are scrapped when they fail. How should each motor type be classified? Show the answer 50 HP Homogenizer drive motor : Model as an asset using a rotating item record. It carries a unique serial number, tracks operating hours, moves between the machine, storeroom, and repair shop, and accumulates overhaul costs across its lifecycle. Fractional exhaust fan motor : Model as a spare part in Item Master. When a fan motor fails, a replacement is issued from the storeroom to the work order , and the failed motor is discarded. Common classification mistakes ¤ When classifying facility records, avoid these common mistakes: Creating a matching location for every asset record. Modeling consumable wear parts, bolts, or gaskets as asset records. Creating asset records for rooms, buildings, or outdoor areas. Failing to use the Spare Parts tab for approved equipment bills of materials. Treating throwaway non-rebuildable items as serialized assets . A clean classification model keeps your asset register concise, your storeroom inventory accurate, and your hierarchy trees easy to navigate. Classification decision checklist ¤ Before loading records into Maximo Application Suite Select, verify each classification decision: Table 2: Classification checklist ¤ Check Classification item What to verify [ ] Places as locations Buildings, rooms, and storerooms are created in the Locations application. [ ] Maintainable machines as assets Equipment with serial numbers, PM schedules, or runtime meters is created in the Assets application. [ ] One location holds multiple assets Rooms contain multiple assets rather than creating artificial 1:1 location records. [ ] Consumables in Item Master Wear parts, gaskets, seals, and fuses are cataloged in Item Master, not the Assets application. [ ] Spare Parts tabs populated Replacement parts are linked to parent assets on the Spare Parts tab for fast work order selection. [ ] Rotating items identified Rebuildable motors and pumps that cycle through storerooms are configured as rotating items . docs.text: How do I get data into the system? ¤ Use Data Management to import your existing records into IBM Maximo Application Suite Select from a CSV file. This is how you bring in locations , assets , items , and other data in bulk during setup, or any time you need to add or update a large number of records. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Always download the export template first. The template shows you the exact column names and format the system expects. Keep your CSV file under 500 KB. Larger files need to be split into smaller batches. Import one data type at a time, in the correct sequence. See What is the correct load order? for the import sequence. Format ID columns as text in your spreadsheet application before entering data. Spreadsheet applications such as Microsoft Excel can silently reformat IDs as numbers, which breaks the import. Run a small test batch of 5 to 10 records before importing hundreds. This lets you catch format problems quickly. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: What you can import ¤ Data type When to import Locations Sites , buildings, areas, and functional locations where assets are installed Assets Equipment and infrastructure your organization maintains Items Inventory parts and materials stocked in your storeroom GL accounts Cost codes and account structures How to get the correct template ¤ Before filling in your data, use the Data Management application to download a template or export sample records with the correct column names and structure. What to do: In the Find navigation item field, search for Data Management and open it. Select the data type or object structure you want to import, such as locations or assets . Click Export data or download the template for that data type. Open the downloaded CSV file in a spreadsheet application to review the required columns and format. Note If you need a breakdown of the specific column fields for each data type, see Which object structure do I use for each data type? and How do I prepare data for import? . How to import your data ¤ Once your CSV file is prepared and validated: What to do: In the Find navigation item field, search for Data Management and open it. docs.text: Always download the export template first. The template shows you the exact column names and format the system expects. Keep your CSV file under 500 KB. docs.text: How do I plan my asset hierarchy? ¤ Your asset hierarchy is the equipment breakdown structure of your facility. It organizes machinery, subassemblies, and critical maintainable components into a parent-child relationship operating within your locations . When onboarding data into Maximo Application Suite Select, planning your asset hierarchy follows the creation of your location hierarchy, as outlined in What is the correct load order? and How do I plan my location hierarchy? . Looking to verify your asset hierarchy structure right away? Skip to asset hierarchy planning checklist ↓ An asset hierarchy organizes equipment into parent machines and their components. It allows maintenance teams to track the lifecycle of serialized equipment, schedule overhauls at the machine or component level, and move subassemblies across the plant without losing work history. A small operation can keep it simple. Avoid adding consumable parts, which clutter drilldown trees. Video 1: Building an effective asset hierarchy (about 2 minutes). [Video in production, placeholder preview for design review] Core principles for planning your hierarchy ¤ Before loading equipment records into the system, apply these five best practices with your maintenance planners, reliability engineers, and storeroom managers. 1. Distinguish maintainable equipment from consumable spare parts ¤ The most critical decision in asset hierarchy design is separating serialized, maintainable equipment from consumable replacement parts. Apply the nameplate and overhaul test to every item : Asset : A piece of equipment that carries a unique serial number or manufacturer nameplate, undergoes preventive maintenance or repair, and tracks its own cost and operating history over time. Examples include Filler FL-02 , a drive motor, or a centrifugal pump. Spare part : A consumable or non-serialized item that is issued to a work order and replaced during maintenance. Examples include gaskets, o-rings, mechanical seals, bearings, filters, and fuses. Creating asset records for consumable wear parts creates thousands of unnecessary records that clutter search results and navigation trees. Keep consumable wear parts in the Item Master and associate them directly with the parent asset . Quick test: Should this be a child asset ? ¤ Create a child asset only if one or more of the following are true: It is maintained independently. It has its own maintenance history. It can be replaced, rebuilt, or transferred separately. It needs its own inspections, meters , or work orders . If the component is simply replaced when it fails and does not require separate tracking, it is probably a spare part rather than an asset . 2. Keep the hierarchy shallow ¤ While the database supports deep nesting, asset hierarchies work best when they stop at units that are maintained independently. Many organizations need only two or three levels: Parent machine package → Subassembly → Maintainable component For example, a packaging machine package contains a drive motor subassembly, which contains a gearbox component. Do not attempt to model every bolt, bracket, or hose in the asset tree. If an item is not independently maintained, tracked with a meter , or transferred between machines as a complete unit, stop at the subassembly level. 💡 Tip: Managing spare parts with the Spare Parts tab ¤ To make replacement parts easy for technicians to find without turning them into child assets , add stocked items from the Item Master to the Spare Parts tab of the parent asset . Technicians can view approved part numbers, verify storeroom availability, and reserve parts directly on active work orders . 3. Anchor every parent asset to a valid location ¤ Every top-level parent asset must be assigned to an operating location in your location hierarchy, such as Filling line room . When a parent asset is assigned to a location , child subassemblies inherit that location context automatically. When you move a parent asset to a new room or send it to the storeroom for rebuild, child components move along with the parent. 4. Standardize naming and import from the top down ¤ Establish consistent, descriptive naming conventions that combine an equipment code with an operational description, such as ASSET-FL02 / Filler FL-02 and MTR-DRV-01 / Filler FL-02 drive motor . When preparing spreadsheet files for data loading: Locations first : Ensure all operating locations exist in the system before importing assets . Top-level parent assets second : Load main equipment packages with their location references. Child subassemblies third : Load child records referencing their parent asset identifiers. Spare parts lists fourth : Attach stocked item records to assets after asset records exist. What a good asset hierarchy looks like ¤ In this sample ice cream plant equipment model, the asset hierarchy represents the filling line machinery installed inside Filling line room : Filler FL-02 is the top-level parent asset anchored to the operating location Filling line room . Drive motor is a critical serialized subassembly under Filler FL-02 with its own runtime meter and overhaul schedule. Nozzle assembly is a mechanical subassembly under Filler FL-02 that receives regular rebuilds. Nozzle body and Shutoff valve are maintainable child components under Nozzle assembly. Consumable seals, o-rings, and gaskets for the nozzle assembly live on the Spare Parts tab from Item Master, not as child asset records. Figure 1: Sample asset hierarchy for the Filling line system Why this structure works ¤ This equipment structure delivers clean maintenance history and streamlined navigation for everyday operations: Targeted work order history : Technicians can raise a repair work order against Drive motor to log electrical diagnostics, or against Filler FL-02 for general line servicing. Fast drilldown navigation : Technicians navigating in Maximo Mobile or the desktop applications find any maintainable component in two to three clicks from the main filler record. Clean separation of wear parts : Because o-rings and gaskets are cataloged on the Spare Parts tab, storeroom clerks issue parts against the work order without generating orphaned asset records. Independent equipment tracking : If the Drive motor is swapped out during a breakdown, the motor asset record retains its full rebuild history as it moves to the repair shop, while the replacement motor links to Filler FL-02 . Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your understanding before building your equipment hierarchy. Problem 1: Are wear parts and consumables child assets ? ¤ Your maintenance planner wants to create child asset records under Filler FL-02 for mechanical seals, o-rings, and flange gaskets so technicians can select them during repairs. Figure 2 shows the over-assetized hierarchy where consumable wear parts, including o-rings, mechanical seals, and flange gaskets, are incorrectly modeled as individual child asset records underneath Nozzle assembly . Figure 2: Problem 1: Over-assetized hierarchy with consumable parts modeled as child assets What happens if you model these consumable items as child assets ? Show the answer Creating asset records for consumables results in severe over-assetization. The asset register becomes bloated with thousands of static parts that do not undergo individual preventive maintenance or carry serial numbers. Technicians face cluttered drilldown trees, and storeroom inventory counts cannot sync properly with asset records. What to do instead: Keep consumable wear parts in the Item Master and link them to the parent asset using the Spare Parts tab. Technicians can view the approved bill of materials, check storeroom stock, and charge items directly to work orders . Figure 3 shows the corrected asset structure where maintainable child assets Nozzle body and Shutoff valve remain under Nozzle assembly , while consumable o-rings and gaskets are cataloged in Item Master and linked through the Spare Parts tab. Figure 3: Solution 1: Correct asset hierarchy with consumable wear parts managed on the Spare Parts tab Problem 2: What happens when Filler FL-02 moves to a new line? ¤ Filler FL-02 is moved from Filling line room to a newly constructed packaging suite in another building. How do child subassemblies, such as Drive motor and Nozzle assembly , handle the move? Show the answer When a parent asset moves to a new operating location , all child assets in its hierarchy automatically move with it to the new location . The parent-child relationship remains intact, and historical work orders remain linked to both the equipment and the previous location . Figure 4 illustrates moving parent asset Filler FL-02 from location Filling line room to location Packaging suite , showing how child subassemblies Drive motor and Nozzle assembly as well as child components Nozzle body and Shutoff valve automatically inherit the new location . Figure 4: Problem 2: Child subassemblies automatically inherit parent asset relocation What to do instead: Move the top-level parent asset record to the new location . The system updates the location reference across all child subassemblies in a single operation. Problem 3: Should a building or room be modeled as an asset ? ¤ A team member creates an asset record named Production building and places all equipment inside that asset record instead of creating a location record. What goes wrong when supervisors run building maintenance reports? Show the answer Buildings, rooms, and areas are places, not movable equipment. Modeling rooms as assets disables filtering by location in Maximo Mobile and prevents accurate tracking when equipment moves between rooms. Figure 5 contrasts the incorrect model where Production building is created as an asset record holding Filler FL-02 against the correct model where Production building is created as a location record holding asset Filler FL-02 . Figure 5: Problem 3: Comparison of modeling places as locations versus assets What to do instead: Model buildings, floors, and rooms in the location hierarchy under the Locations application. Anchor equipment records, such as Filler FL-02 , into their respective operating location records. Problem 4: In what order do you load parent and child asset records? ¤ You are importing equipment data from a spreadsheet with rows sorted in the following order: Nozzle body : Child component Nozzle assembly : Subassembly Filler FL-02 : Parent machine Filling line room : Operating location What happens when you run the import in this sequence? Show the answer The import fails. Nozzle body fails because its parent Nozzle assembly does not exist yet. Nozzle assembly fails because Filler FL-02 is missing. Filler FL-02 fails because its operating location Filling line room has not been loaded into the database. What to do instead: Sort import rows top-down: Filling line room : Location Filler FL-02 : Top-level parent asset Drive motor , Nozzle assembly : Subassemblies Nozzle body , Shutoff valve : Child components Always verify your import count against the number of rows in your source spreadsheet. Follow data formatting guidelines in How do I prepare data for import? and review sequencing in What is the correct load order? . Common planning mistakes ¤ When designing an asset hierarchy, avoid these common mistakes: Creating assets for every component, no matter how small. Tracking spare parts as assets . Adding hierarchy levels that provide no maintenance or reporting value. Creating separate assets that will never have their own work history. Building a hierarchy that is difficult to navigate or maintain. A good asset hierarchy reflects how equipment is maintained, inspected, and reported on. Focus on maintainable equipment rather than trying to model every physical component. Asset hierarchy planning checklist ¤ Before loading your asset hierarchy into Maximo Application Suite Select, verify each planning requirement: Table 1: Asset hierarchy planning checklist ¤ Check Planning item What to verify [ ] Maintainable equipment only Every asset record represents serialized, maintainable equipment, not consumable wear parts. [ ] Spare parts cataloged Consumables, o-rings, and gaskets are organized in Item Master for use on the Spare Parts tab. [ ] Valid operating locations Every top-level parent asset is assigned to an existing location record. [ ] Shallow hierarchy depth The equipment structure stops at maintainable units. Many organizations need only two or three levels. [ ] Standardized naming Equipment identifiers and asset tags follow consistent naming conventions. [ ] Top-down import sequence Spreadsheet records are ordered so parent assets and locations exist before child records load.
