docs.text: How do I plan my location hierarchy? ¤ Your location hierarchy is the map of the places where your assets are operated, stored, or repaired. It organizes those places into a clear parent-child structure. A place can be a building, a room, a section of a map grid, or a telephone pole. When loading data into Maximo Application Suite Select, locations must be established before you load equipment, inventory , or work orders , as outlined in What is the correct load order? . Looking to verify your location hierarchy structure right away? Skip to location hierarchy planning checklist ↓ A location hierarchy lets you find work across an entire building or drill down to a single room. How much structure you need depends on your operation. A plant with a few rooms needs far less than a site with many buildings and floors. Video 1: Building an effective location hierarchy (about 2 minutes). [Video in production, placeholder preview for design review] Core principles for planning your hierarchy ¤ Before loading records into the system, follow these five best practices with your maintenance planners, supervisors, and operations team. 1. Map your layout on paper first ¤ Before creating records in the system, sketch the facility on paper or a whiteboard. Distinguish clearly between locations , assets , and storerooms: Location : A place where work happens or where equipment is operated, stored, or repaired, such as Production building or Filling line room . A location accumulates the long-term history of that place. Asset : Maintainable equipment operating at a location , such as Filler FL-02 or a motor. Assets can move between locations or into a storeroom, retaining their own lifecycle history wherever they go. Storeroom : A specialized location used specifically to receive, store, and issue inventory items , such as Main storeroom . Ask yourself: "Is this a place where work occurs, or a piece of equipment that could be moved, replaced, or overhauled?" 2. Choose one clear primary structure, usually based on place ¤ The primary location hierarchy usually follows the places where work happens, for example: Top-level location → Building or area → Floor or zone → Room or position A location does not have to be a building with floors and rooms. It can be a section of a map grid or a telephone pole. Choose levels that fit how your operation is laid out. When you search for work in a building, the results include the locations under it. If you group locations by what they are used for, such as all restrooms or all compressor rooms across multiple buildings under one branch, a search for Production building will miss any rooms placed outside that building's branch. Can I organize the same locations more than one way? ¤ Yes. Maximo Application Suite Select lets you organize locations into more than one system. A system is a hierarchy of locations . The same location can belong to more than one system. Primary system : The physical layout of your operation, such as plant, building, and room. You can have only one primary system. Secondary systems : Other groupings of the same locations , based on how equipment works together, such as refrigeration, heating and cooling, or electrical. For example, in the ice cream plant, the primary system follows the physical layout. A secondary Refrigeration system can group Cold storage and Freezer Tunnel , so a supervisor can see everything that keeps product cold in one view. The primary system is not affected, and a search for Production building still covers every room in that building's branch. Keep your primary system based on place. Use secondary systems for functional views, so you do not have to change the physical layout to get them. TODO: Confirm with a subject matter expert [SME confirmation required: confirm whether Maximo Application Suite Select also supports network systems, and how an administrator creates a secondary system. The previous version of this page mentioned network systems.] 💡 Tip: Grouping by function ¤ If you want to view locations by how equipment works together, such as everything that keeps product cold, add a secondary system instead of changing the primary hierarchy. See Can I organize the same locations more than one way? If you want to find locations by type, such as all restrooms or all electrical closets across a facility, use Classifications or location attributes. Some organizations also define locations by function, so that history stays with the location as the assets in it are swapped. For example, an air conditioning compressor can be both an asset and a location in an HVAC system. For more about items that are both, see How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? . TODO: Confirm with a subject matter expert [SME confirmation required: confirm how functional locations work in Maximo Application Suite Select, and how to describe an item that is both an asset and a location .] Quick test: Should this be a location ? ¤ Create a location only if all of the following are true: It is a place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired, or a functional position that keeps its history when equipment is swapped. Maintenance work might be planned, performed, or reported for it. It needs its own maintenance history, costs, or operational context. If the item moves with the equipment when it is repaired, replaced, or transferred, it is probably an asset rather than a location . 3. Decide how deep to go: stop at the maintainable level ¤ More levels are not always better. Extra levels make drilldown navigation slower for technicians in the field. For every level you consider adding, ask this rule-of-thumb question: "Will someone plan, assign, or report maintenance work at this specific level?" If yes , create the location record. If no , stop at the parent level. For example, if maintenance is scheduled for Cold storage as an entire room, do not create sub- locations for every individual shelf or rack. Start with only the levels you need. A small operation might need only two or three levels, and a site with many buildings and floors might need more. You can add sub- locations later as your maintenance processes mature. Do I need a deep hierarchy? ¤ Not always. A hierarchy helps most when you can use it to find things, such as picking a building and drilling down to a floor or room. If your locations do not nest, a flat list is fine. For example, a series of telephone poles does not need levels above or below them. Add structure only where it helps people find or group their work. 4. Connect every child location to a valid parent ¤ Except for the top-level location , every operational location in your hierarchy must have an assigned parent location . Locations created without a parent become orphaned records. They do not appear in hierarchy drilldown navigation trees and are not included when you search for a parent facility. 5. Standardize naming and import from the top down ¤ Establish consistent, descriptive naming conventions across the facility. Combine a clear code with an easily recognized name, such as BLD-PROD / Production building and RM-MIX / Mixing room . When importing data from spreadsheets: Sort your records top-down : Parents must exist before child records are added. Import order : Top-level location , then parent locations , then child locations , then assets . If child rows appear before their parents in an import file, the database cannot resolve the parent reference, leading to import errors and orphaned records. What a good location hierarchy looks like ¤ In this sample ice cream plant, the structure follows the layout of the plant from the top-level location down to individual rooms: Ice cream main plant is the top-level location that all other locations sit under. Production building is a primary parent location that groups related production spaces. Mixing room , Filling line room , and Packaging zone are child locations under Production building. Cold storage and Main storeroom are separate operating locations directly under Ice cream main plant . Figure 1: Sample location hierarchy for Ice cream main plant Why this structure works ¤ This layout succeeds because it mirrors the physical layout of the plant while meeting everyday operational and reporting needs: Work found by building : Work orders assigned to Mixing room , Filling line room , or Packaging zone appear when you search for Production building . Supervisors can review work for the whole building or drill down into a single room. Targeted context for technicians : When technicians open Filling line room in Maximo Mobile or the desktop application, they see only the equipment, safety requirements, and open work orders relevant to that specific room, without clutter from other areas. Clear separation of storerooms and production areas : Main storeroom is designated as an inventory location for receiving, storing, and issuing parts. Keeping storerooms separate from operating production rooms prevents inventory transactions from mixing with equipment maintenance history. Independent tracking for standalone facilities : Cold storage sits directly under Ice cream main plant because it is a separate physical structure with its own refrigeration systems and temperature controls, allowing its costs and work to be tracked independently of the main production building. Fast, shallow drilldown : Technicians reach any room in only two navigation steps from Ice cream main plant . This shallow depth keeps navigation fast in the field while providing all the detail required for work management. Equipment mobility : When assets such as fillers, motors, or pumps are replaced, moved to another room, or sent for overhaul, the location hierarchy remains stable while the asset records track their own movement history. Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your understanding before building your own hierarchy. Problem 1: Which place is each restroom in? ¤ The plant has two restrooms. In the hierarchy below, both are placed under a separate parent location named Restrooms . Figure 2 illustrates the flawed functional grouping where restrooms across different areas, Production building restroom and Packaging zone restroom , are grouped together under a separate Restrooms parent instead of within their respective physical buildings. Figure 2: Problem 1: Restrooms grouped by functional use instead of physical location A supervisor searches for the work orders for Production building for the past quarter. What goes wrong? Show the answer The Production building restroom is omitted from the results because it sits under Restrooms , not under Production building . The hierarchy was grouped by functional use rather than physical location . What to do instead: Place each restroom under the physical area where it is located. Production building restroom belongs under Production building . Packaging zone restroom belongs under Packaging zone . Figure 3 shows the corrected physical structure where Production building restroom sits directly under Production building , and Packaging zone restroom sits under Packaging zone . Figure 3: Solution 1: Restrooms placed within their physical parent locations If you need to find all restrooms across the plant, assign a common Classification or type rather than creating a functional branch in your primary location hierarchy. Problem 2: Where is the Packaging zone? ¤ In the hierarchy below, Packaging zone was added without selecting a parent location . Figure 4 shows an orphaned record condition where Packaging zone is created without a parent connection, leaving it disconnected from Production building . Figure 4: Problem 2: Packaging zone created as an orphaned record without a parent What happens when a planner opens Production building in the drilldown tree? Show the answer Production building displays only Mixing room and Filling line room . Packaging zone is missing from the tree view and from searches for the building. Because Packaging zone has no parent, it exists as an orphaned record with no connection to Production building . What to do instead: Assign Production building as the parent location for Packaging zone . Figure 5 shows the resolved hierarchy where Packaging zone is properly connected to parent location Production building . Figure 5: Solution 2: Packaging zone connected to Production building parent location Problem 3: How many levels should the plant have? ¤ Your maintenance team wants to add sub- locations under Cold storage for every rack, shelf, and bin. A colleague argues that more detail is always better. What question should you ask before creating these sub- locations ? Show the answer Ask: "Will anyone plan, perform, or report maintenance work at an individual shelf level?" If maintenance is performed on the refrigeration units, doors, and ambient room space, not individual storage shelves, stop at Cold storage . Adding unnecessary levels makes the hierarchy harder to navigate without providing actionable maintenance data. The right depth depends on your operation, so a small plant often needs fewer levels than a large site . If parts or items need shelf-level tracking, that is handled through inventory bins in storerooms, not operational location records. Problem 4: In what order do you load location records? ¤ You are importing location records from a spreadsheet with rows in the following sequence: Packaging zone Mixing room Production building Ice cream main plant What happens when you run the import in this order? Show the answer Packaging zone and Mixing room fail to import because their parent, Production building , does not exist in the database yet. Production building then fails because Ice cream main plant has not been loaded yet. What to do instead: Sort import rows top-down: Ice cream main plant : Top-level location Production building : Parent location Mixing room , Filling line room , Packaging zone : Child locations Always verify your import count against the number of rows in your source spreadsheet. Prepare your spreadsheet formatting by following How do I prepare data for import? . For details on sequencing, see What is the correct load order? , and see How do I fix import errors? if rows fail to load. Common planning mistakes ¤ When designing a location hierarchy, avoid these common mistakes: Grouping locations by function in your primary hierarchy when you need reports by building or area. Use a secondary system for functional views. Creating a location for every movable piece of equipment. Adding levels that nobody will maintain, report on, or navigate to. Designing only for today's facility without considering future expansion. Creating orphan locations that are not connected to a parent location . A simple hierarchy that reflects the layout of your operation is easier to maintain than a highly detailed one. Location hierarchy planning checklist ¤ Before loading your location hierarchy into Maximo Application Suite Select, verify each requirement: Table 1: Location hierarchy planning checklist ¤ Check Planning item What to verify [ ] Places and positions Every location record represents a place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired, or a functional position, not a movable piece of equipment. [ ] One clear primary structure The primary system follows one consistent structure, usually from the top-level location to building to room. Functional views use secondary systems, and groupings by type use classifications. [ ] Valid parent connections Every child location connects to an existing parent location to prevent orphan records. [ ] Maintainable depth The structure stops at the level where work is planned, assigned, or reported. A small operation might need only a few levels. [ ] Standardized naming Location codes and identifiers follow consistent naming conventions across the hierarchy. [ ] Top-down import sequence Spreadsheet rows are sorted so that parent locations exist before child records are imported. Use a secondary system for functional views. Creating a location for every movable piece of equipment. Adding levels that nobody will maintain, report on, or navigate to. Designing only for today's facility without considering future expansion. Creating orphan locations that are not connected to a parent location . A simple hierarchy that reflects the layout of your operation is easier to maintain than a highly detailed one.

docs.text: How do I plan my preventive maintenance strategy? ¤ A successful preventive maintenance strategy prevents equipment breakdowns, stabilizes labor schedules, and ensures replacement parts are staged before work begins. Creating maintenance records without a strategic design leads to work order overload, missed service dates, or unnecessary teardown inspections that cause equipment defects. Planning your preventive maintenance strategy in Maximo Application Suite Select involves selecting between time-based and usage-based frequencies, choosing fixed versus floating schedules, buffering lead times for parts staging, and organizing multi-stop routes. Looking to verify your PM strategy right away? Skip to PM strategy planning checklist ↓ Core principles for designing a PM strategy ¤ Before configuring schedules in the PM application, establish your maintenance strategy with your reliability engineers, planners, and operations team. 1. Balance time-based and usage-based triggers ¤ Equipment operating under constant loads benefits from calendar schedules, while machinery with fluctuating production cycles requires usage-based runtime triggers. Figure 1 outlines the decision framework for selecting maintenance frequencies based on operating patterns: 24/7 continuous operation : time-based schedule using fixed calendar days, weeks, or months. Variable batch production : usage-based schedule driven by continuous run hours or cycles. Intermittent seasonal operation : combined schedule triggered by whichever threshold occurs first, calendar elapsed time or meter run hours. Figure 1: Decision framework for preventive maintenance frequency Table 1: Matching equipment types to maintenance triggers ¤ Schedule type How interval is calculated Best suited for Ice Cream Plant example Time-based Fixed calendar days, weeks, or months Continuously running utility systems Monthly emergency lighting and safety valve inspections Usage-based Cumulative continuous meter run hours or cycles High-wear production machinery with fluctuating shift schedules 500-hour bearing lubrication on Filler FL-02 drive motor Combined Elapsed calendar time or accumulated run hours, whichever occurs first Standby machinery or seasonal backup systems Cold Storage backup compressor serviced every 6 months or 250 run hours 2. Choose fixed versus floating intervals carefully ¤ Understanding the difference between fixed and floating schedules is one of the most critical decisions in maintenance planning: Fixed schedule: Calculates the next due date based on the Target Start Date of the previous work order . A monthly PM scheduled for the first of the month always generates on the first of the month, regardless of when technicians complete the physical work. Floating schedule: Calculates the next due date based on the Actual Completion Date of the previous work order . If a monthly PM due on January 1 is finished late on January 15, the next work order is scheduled for February 15. 💡 Tip: Beware of the floating PM halting trap ¤ While a floating PM work order remains open in In Progress or Waiting on Material status , the system cannot calculate the next due date. If a technician forgets to close a floating work order , future preventive maintenance on that machine stops generating entirely without warning. Use fixed schedules for regulatory inspections and reserve floating schedules for usage-based overhauls. 3. Buffer work generation with realistic lead times ¤ Lead time specifies how many days before the maintenance due date Maximo Application Suite Select generates the work order . Set lead times based on your physical storeroom procurement cycles and shift planning routines: Standard lead time: 7 to 14 days: Gives supervisors time to verify parts availability in the storeroom, assign qualified crafts , and coordinate equipment downtime with production supervisors. Zero lead time penalty: If lead time is left at zero, work orders appear on their due date, leaving zero preparation time and causing immediate parts shortages. What a good PM strategy looks like ¤ In our sample ice cream plant, the maintenance strategy combines calendar routines, usage-based triggers, and consolidated routes. Figure 2 illustrates the three maintenance streams that feed into the automated generation engine: Fixed calendar PMs : recurring safety and facility audits scheduled on fixed calendar intervals. Meter run-hour PMs : usage-based servicing for production machines like Filler FL-02 and pumps. Multi-stop routes : consolidated inspection rounds, such as the daily Cold storage walk-through. Automated cron processing : background tasks evaluate lead times and generate work orders 7 days in advance for supervisor assignment. Figure 2: Architecture of an integrated plant preventive maintenance strategy Why this strategy works ¤ Prevents over-maintenance: Variable-speed production machinery triggers maintenance only after true operating wear, saving labor and consumable seal costs. Guarantees regulatory compliance: Hygiene, sanitation, and safety inspections run on fixed calendar dates that cannot drift over time. Eliminates parts delays: A mandatory 7-day lead time ensures replacement gaskets and food-grade lubricants are staged before technicians open equipment panels. Reduces work order volume: Low-risk walk-through checks across 45 cold storage valves are bundled into a single routed work order rather than 45 separate tickets . Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your strategy before creating PM records. Problem 1: The silent halting trap on a floating schedule ¤ A maintenance planner creates a floating monthly preventive maintenance schedule for Filler FL-02 . A technician completes the physical lubrication on January 10 but forgets to advance the work order status from In Progress to Completed. What happens to scheduled maintenance for February and March? Show the answer No work orders are generated for February, March, or any subsequent month. Because floating schedules calculate next due dates from the completion timestamp of the previous work order , the open ticket blocks all future generation. Maintenance halts silently until someone investigates the backlog. What to do instead: Use fixed schedules for recurring time-based servicing, or establish a daily supervisor dashboard triage routine to close completed work orders promptly. Problem 2: The premature calendar PM on idle equipment ¤ A plant sets a fixed 30-day lubrication PM on the packaging room conveyor drive motor. Due to seasonal supply constraints, the filling line was shut down for three weeks during the month and only operated for 20 hours. What happens when the calendar PM generates on schedule? Show the answer Technicians perform an unnecessary lubrication service on a machine that experienced almost zero mechanical wear. Over-lubricating bearings can blow out grease seals and introduce particulate contamination. What to do instead: Switch the conveyor motor from a calendar frequency to a meter -based schedule triggered every 300 continuous operating run hours. Problem 3: The zero lead time material bottleneck ¤ A planner configures quarterly pump rebuild schedules with zero days lead time. When work orders generate on the first day of the quarter, technicians immediately open the tickets and walk to the storeroom. What happens at the storeroom counter? Show the answer The required mechanical seal kits are out of stock. Because the work order generated on its due date, the inventory clerk had zero advance notice to reorder parts. The work order stalls in Waiting on Material status for two weeks, turning a planned PM into an overdue compliance failure. What to do instead: Configure a 14-day lead time on the PM record. When the work order generates two weeks early, the system reserves storeroom stock and alerts the inventory clerk to replenish low balances before work starts. Problem 4: Work order clutter from individual minor inspections ¤ A facility creates 60 separate monthly PM records to inspect each individual fire extinguisher and emergency eyewash station across the production building. What happens to technician productivity and supervisor assignment queues? Show the answer Technicians spend more time opening, logging labor on, and closing 60 individual records than performing the actual physical checks. Supervisor work queues become overwhelmed with dozens of trivial tickets . What to do instead: Group all 60 inspection points into a single multi-stop Route attached to one monthly PM schedule. The system generates one consolidated work order with 60 sequential room stops. Common PM planning mistakes ¤ When planning preventive maintenance schedules, avoid these frequent pitfalls: Creating separate standalone PMs for every minor component instead of using Master PMs and Routes. Setting floating schedules on compliance-critical assets where dates must not drift. Leaving lead time at zero, which causes parts shortages on the scheduled start date. Scheduling invasive teardown inspections on sealed components when non-destructive condition monitoring is more effective. Activating dozens of new PM schedules simultaneously on day one, which overwhelms the maintenance team with sudden work spikes. PM strategy planning checklist ¤ Use this checklist to verify your maintenance strategy before activating schedules. Table 2: PM strategy verification checklist ¤ Check Planning item What to verify [ ] Schedule type alignment Continuous machines use meter run hours; fixed facilities use calendar intervals [ ] Fixed vs floating validation Regulatory and safety checks use fixed intervals to prevent schedule drift [ ] Lead time buffering All PM records have a lead time of 7 to 14 days for material verification [ ] Standardized job plans linked Every PM record references an active Job Plan with task steps and material lists [ ] Route consolidation Minor walk-through checks are bundled into multi-stop routes [ ] Meter configuration verified Usage-based PMs connect to continuous meters with active daily run rates Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next steps: Setup and execution ¤ How do I set up meters and meter groups? : Configure continuous run-hour meters and rollover limits. docs.text: How do I plan my storeroom and inventory strategy? ¤ An effective storeroom and inventory strategy ensures critical spare parts are on hand when machines break down, prevents expensive stockouts, and eliminates excess capital tied up in slow-moving materials. Without structured storeroom management, maintenance teams suffer frequent job delays and inventory counts drift into inaccurate negative balances. Planning your storeroom and inventory strategy in Maximo Application Suite Select involves designing physical storeroom layouts, classifying consumable versus rebuildable rotating items , establishing dynamic reorder points, and implementing regular cycle counts. Looking to verify your storeroom and inventory strategy right away? Skip to storeroom strategy planning checklist ↓ Core principles for designing a storeroom strategy ¤ Before cataloging items in the Item Master or creating warehouses in the Storerooms application, establish your inventory strategy with your maintenance, procurement, and warehouse teams. 1. Separate physical storerooms from operational locations ¤ In Maximo Application Suite Select, a storeroom is a specialized location record designated for inventory control. Keep storeroom records strictly distinct from operating rooms: Operating location : Where production occurs and machinery operates, such as Filling line room . Work orders and downtime are tracked against operating locations . Storeroom location : Where items and spare parts are securely held, received, and issued, such as Main storeroom . Inventory transactions, stock balances, and unit costs are tracked at storerooms. Figure 1 maps the material and financial flow from storeroom inventory to work orders and physical locations : Storeroom location : Main storeroom holds stocked spare parts. Material issue : items are issued and charged directly to an active work order , such as Filler FL-02 . Operating location : Filling line room provides the physical space where the equipment operates. Cost tracking : maintenance and material expenses are tracked against both the asset and the location . Figure 1: Financial and material flow between storeroom, work order, and operating location 2. Distinguish consumable materials from rotating rebuildable assets ¤ Every item stocked in inventory must be categorized as either a consumable item or a rotating item : Consumable item , non-rotating: Standard wear parts, such as flange gaskets, o-rings, drive belts, and filters. Tracked as physical stock quantities in storeroom bins. When issued, the part is consumed by the work order and discarded upon replacement. Rotating item : Expensive, rebuildable serialized equipment, such as 50 HP drive motors, sanitary pumps, and gearboxes. Tracked simultaneously as an inventory item in storerooms and as an individual asset in the Assets application. When pulled from a machine, the failed unit returns to the storeroom for repair rather than being scrapped. Table 1: Consumable items versus rotating items comparison ¤ Item classification Tracking method Financial impact upon issue Repair handling Ice Cream Plant example Consumable item Quantity balance in storeroom bin Material cost charged directly to work order Discarded and replaced with new stock Food-grade silicone gasket kit for Filler FL-02 Rotating item Quantity balance plus serialized asset record Material usage and asset location transfer recorded Sent to rebuild shop and returned to storeroom stock Rebuildable 50 HP homogenizer pump drive motor 💡 Tip: Use the Attach to Parent Asset on Issue toggle ¤ For rotating items that operate as subassemblies on parent machines, enable Attach to Parent Asset on Issue in the Item Master. When a storeroom clerk issues the replacement motor to Filler FL-02 , Maximo Application Suite Select automatically links the new motor as a child asset to the filler in a single transaction. 3. Establish automated reorder points and safety stock ¤ Automating inventory replenishment prevents emergency stockouts while avoiding over-purchasing. Configure reorder parameters on the Inventory record for each stocked item : Safety stock: Minimum buffer held to protect against supplier shipping delays or unexpected breakdown spikes. Reorder point: Threshold that triggers reordering when the calculation Current Balance + On Order - Reserved drops to or below this level. Economic order quantity: Minimum cost-effective batch size to purchase from vendors. What a good storeroom strategy looks like ¤ In our sample ice cream plant, the inventory strategy combines a secure central storeroom, satellite staging cribs, and structured rotating pools. Figure 2 illustrates the storeroom topology and replenishment architecture: Central storeroom : Main storeroom securely stores high-value spares and rotating items . Issue counter : handles rapid barcode checkout for major jobs like Filler FL-02 overhaul . Satellite crib : receives bulk restocks from the main storeroom to hold consumable parts close to active areas like Cold storage for jobs like Refrigeration routine . Automated replenishment : system calculations monitor stock buffers to trigger timely reorders before stockouts occur. Figure 2: Sample storeroom topology and inventory replenishment flow Why this strategy works ¤ Secures high-value rotating spares: Rebuildable motors and expensive sanitary valves remain controlled in the central warehouse until officially reserved on approved work orders . Minimizes technician transit time: High-frequency consumables like sanitizing lubricants and cold-temperature seals live in an unlocked satellite cabinet near the cold storage facility. Maintains 100% stock accuracy: Storeroom staff conduct weekly cycle counts using Count Books, preventing inventory balance discrepancies before scheduled PMs run. Prevents stockouts on critical lines: Automated reorder calculations alert procurement two weeks before packaging line consumables deplete. Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your inventory strategy before adding items . Problem 1: The ghost stockout from unrecorded counter withdrawals ¤ Technicians frequently grab mechanical seals from storeroom shelves during emergency repairs without logging an issue transaction on their work orders . What happens when the scheduled monthly PM work order for Filler FL-02 generates two weeks later? Show the answer The system shows 4 seals in stock, so the work order is approved. However, when the technician arrives at the storeroom bin, the shelf is completely empty. The job stalls in Waiting on Material status , and the plant faces unexpected downtime because unrecorded withdrawals created ghost inventory . What to do instead: Require all item checkouts to be recorded at the counter using the Issues and Transfers role-based app, and perform weekly cycle counts in Count Books to catch discrepancies early. Problem 2: Over-stocking low-cost bolts while stocking out of critical seals ¤ A facility stocks $40,000 worth of standard hardware bolts that can be purchased locally in 2 hours, but holds zero custom mechanical seal kits for Filler FL-02 that have an 8-week supplier lead time. What happens when Filler FL-02 suffers an unexpected seal failure? Show the answer The filling line is shut down for weeks waiting for international replacement shipments, costing tens of thousands of dollars in lost production, while valuable working capital sits locked up in excess hardware bolts. What to do instead: Conduct an inventory criticality review. Set high safety stock and automated reorder points on long-lead critical spares, and maintain lean just-in-time minimums for locally available commercial hardware. Problem 3: The throwaway motor trap ¤ A maintenance team purchases ten 50 HP drive motors for production pumps. In Item Master, the planner forgets to check the Rotating? box and catalogs the motors as standard consumable items . What happens when the first motor fails and is replaced? Show the answer The technician issues the replacement motor as a consumable material. The old motor is removed, but because it has no serialized asset record, its lifetime overhaul history, rewind dates, and run-hour meter logs are permanently lost. The repair shop cannot track whether this specific motor has failed multiple times. What to do instead: Mark rebuildable equipment as Rotating in the Item Master before creating inventory balances, and track the individual units as serialized assets . Problem 4: Creating a storeroom as an asset record ¤ A data entry clerk creates Main storeroom as an asset record in the Assets application so that equipment can be linked to it. What happens when inventory clerks attempt to receive purchase orders or issue parts? Show the answer Inventory applications like Inventory , Count Books, and Issues and Transfers store items in storerooms, so parts cannot be stocked inside asset records. What to do instead: Create Main storeroom in the Storerooms application. Common storeroom planning mistakes ¤ When planning your storerooms and inventory catalogs, avoid these frequent mistakes: Allowing open, unmonitored access to storeroom bins without barcode issue logging. Failing to mark rebuildable motors and pumps as Rotating items in Item Master. Setting reorder points to zero, disabling automated stock replenishment calculations. Neglecting to link stocked items to the Spare Parts tab of parent asset records. Skipping periodic cycle counts, which allows physical stock and database balances to drift. Storeroom strategy planning checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm your inventory strategy is ready for operations. Table 2: Storeroom strategy verification checklist ¤ Check Planning item What to verify [ ] Dedicated storerooms Storerooms are created in the Storerooms application, separate from operating locations and assets [ ] Rotating items classified Rebuildable motors and pumps have the Rotating checkbox enabled in Item Master [ ] Critical spares identified Long-lead replacement parts have defined safety stock and reorder points in Inventory [ ] Spare Parts tabs linked Consumable gaskets and seals are linked to parent machines for fast technician lookup [ ] Barcode issue process ready Storeroom counter staff use Issues and Transfers for rapid material checkout [ ] Cycle counting schedule set Periodic physical inventory audits are planned using Count Books Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next steps: Setup and execution ¤ How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? : Master the four-question classification framework. How do I issue parts? : Execute fast counter checkouts using the Issues and Transfers app. How do I track stock levels? : Monitor minimum balances, reservations, and reorder triggers. Configure reorder parameters on the Inventory record for each stocked item : Safety stock: Minimum buffer held to protect against supplier shipping delays or unexpected breakdown spikes. Reorder point: Threshold that triggers reordering when the calculation Current Balance + On Order - Reserved drops to or below this level. Economic order quantity: Minimum cost-effective batch size to purchase from vendors.
docs.title: 3. Establish automated reorder points and safety stock

docs.text: In our sample ice cream plant, the inventory strategy combines a secure central storeroom, satellite staging cribs, and structured rotating pools. Figure 2 illustrates the storeroom topology and replenishment architecture: Central storeroom : Main storeroom securely stores high-value spares and rotating items . Issue counter : handles rapid barcode checkout for major jobs like Filler FL-02 overhaul . Satellite crib : receives bulk restocks from the main storeroom to hold consumable parts close to active areas like Cold storage for jobs like Refrigeration routine . Automated replenishment : system calculations monitor stock buffers to trigger timely reorders before stockouts occur. Figure 2: Sample storeroom topology and inventory replenishment flow
docs.title: What a good storeroom strategy looks like

docs.text: Secures high-value rotating spares: Rebuildable motors and expensive sanitary valves remain controlled in the central warehouse until officially reserved on approved work orders . Minimizes technician transit time: High-frequency consumables like sanitizing lubricants and cold-temperature seals live in an unlocked satellite cabinet near the cold storage facility. Maintains 100% stock accuracy: Storeroom staff conduct weekly cycle counts using Count Books, preventing inventory balance discrepancies before scheduled PMs run. Prevents stockouts on critical lines: Automated reorder calculations alert procurement two weeks before packaging line consumables deplete.
docs.title: Why this strategy works

docs.text: Review these common planning scenarios to test your inventory strategy before adding items .
docs.title: Spot the problem: test your plan

docs.text: Technicians frequently grab mechanical seals from storeroom shelves during emergency repairs without logging an issue transaction on their work orders . What happens when the scheduled monthly PM work order for Filler FL-02 generates two weeks later? Show the answer The system shows 4 seals in stock, so the work order is approved. However, when the technician arrives at the storeroom bin, the shelf is completely empty. The job stalls in Waiting on Material status , and the plant faces unexpected downtime because unrecorded withdrawals created ghost inventory . What to do instead: Require all item checkouts to be recorded at the counter using the Issues and Transfers role-based app, and perform weekly cycle counts in Count Books to catch discrepancies early.
docs.title: Problem 1: The ghost stockout from unrecorded counter withdrawals

docs.text: A facility stocks $40,000 worth of standard hardware bolts that can be purchased locally in 2 hours, but holds zero custom mechanical seal kits for Filler FL-02 that have an 8-week supplier lead time. What happens when Filler FL-02 suffers an unexpected seal failure? Show the answer The filling line is shut down for weeks waiting for international replacement shipments, costing tens of thousands of dollars in lost production, while valuable working capital sits locked up in excess hardware bolts. What to do instead: Conduct an inventory criticality review. Set high safety stock and automated reorder points on long-lead critical spares, and maintain lean just-in-time minimums for locally available commercial hardware.
docs.title: Problem 2: Over-stocking low-cost bolts while stocking out of critical seals

docs.text: A maintenance team purchases ten 50 HP drive motors for production pumps. In Item Master, the planner forgets to check the Rotating? box and catalogs the motors as standard consumable items . What happens when the first motor fails and is replaced? Show the answer The technician issues the replacement motor as a consumable material. The old motor is removed, but because it has no serialized asset record, its lifetime overhaul history, rewind dates, and run-hour meter logs are permanently lost. The repair shop cannot track whether this specific motor has failed multiple times. What to do instead: Mark rebuildable equipment as Rotating in the Item Master before creating inventory balances, and track the individual units as serialized assets .
docs.title: Problem 3: The throwaway motor trap

docs.text: A data entry clerk creates Main storeroom as an asset record in the Assets application so that equipment can be linked to it. What happens when inventory clerks attempt to receive purchase orders or issue parts? Show the answer Inventory applications like Inventory , Count Books, and Issues and Transfers store items in storerooms, so parts cannot be stocked inside asset records. What to do instead: Create Main storeroom in the Storerooms application.
docs.title: Problem 4: Creating a storeroom as an asset record

docs.text: When planning your storerooms and inventory catalogs, avoid these frequent mistakes: Allowing open, unmonitored access to storeroom bins without barcode issue logging. Failing to mark rebuildable motors and pumps as Rotating items in Item Master. Setting reorder points to zero, disabling automated stock replenishment calculations. Neglecting to link stocked items to the Spare Parts tab of parent asset records. Skipping periodic cycle counts, which allows physical stock and database balances to drift.
docs.title: Common storeroom planning mistakes

docs.text: How do I prepare data for import? ¤ Data Management is the primary application used to import records into IBM Maximo Application Suite Select. Use this guide to clean, format, and structure your spreadsheets or legacy CSV files before uploading them into Data Management. Looking to validate your CSV file right away? Skip to pre-import data validation checklist ↓ 💡 Tips: Best practices for data preparation ¤ Start with a template : Download official templates or export existing records directly from Data Management to see the required column names and structure. Validate data first : Check all values against system data such as site IDs and failure classes before uploading. Use text format : Prevent spreadsheet software from corrupting leading zeros or converting numbers to scientific notation. Test with small batches : Verify format with a small batch of 5 to 10 records before importing thousands. Keep error logs : Document preview errors to correct source files efficiently. Common preparation steps ¤ Use the correct file format ¤ What to do : Save files as CSV format, using comma delimiters Use UTF-8 encoding for special characters Format ID columns as text in Excel before entering data Validate field names and structure ¤ What to check : Column names match system field names exactly All required fields are included Field names are correct, which are case-sensitive What to do : Use a template or export an existing record to see the correct structure. Prevent Excel from corrupting data ¤ Excel can corrupt data in several ways: Dates : Converts text to dates, such as converting 01-02 to Jan 2 IDs : Removes leading zeros, such as converting 001 to 1 Long numbers : Converts long numbers to scientific notation What to do : Format all columns as text in Excel before entering data, or use a plain text editor to create the CSV. Clean your data ¤ What to check : Remove extra spaces from all fields Ensure consistent formatting Validate data against system values, such as status codes and site IDs Check for duplicate IDs Check referenced data before importing ¤ Verify that supporting records exist before importing locations or assets . Missing referenced data is a common cause of import failures. For location imports ¤ What to check : Table 1: Location fields to check before import ¤ Field Required when GL accounts Your organization tracks maintenance costs by cost centre Service addresses Locations need to appear on maps or work order dispatch Calendars and shifts Scheduling work or calculating availability at this location Failure classes You want structured failure reporting on work orders for this location Classifications and specifications You want to search or report on locations by equipment type What to do : Create missing referenced records before importing locations , or update the import file to use existing values. For asset imports ¤ What to check : Table 2: Asset fields to check before import ¤ Field Required when GL accounts Tracking maintenance costs by cost centre Service addresses Assets need to appear on maps or work order dispatch Failure classes Technicians need to select failure codes on work orders for this asset . Without this, the Failure Reporting tab is empty Rotating items Only when the asset is a rotating, serialised item tracked by individual asset record Vendors and manufacturers Tracking warranty, procurement, or service history by supplier Classifications and specifications You want to search, filter, or report on assets by type or specification What to do : Verify all referenced records exist before importing assets . Create missing records or correct values in the import file. Use consistent date formats ¤ Date formats are a common source of import errors. Follow these guidelines to prevent date-related failures. What to do : Use one accepted date format consistently throughout the file Do not mix regional date formats, such as MM/DD/YYYY and DD/MM/YYYY Avoid ambiguous dates such as 01/02/2026 unless the accepted format is clear Format date columns as text in Excel before entering values Test a small batch that includes date values before importing the full file Common date format issues : Excel automatically converts dates to its default format Mixed formats cause some records to fail while others succeed Ambiguous dates are interpreted incorrectly What to do : Verify the expected date format for your system and apply it consistently to all date fields. Import hierarchies in the correct order ¤ For locations and parent-child relationships: What to do : Import in order: Top-level records first: parent locations Second-level records next Lowest-level records last: child locations Break large imports into batches ¤ What to do : Break files into smaller batches of 1,000 to 5,000 records at a time This prevents timeouts and makes troubleshooting easier Preview before importing ¤ Use preview/import validation : Always preview your import before committing it. This shows: Which records will succeed Which records will fail What errors need to be fixed Without validation If you skip validation, errors are only discovered after processing. This can result in: Partial imports with missing records Incorrect data in the system Time wasted troubleshooting after the fact What happens next? ¤ After preparing your data: Preview the import to validate Fix any errors identified Process the import Verify records were created successfully Pre-import data validation checklist ¤ Before uploading your file into Data Management, verify each data preparation step: Table 3: Pre-import data validation checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] CSV file encoding File is saved in CSV format with UTF-8 encoding [ ] Text column formatting ID, code, and date columns are formatted as Text in spreadsheet software [ ] Leading zeros preserved Asset numbers, location codes, and part identifiers retain leading zeros [ ] Header row alignment Column names match system attribute names and case sensitivity [ ] Mandatory site and org keys Every row contains valid SITEID and ORGID values [ ] Top-down hierarchical sort Parent locations and parent assets appear in rows before their child records [ ] Hierarchy plan agreed Your location and asset hierarchies are planned and agreed with your planners and supervisors before you load [ ] Referenced data verified Status codes, failure classes, crafts , and vendors exist in the system [ ] Batch size limit Large datasets are split into batches of 1,000 to 5,000 rows Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Get data into the system ¤ With your CSV files prepared and validated, upload them into Data Management and preview your records before importing. docs.text: How do I set up failure codes ? ¤ Structured failure codes convert subjective technician remarks into standardized reliability data. When technicians record repairs using consistent failure codes , maintenance engineers can track defect trends, identify recurring root causes, and justify equipment redesigns or warranty claims. In Maximo Application Suite Select, failure codes are organized into a four-tier hierarchy headed by a Failure Class, followed by Problem, Cause, and Remedy codes configured in the Failure Codes application. Select includes some failure codes . You can use them as they are, or add your own to match your equipment. Looking to verify your failure code configuration right away? Skip to failure code setup verification checklist ↓ The four-tier failure hierarchy architecture ¤ A failure hierarchy structures failure reporting from initial symptom down to corrective action. Figure 1 illustrates the four-tier failure hierarchy architecture: Tier 1 (Failure Class) : broad equipment category, such as PUMPS . Tier 2 (Problem) : observed operational symptom, such as LEAK for fluid leaks or HIGH_TEMP for heat issues. Tier 3 (Cause) : underlying mechanical defect, such as SEAL_WEAR . Tier 4 (Remedy) : corrective action taken, such as REPLACE_SEAL . Figure 1: Four-tier failure code hierarchy architecture Table 1: Four-tier failure code hierarchy with plant examples ¤ Level Code type What it describes Ice Cream Plant example Level 1 Failure Class Broad equipment family or machine type PUMPS (Sanitary and utility pumps) Level 2 Problem The observed failure symptom or operational defect LEAK (Fluid leaking from pump casing) Level 3 Cause The underlying mechanical or operational root cause SEAL_WEAR (Carbon seal face worn beyond tolerance) Level 4 Remedy The specific corrective action that resolved the failure REPLACE_SEAL (Installed new food-grade mechanical seal kit) Step 1: Create a failure hierarchy in Failure Codes ¤ Failure codes and hierarchies are created at the Organization level in the Failure Codes application. Building a failure tree in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Failure Codes and open it. Click New Failure Code . In the Failure Class field, enter a clear identifier, such as PUMPS . In the Description field, enter Sanitary and Utility Pumps Failure Class . In the Problems table, click New Row to add failure symptoms: In the Problem field, enter LEAK . In the Description field, enter Liquid product or lubricant leak . With the LEAK problem row selected, go to the Causes table below and click New Row : In the Cause field, enter SEAL_WEAR . In the Description field, enter Mechanical seal wear or face scoring . With the SEAL_WEAR cause row selected, go to the Remedies table and click New Row : In the Remedy field, enter REPLACE_SEAL . In the Description field, enter Replaced mechanical seal assembly . Repeat steps 5 through 7 to add remaining problems, causes, and remedies. Click Save . 💡 Tip: Reuse branches with Copy Failure Hierarchy ¤ Many equipment types share identical mechanical failure paths. Instead of retyping problem, cause, and remedy trees for every machine class, use the Copy Failure Hierarchy action in the Failure Codes application to duplicate branches from existing failure classes in seconds. Step 2: Assign Failure Classes to assets ¤ For technicians to select failure codes on work orders , the asset must have an assigned Failure Class. Linking a failure class to an asset record ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Assets and open it. Open the target equipment record, such as Filler FL-02 . On the main Asset tab, locate the Failure Class field. Select the matching failure class, such as FILLERS or ROTATING_PUMP . Click Save . Figure 2 outlines the failure class inheritance and field reporting workflow: Asset record : equipment record Filler FL-02 holds configured failure class PUMPS . Work order header : when the asset is added to a corrective work order , PUMPS is inherited automatically. Field closure : during job completion, the technician accesses the Failure Reporting tab. Cascading selection : the technician navigates the filtered PUMPS hierarchy to log Problem LEAK , Cause SEAL_WEAR , and Remedy REPLACE_SEAL . Figure 2: Failure class inheritance and field reporting flow How failure codes behave on work orders ¤ Understanding how failure codes transfer to work orders ensures smooth field reporting: Automatic inheritance: When an asset is added to a work order , its Failure Class copies automatically to the work order header. Precedence rule: If both an asset and a location are specified on a work order and each has a different failure class, the asset failure class takes precedence. Mandatory reporting: For emergency and breakdown work types, configure work order rules to require Problem, Cause, and Remedy selection before advancing status to Completed. Common failure code design mistakes ¤ To maintain clean reliability analytics, avoid these common design traps: Creating too many failure classes: Keep your initial failure class list focused on 5 to 10 major equipment families, such as Pumps, Motors, Conveyors, Refrigeration, and Electrical. Avoid creating a unique failure class for every individual machine model. Using vague problem descriptions: Do not create codes named Broken , Damaged , or Failed . Use specific physical symptoms, such as High Vibration , Overheating , Jammed , or Leaking . Omitting remedy codes: Recording only what broke without recording which remedy succeeded prevents reliability teams from knowing which repair procedures are most effective. Failure code setup verification checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm your failure hierarchies are ready for operational use. Table 2: Failure code configuration checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Core failure classes established Top-level classes exist for all major plant equipment families [ ] 4-tier depth completed Each problem branch has linked cause codes and associated remedies [ ] Descriptive naming applied Codes use clear alphanumeric identifiers with concise plain-language descriptions [ ] Asset records populated Operating equipment records have a valid Failure Class assigned on their main tab [ ] Mobile visibility verified Technicians can view and navigate the failure hierarchy on mobile work order cards [ ] Mandatory on corrective work Failure reporting is required before closing emergency or unscheduled repair work orders Related topics ¤ What happens when an asset fails? How do I reduce downtime ? How do I make data reliable? How do I standardize across teams?

docs.text: How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? ¤ Set up your workforce resources before you start assigning work. Crafts define the skills in your organization. Labor records represent the people. Crews group people together so you can assign a whole team to a job in one step. These records work together. You need to set them up in the correct order. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Set up crafts before labor . A labor record must reference a valid craft . Set up a calendar before creating a crew . The crew 's calendar controls when its members show as available. Match the calendar and shift on each labor record to the crew they belong to. A mismatch is the most common reason crew members show as unavailable when you try to assign work. Leave the End Date blank on labor assignments to a crew unless the assignment has a fixed end. This keeps the member permanently assigned until you need to change it. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Labor and crew terminology ¤ Term What it means Craft A skill or trade, such as Electrician or Mechanic, used to match the correct person to the correct job Calendar Defines working days and shifts. Must be assigned to both the crew and each member. Labor A person who performs work or records time Crew type A template that defines the positions and crafts a crew requires, such as Leader and Helper Crew A named group of people assembled to work together, built from a crew type Setup order ¤ Set these up in sequence. Each step depends on the one before it. Crafts → Calendar → Labor → Crew type → Crew Step 1: Create crafts ¤ Crafts represent the skills in your workforce. Select includes some crafts and skill levels. You can use them as they are, or add your own. In the Find navigation item field, search for Crafts and open it. Create a new craft record. Enter a craft ID and description, for example, MECH, Mechanic or REFRIG, Refrigeration technician . Set the default rate if applicable. Save. Repeat for each skill type in your organization. Step 2: Set up a calendar ¤ Crews need a calendar to define when their members are available. If you have not already created a calendar for your workforce, do this before creating crew types. See How do I schedule work? for steps to create shifts and calendars. Step 3: Create labor records ¤ Labor records represent the individuals who perform work. Select creates a labor record for a person when you create their user, so you usually update the existing record instead of creating a new one. docs.text: How do I set up maps? ¤ Map Manager lets you configure a map so that users can see the location of assets , work orders , and service addresses on a visual map inside the application. Once a map is configured and enabled, it appears in spatially enabled applications for all users. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Keep your first map simple. One basemap service is enough to get started. You can add more map services later. Use a descriptive name for each map service so it is easy to identify if you add more later. If users will be viewing maps on mobile devices, use the same map configuration. Mobile users see the same map as desktop users. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Map terminology ¤ Term What it means Map Manager The application where you create and configure maps Map provider The mapping service that supplies the background map, such as OpenMap Basemap The background map layer that shows geography, streets, or satellite imagery Map service A URL that points to a map tile or layer from your map provider Initial extent The default view that opens when a user first opens the map What you need before you start ¤ A basemap URL from your map provider. OpenMap supports public ArcGIS basemap URLs, which do not require an account or license to use. The name of the applications you want maps to appear in. How to set up a map ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Map Manager and open it. Click New Map . Enter a unique name and a short description for the map. Select Enable Map to activate this configuration. Set the Map Provider to OpenMap . In the Map Services table, click Add Row . Enter a name for the map service, for example, Basemap . Enter the basemap URL. For example, to use a public ArcGIS basemap : https://services.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/World_Street_Map/MapServer Set the Order value. The basemap should have the highest order value in the list. Set the Initial Extent for the map. Pan and zoom to the geographic area your organization works in, then save the extent. Save the map record. Confirm the map is working ¤ After saving, open the Locations or Assets application and open a record that has a location or address. A map panel should appear on the record showing your configured basemap . If the map does not appear, check that: The map record has Enable Map selected. The basemap URL is accessible from the application. If your map does not load In some environments, the application's security policy may block external map tile servers. If the map panel appears but the map does not load, contact IBM support. In Maximo Application Suite Select, system-level security settings are managed by IBM. Continue building your skills ¤ Automate your notifications ¤ With your map in place, keep your team informed. Set up email and push notifications so people know when work is assigned or updated. How do I automate communication? Configure Maximo Mobile for field teams ¤ Let technicians, supervisors, and inventory clerks use a mobile app to access their work from anywhere. docs.text: How do I set up meters and meter groups? ¤ Meters track equipment usage, operating conditions, and physical measurements. In Maximo Application Suite Select, meter readings drive automated preventive maintenance schedules based on run hours and trigger corrective work orders when readings breach safety limits. You enter meter readings manually. Select does not receive readings automatically from sensors or IoT devices. Setting up meters involves defining meter definitions at the system level, grouping related meters into reusable templates, and attaching those meters to assets and locations . Looking to verify your meter setup right away? Skip to meter setup verification checklist ↓ The three meter types in Maximo Application Suite Select ¤ Before creating meters , select the appropriate meter type based on how the measurement behaves. Figure 1 outlines the decision framework for selecting meter types: Continuous meter : for cumulative values that always increment, such as run hours or cycles, driving usage-based preventive maintenance . Gauge meter : for numeric values that fluctuate up and down, such as temperature or pressure, driving condition monitoring limits. Characteristic meter : for qualitative observations, such as fluid clarity or physical wear, evaluating values from an ALN domain . Figure 1: Decision framework for selecting meter types and operational applications Table 1: Comparison of meter types and operational applications ¤ Meter type Measurement behavior Allowable values Operational application Ice Cream Plant example Continuous Always increments upward until hardware rollover Positive numbers only Drives usage-based PM generation Run hours on the Filler FL-02 drive motor Gauge Fluctuates up and down Numeric values, including negative numbers Triggers Condition Monitoring alerts Ambient temperature in Cold Storage Room Characteristic Qualitative visual or physical observations Alphanumeric values defined in an ALN domain Triggers Condition Monitoring alerts Lubricant clarity rated as Clear, Cloudy, or Dark Step 1: Define meters in the Meter application ¤ Meters are created once at the system level and can then be applied across multiple assets and locations . Creating a meter in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Meter and open it. Click New Meter . In the Meter field, enter a unique identifier, such as RUNHOURS . In the Description field, enter Operating Run Hours . In the Meter Type field, select CONTINUOUS , GAUGE , or CHARACTERISTIC . Configure type-specific settings: For Continuous meters : In the Reading Type field, select ACTUAL if workers log the total odometer reading, or DELTA if workers log only hours run during the shift. Enter the Unit of Measure , such as HOURS . For Gauge meters : Enter the Unit of Measure , such as CELSIUS or PSI . For Characteristic meters : In the Domain field, select the ALN domain containing allowable inspection values. Click Save . Step 2: Bundle meters into Meter Groups ¤ If your facility operates multiple machines that share the same set of meters , group them into a Meter Group. When you assign the group to an asset , all bundled meters attach automatically in a single step. Creating a meter group in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Meter Groups and open it. Click New Meter Group . In the Meter Group field, enter an identifier, such as ROTATING_PUMP . In the Description field, enter Rotating Pump Standard Meter Package . Check Apply New Meters Where Group Is Used? so that any future meters added to this group cascade to existing assets automatically. In the Meters in Meter Group table, click New Row to add individual meters : In the Meter field, select RUNHOURS . In the Sequence field, enter 10 . Click New Row , select VIB_VELOCITY , and enter 20 . Click New Row , select OIL_COND , and enter 30 . Click Save . 💡 Tip: Order meters by inspection sequence ¤ Use the Sequence field in Meter Groups to arrange meters in the order a technician reads physical gauges on the machine. This layout matches field data entry on mobile devices and eliminates scrolling. Step 3: Attach meters to assets ¤ Once meters and meter groups exist, attach them to equipment records on the Meters tab in the Assets application. Configuring an asset meter in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Assets and open it. Open the target equipment record, such as Filler FL-02 . Open the Meters tab. If attaching a group: In the Meter Group field, select ROTATING_PUMP . All bundled meters populate the table. If attaching a single meter : In the Meters table, click New Row and select the meter . For Continuous meters , configure calculation parameters in the details section: In the Average Calculation Method field, select STATIC to manually set daily consumption, or select ALL to let the system calculate rolling daily usage from entered readings. In the Average Units / Day field, enter the expected daily run rate, such as 16.0 hours per day. In the Rollover Point field, enter the physical dial limit, such as 999999 . Click Save . Figure 2 illustrates the continuous meter projection workflow across five stages: Attach meter to asset : assign the continuous meter to the equipment record. Configure daily average : establish the expected daily operating rate, such as 16 hours per day. Log meter reading : enter cumulative runtime observations, such as 1,200 operating hours. Link to PM schedule : define maintenance trigger intervals, such as every 500 runtime hours. Project due date : background processes calculate when thresholds will be reached and forecast work order generation. Figure 2: Continuous meter setup and automated preventive maintenance projection Step 4: Record and manage meter readings ¤ Technicians enter readings during daily inspections, on work orders , or directly in the Assets application. Entering a meter reading ¤ In the Assets application, open the equipment record. In the Select Action menu, click Enter Meter Readings . In the New Reading field for each active meter , enter the observed value. If a continuous meter hardware dial rolled over past its limit, check the Rollover box to allow a lower numeric entry. Click OK . Resetting or replacing broken meters ¤ If a physical gauge or runtime meter fails and is replaced with a new unit: Open the equipment record in the Assets application. In the Select Action menu, click Reset/Replace Meters . Select the continuous meter row. In the Last Reading field, enter the starting value on the replacement meter . If resetting overhaul counters, update Since Last Overhaul or Since Last Repair to zero. Click OK . Common meter setup pitfalls ¤ Avoid these common configuration errors that disrupt automated maintenance: Missing Average Units per Day: If this field is zero or blank on a continuous meter , background cron tasks cannot project future maintenance dates, and PM work orders will fail to generate ahead of time. Using Continuous type for fluctuating values: Never select Continuous for temperatures or pressure levels. If a temperature drops from 40 to 35 degrees, the system treats the drop as an error or rollover. Use Gauge instead. Forgetting the Rollover point: Leaving the rollover limit blank causes the system to reject readings when mechanical dials cycle from 999999 back to 0. Meter setup verification checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm your meters are configured properly. Table 2: Meter setup verification checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Proper meter type Continuous meters are used for cumulative run hours; Gauge meters are used for fluctuating levels [ ] ALN domains on characteristics Characteristic meters have an active ALN domain linked for picklist selections [ ] Daily run rate configured All continuous asset meters have a positive Average Units / Day value populated [ ] Rollover point defined Mechanical meters have their hardware maximum rollover value specified [ ] Meter group cascade toggle Meter groups have the auto-apply toggle checked to simplify future fleet updates [ ] Condition monitoring links Gauge meters on critical equipment are linked to active measurement points Related topics ¤ How do I detect issues early? docs.text: What are ticket templates? ¤ A ticket template is a saved set of values that fills in a service request for you. Use one for requests that come up often, so people do not type the same details each time. When you apply a ticket template to a service request, the system fills in the fields that the template defines. It can also add the activities that the work needs. Looking to verify a ticket template setup right away? Skip to ticket template verification checklist ↓ Each ticket template has a class that sets the type of ticket it applies to. The three classes are service request, problem, and incident. [SME confirmation required: Confirm whether Select has a Tickets application.] 💡 Tips for success ¤ Change the status of a new template to ACTIVE. Other people cannot apply a template until it is active. Create one template for each common request, such as a leaking pipe or a spill on the floor. A narrow template fills in more fields correctly than a general one. Add a job plan to a template when the same steps always follow the request. You reuse the steps instead of listing them again. Duplicate a template to make a similar one. The copy gets a new ID and starts in draft status . Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Ticket template terms ¤ Term What it means Ticket template A saved set of values that fills in fields on a service request Class The type of record that the template can be applied to. The template class must match the class of the record Status Controls whether other people can apply the template. Only ACTIVE templates can be applied Site Optional. Limits which organizations see the template in their list Activity A step of work that the system creates when the template is applied Job plan An existing set of steps that you can add to a template instead of listing activities one by one How do I find the Ticket Templates application? ¤ Use the Find navigation item field at the top of the menu and search for Ticket Templates. What does a ticket template fill in? ¤ When someone applies a template to a service request, the system puts the values from the template into the fields on the request. For example, with a template for a home VPN request, the system categorizes the request, sets the internal priority, and supplies other predefined values. A template can also include: A classification, at the template level or for an individual activity. A list of activities, in a set order. An existing job plan , instead of or as well as activities. [SME confirmation required: Confirm which fields, classifications, and activities a ticket template can set in Select.] How do ticket templates work with service requests? ¤ Select includes some ticket templates. Service request categories use them. When a requester picks a category, the template for that category can ask questions that fit it, such as whether there is a leak or a spill. A category that does not need questions can ask for a general summary of the request. [SME confirmation required: Confirm how service request categories use ticket templates in Select, how the questions and answers are defined, and which templates are included.] When can someone apply a ticket template? ¤ Someone can apply a template to a service request when: The template status is ACTIVE. The template class matches the class of the service request. The template is in the list for the organization of the request. A template with a site is listed for the organizations of that site . A template with no organization is listed for all organizations. A new or duplicated template starts in draft status . Change the status to ACTIVE before other people can use the template. A closed template can no longer have its classification changed. Table 2: Ticket template statuses ¤ Status What it allows DRAFT Use this status while you create or finalize the template. When you move the template out of draft, you cannot set it back to draft ACTIVE Other people can apply the template to a ticket INACTIVE Other people cannot apply the template. Use it when you do not want people to use the template, when you are not using it now, or when you want to keep it for your records Use the Change Status action to move a template between statuses. What happens when activities are added? ¤ When you apply a template that has activities, the system creates a child activity work order for each activity. If the template has a job plan , the system creates one more child activity work order based on that job plan . A job plan must have the status ACTIVE before you can add it to a template. Example: A request for a new starter ¤ Your plant needs a template for a new employee. You create a template called New Employee and add four activities in order. Table 3: Activities in the New Employee template ¤ Sequence Description 10 Create a security badge 20 Create IT accounts 30 Issue PC 40 Issue cell phone When someone applies the template to a service request, the system creates one activity for each row. If a job plan already contains these four steps, you can add that single job plan instead.
