docs.text: How do I fix import errors? ¤ Import errors can occur with locations or assets . This guide helps you troubleshoot and fix common import problems. Quick navigation ¤ Jump to the section you need: Location import errors Location hierarchy errors Location referenced data errors Asset import errors Asset hierarchy errors Asset referenced data errors Common issues across all import types Date and CSV formatting errors Location import errors ¤ Location imports are error-prone because of parent-child relationships and hierarchies. Location hierarchy errors ¤ Hierarchy imports require careful attention to parent-child relationships. Parent locations not created first ¤ Child locations can't be created if their parent doesn't exist yet. Example : You can't create "Ice Cream Plant A > Production Building > Filling Line 2" if "Ice Cream Plant A" and "Production Building" don't exist. What to do : Import locations in order: Top-level locations first : load facilities with no parent, such as Ice cream main plant . Second-level locations next : load buildings that reference the top-level plant, such as Production building . Lowest-level locations last : load rooms that reference the building, such as Filling line room . Figure 1 contrasts the correct top-down import sequence with a missing-parent validation error: Correct top-down load sequence : top-level location Ice cream main plant loads first with no parent, followed by second-level location Production building referencing the plant, followed by lower-level location Filling line room referencing the building. Hierarchy import error condition : attempting to import child record Filling line room before its parent Production building exists causes the data loader to reject the child record with a validation failure. To fix this, import Production building first, then re-import Filling line room . Figure 1: Location hierarchy import sequence and parent validation Incorrect object structure ¤ Location hierarchies require specific object structure in the import file. What to do : Use the system's location hierarchy template or export an existing hierarchy to see the correct format. Incorrect hierarchy relationships ¤ Parent-child relationships must be defined correctly in the import file. What to check : Parent location IDs are correct Hierarchy levels are properly defined System location references are valid What to do : Verify all parent locations exist before importing child locations . Import hierarchies sequentially Hierarchies require sequential loading from the top down. Import parent locations first, then their children. Location referenced data does not exist ¤ Location imports fail when they reference supporting records that don't exist in the system. What to check : GL account exists and is valid Service address is defined Calendar and shift are configured Failure class is set up Bill-to or ship-to address for the site is correct Classification or specification is available What to do : Create or correct the referenced record, or update the import file to use an existing value Make sure values in the import file match system values exactly, which are case-sensitive Verify spelling and IDs are correct 💡 Tips for successful location imports ¤ Import hierarchies in order : Parents before children Verify referenced data : Check that supporting records exist Start with a template : Export existing records to see correct format Validate data first : Check all values against system data Use text format : Prevent Excel from corrupting data Test with small batches : Verify format before importing thousands of records Asset import errors ¤ Asset imports fail due to object structure , data issues, or missing referenced records. Common asset import problems and solutions ¤ Table 1: Common asset import problems and solutions ¤ Problem What happens Solution Parent doesn't exist Child asset fails Import parents first Excel corrupts IDs Leading zeros removed Format as text in Excel Missing required fields Record skipped Validate all required fields Invalid status codes Import fails Use valid status values File too large Timeout or failure Break into smaller batches Asset hierarchy errors ¤ If using parent-child asset relationships, hierarchy errors can cause import failures. What to check : Parent asset exists before importing child assets Parent asset ID is correct in the import file Parent asset exists at the expected site and location What to do : Import parent assets before child assets or subassemblies Verify that each child asset references the correct parent asset Confirm the parent asset location matches expectations Asset referenced data does not exist ¤ Asset imports fail when they reference supporting records that don't exist in the system. What to check : GL account exists and is valid Service address is defined Calendar and shift are configured Failure class is set up Rotating item is created, if applicable Vendor or manufacturer exists Type value is valid Classification or specification is available What to do : Verify that referenced records exist in the system Correct spelling, IDs, and values in the import file Create missing referenced records before importing assets Revalidate the file before importing again 💡 Tips for successful asset imports ¤ Verify referenced data : Check that supporting records exist Start with a template : Export existing records to see correct format Validate data first : Check all values against system data Use text format : Prevent Excel from corrupting data Test with small batches : Verify format before importing thousands of records Common causes of asset import failures ¤ Wrong object structure ¤ The import file must match the expected object structure exactly. What to check : File structure matches ASSET object All required fields are included Field names are correct What to do : Use a template or export an existing asset to see the correct structure. Missing mandatory fields ¤ Assets have required fields that must be populated. Common required fields : Asset ID Description Site Status What to do : Review the import file to ensure all mandatory fields have values. Data errors in file ¤ Problems with the data itself cause import failures. Common data errors : Invalid status codes Non-existent site references Incorrect data types, such as text in number fields Invalid dates What to do : Validate data against system values before importing. Table 2: Common data import error messages and solutions ¤ Error message or symptom Cause Corrective action Parent record not found Child location or asset is listed before its parent record Sort spreadsheet rows top-down so parent records load before child records Invalid site identifier SITEID column is blank or contains a site code that does not exist Verify the exact SITEID code in the Organizations application Leading zero truncated Spreadsheet software converted numerical ID columns to numbers Format ID columns as Text before populating data or editing CSV files Invalid status code Status column uses unapproved status values or non-standard synonyms Use valid initial statuses such as NOT READY , OPERATING , or DRAFT Referenced record does not exist Supporting failure class, craft , or GL account is missing Create the supporting record in its respective application first Why are only some asset records imported? ¤ Partial imports happen when some records pass validation and others don't. Import limits are exceeded : Some systems have limits on: Number of records per import File size Processing time What to do : Break large imports into smaller batches of 1,000 to 5,000 records at a time. Errors stop processing mid-file : If a critical error occurs, the import might stop processing remaining records. What to do : Review error logs to identify where processing stopped, fix the error, and re-import remaining records. Validation failures block individual records : Each record is validated independently. Invalid records are skipped while valid ones are imported. What to do : Review the error file, fix failed records, and import them separately. Common issues across all import types ¤ Date values are invalid or reformatted ¤ Date formatting is a common source of import errors across all record types. Common causes : Excel changed the date format automatically The file uses mixed date formats, such as MM/DD/YYYY and DD/MM/YYYY The date format is ambiguous, such as 01/02/2026 Date values do not match the expected import format What to do : Format date columns as text in Excel before entering values Use one consistent date format throughout the file Re-export or use a template to confirm the expected format Test a small import that includes date values before importing the full file Excel formatting corrupts data ¤ Excel can corrupt data in several ways: Dates : Converts text to dates, such as converting 01-02 to Jan 2 IDs : Removes leading zeros, such as converting 001 to 1 Long numbers : Converts long numbers to scientific notation What to do : Format all columns as text in Excel before entering data, or use a plain text editor to create the CSV. Lack of pre-validation leads to late errors ¤ Without validation, errors aren't discovered until after processing starts. What to do : Always use the preview/validation function before committing the import. Parent-child relationships missing or loaded in wrong order ¤ Importing child records before parents causes failures. What to do : Sort your import file so parent records come before child records. Why shouldn't I load very large datasets in a single file? ¤ Bulk imports have constraints when loading very large volumes in a single batch. Constraints ¤ UI session timeouts : Long-running imports can time out in the web interface. Not designed for massive single-file batches : CSV imports work best with manageable batch sizes, typically under 5,000 records per file. Better suited for smaller datasets : For large imports, consider: Breaking into smaller batches of under 5,000 records Loading parent records before child records in separate files Using Data Management to monitor and track import status What happens next? ¤ To resolve import failures: Review error logs and error file Fix data issues in source file Ensure parent records exist for hierarchies Verify referenced data exists Preview/validate before importing Process the corrected import Verify records were created successfully Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Verify the system is working ¤ Once your data is successfully loaded, track work orders , costs, and equipment health across your facility. What metrics matter? Related skills ¤ What is the correct load order? : Review dependencies and ensure parent records exist before children. How do I plan my location hierarchy? : Map physical places and prevent orphan records. How do I plan my asset hierarchy? : Structure equipment packages and avoid over-assetization. How do I get data into the system? : Return to Data Management to re-import corrected rows. Related topics ¤ Which object structure do I use for each data type? How do I prepare data for import? How do I standardize data? What is an asset ? docs.text: How do I simplify workflows? ¤ Complex maintenance workflows with unnecessary approval stages, redundant data entry, and cluttered application screens create bottlenecks that delay repairs. When a process requires ten clicks where three would suffice, staff bypass the system or delay administrative handoffs. Simplifying workflows involves matching user roles to purpose-built apps, configuring default profile values, automating routine notifications, and removing approval hurdles for low-risk work. Looking to verify workflow simplification right away? Skip to workflow simplification checklist ↓ Core strategies for workflow simplification ¤ To streamline maintenance operations across your plant, focus on four key areas: Role-based routing: Direct field technicians and inventory clerks to streamlined role-based apps while reserving comprehensive desktop applications for planners and system administrators. Default profile values: Configure user defaults for site and storeroom so staff do not manually populate repetitive fields on every transaction. Automated notifications: Use Communication Templates to alert stakeholders automatically when work orders change status . Fast-track approvals: Allow routine preventive maintenance and minor repairs below set financial thresholds to approve automatically upon creation. Table 1: Workflow simplification opportunities across operational areas ¤ Operational area Common complexity bottleneck Simplified approach Work execution Technicians opening multi-tab desktop forms on mobile devices Use the Technician role-based app for fast card-based labor and material logging Storeroom issues Storeroom clerks navigating full inventory master records for daily counter issues Use the Issues and Transfers role-based app for rapid barcode scanning and item checkout Material requests Field staff waiting for manual supervisor approvals on standard consumables Pre-approve stocked gasket and lubricant requests attached to active Job Plans Status updates Senders phoning maintenance planners to check repair progress Trigger automated email notifications via Communication Templates at status changes Matching roles to the right applications ¤ Maximo Application Suite Select provides both comprehensive desktop applications and focused role-based apps. Routing users to the appropriate tool reduces training overhead and accelerates data entry. Table 2: Application routing matrix by operational role ¤ Operational role Recommended role-based app Primary desktop application Key daily responsibilities Field Technician Technician app None required for daily tasks View assigned work orders , record meter readings, log labor time, complete job steps Quality Inspector Inspections app None required for daily tasks Complete safety, hygiene, and environmental condition check sheets Inventory Clerk Issues and Transfers app, Inventory Counting app Inventory , Count Books Issue parts at the counter, transfer stock between storerooms, conduct cycle counts Maintenance Planner Work orders Job Plans, PM, Routes Build multi-step maintenance plans, schedule recurring PMs, coordinate craft routes Reliability Engineer Asset Manager Assets , Condition Monitoring, Failure Codes Manage asset registries, configure upper and lower meter limits, analyze failure trends Figure 1: Simplified work order routing and execution workflow As shown in Figure 1, a simplified routing model processes maintenance work across four distinct stages: Work ingestion : The system or a requester generates a work order . Triage and approval routing : Work splits according to urgency: Emergency and critical work : Routes to the supervisor queue for direct supervisor review. Routine PM and minor repairs : Auto-approves to bypass administrative delays and routes directly to craft assignment. Execution : Both streams converge in the Technician app, where technicians view assigned work orders and execute tasks in the field. Completion : Technicians log labor hours, parts, and notes in the mobile interface, automatically triggering completion notifications to stakeholders. Configuring user profile defaults ¤ When technicians, supervisors, or storeroom clerks create records, having the system auto-populate their home Site and default Storeroom eliminates repetitive keystrokes. Setting default Insert Site in the desktop application ¤ In the navigation bar, click the Profile icon in the upper right header and select Default Information . In the Insert Site field, select your active plant site , such as PLANT01 . In the Default Storeroom field, select your primary physical warehouse, such as CENTRAL . Click OK to save your profile preferences. Future transactions, including work orders and inventory issues, will automatically default to these locations . 💡 Tip: Standardize defaults across security groups ¤ Rather than asking every technician to configure profile defaults individually, system administrators can apply default site and storeroom settings at the security group level during initial user onboarding. Automating status notifications ¤ Instead of requiring maintenance planners to send manual emails to production managers when equipment repairs finish, set up automated email notifications using Communication Templates. Creating an automated notification template ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Communication Templates and open it. Click New Communication Template . In the Template field, enter an identifier, such as WO_COMPLETED_NOTIFY . In the Applies to field, enter WORKORDER . docs.text: Complex maintenance workflows with unnecessary approval stages, redundant data entry, and cluttered application screens create bottlenecks that delay repairs. When a process requires ten clicks where three would suffice, staff bypass the system or delay administrative handoffs. Simplifying workflows involves matching user roles to purpose-built apps, configuring default profile values, automating routine notifications, and removing approval hurdles for low-risk work. Looking to verify workflow simplification right away? Skip to workflow simplification checklist ↓
docs.title: How do I simplify workflows?

docs.text: To streamline maintenance operations across your plant, focus on four key areas: Role-based routing: Direct field technicians and inventory clerks to streamlined role-based apps while reserving comprehensive desktop applications for planners and system administrators. Default profile values: Configure user defaults for site and storeroom so staff do not manually populate repetitive fields on every transaction. Automated notifications: Use Communication Templates to alert stakeholders automatically when work orders change status . Fast-track approvals: Allow routine preventive maintenance and minor repairs below set financial thresholds to approve automatically upon creation.

docs.text: Why aren't technicians using the system? ¤ Low system adoption by maintenance technicians leads to delayed work order reporting, incomplete labor tracking, and missing failure records. When technicians avoid logging into the system, organizations revert to informal paper notes, spreadsheet logs, and verbal handoffs, which makes maintenance tracking unreliable. Technicians generally bypass software not out of reluctance, but because of workflow friction: excessive required fields, confusing desktop interfaces on mobile tablets, slow network synchronization in shielded plant areas, or missing job instructions. Looking to verify field adoption readiness right away? Skip to technician adoption checklist ↓ Identifying adoption friction points ¤ To resolve low adoption, diagnose where field workers encounter resistance in their daily maintenance routine. Table 1: Common adoption barriers and operational remedies ¤ Observed symptom Root cause Corrective action End of shift batch logging Work entry forms require too many clicks during active work Deploy the Technician role-based app with streamlined card views instead of desktop forms Data loss complaints in shielded areas Wireless drops in refrigerated or concrete structures Enable offline data caching in Mobile Properties so data queues locally and syncs automatically Vague work descriptions Free text fields with no structured checklist guidance Attach standardized Job Plans with numbered task steps to preventive maintenance records Incomplete parts recording Finding storeroom item numbers is slow or difficult Pre-load expected materials on job plans so technicians select staged items with a single tap Work orders left in progress Technicians forget to record stop times or final failure codes Set up operational dashboard Work Queue cards that highlight open assignments directly to the team Figure 1: Streamlined mobile workflow overcoming adoption barriers As shown in Figure 1, the streamlined mobile pathway overcomes adoption barriers across four connected elements: Step 1: Start shift : The technician begins their workday and opens the mobile interface. Step 2: Mobile card views : Concise card views replace complex desktop forms with touch-friendly assignment cards. Offline data caching : When technicians work in shielded environments like the Cold Storage Room, the mobile app queues all transactions locally and syncs automatically upon returning to wireless network coverage. Pre-loaded job steps : Structured task execution provides single-tap step check-offs and straightforward failure code selection directly on the device. Streamlining the user experience ¤ Complex desktop screens designed for maintenance planners and database administrators create frustration when presented to field technicians wearing gloves or working on small screens. Switching from desktop forms to the Technician app ¤ The dedicated Technician role-based app presents a clean card layout tailored to field execution. Technicians see assigned work orders , view attached equipment manuals, record meter readings, and log labor hours with minimal taps. 💡 Tip: Keep required fields to an absolute minimum ¤ Audit the mandatory fields required to complete a work order . Every additional mandatory field increases the temptation for technicians to bypass the system or enter dummy placeholder data. Only enforce fields that directly drive regulatory compliance, failure tracking, or inventory reconciliation. Optimizing offline and mobile connectivity ¤ In facilities like the Ice Cream Main Plant, technicians frequently work in heavily insulated areas such as the Cold Storage Room where cellular and WiFi signals cannot penetrate. If the mobile app requires constant connectivity, technicians abandon the device. Configuring offline caching ensures technicians can view job instructions, complete inspection checklists, and record used parts without an active network connection. The device stores all transactions locally and synchronizes with the server once the technician re-enters network coverage. Configuring sync parameters in Mobile Properties ¤ Adjust synchronization settings in the desktop application to prevent timeout errors and ensure responsive background syncing. In the Find navigation item field, search for Mobile Properties and open it. In the Property Name filter, search for sync timeout and batch size properties. Select the property governing offline transaction batching, such as si.offline.download.batchsize . Update the Global Value to an appropriate batch limit, such as 50 records, to reduce synchronization latency over intermittent wireless connections. In the Select Action menu, click Save Properties . Click Live Refresh to apply the updated properties without restarting system services. Engaging technicians through better job preparation ¤ Technicians actively embrace the system when it helps them complete repairs faster rather than acting as a digital time clock. When a work order opens with exact safety procedures, equipment location details, and pre-staged parts lists, the software becomes an indispensable tool. Table 2: Elements of high-value work order preparation ¤ Preparation element Where configured Direct technician benefit Equipment location tags Location / Service Address Shows exact plant room and floor coordinates, eliminating wasted travel time Safety hazard warnings Job Plans Alerts the technician to lockout and tagout requirements before opening panels Pre-specified spare parts Job Plans Lists required replacement seals and gaskets with storeroom bin numbers Technical schematics Asset attachments Provides instant access to wiring diagrams and parts lists directly on mobile devices Technician adoption checklist ¤ Use this checklist to evaluate whether your software setup supports smooth field adoption. docs.text: Why does my data look wrong? ¤ When dashboard reports display unexpected figures, asset counts look inflated, inventory balances show negative numbers, or assets seem disconnected from their physical rooms, data anomalies are almost always the cause. Inaccurate data undermines trust in your maintenance system and distorts performance metrics. In Maximo Application Suite Select, identifying the symptom and tracing it to the underlying configuration allows administrators to correct existing records and prevent recurring errors. Looking to verify data integrity right away? Skip to data quality verification checklist ↓ 💡 Tips for success ¤ Check for duplicate asset records before modifying maintenance history. Duplicates frequently occur when identical machines are imported twice with slightly different naming conventions. Verify parent location links when assets do not appear in hierarchy drill-downs. An operating location without a parent is treated as an isolated top-level site record. Reconcile physical inventory with Count Books when stock balances show negative numbers. Issuing parts before recording purchase receipts creates temporary negative balance discrepancies. Establish standardized classification attributes so that all assets in the same category display consistent technical specifications. Diagnosing common data anomalies ¤ Review this diagnostic guide to match your observed symptom with its root cause and corrective action. Table 1: Common data quality symptoms and corrective actions ¤ Observed symptom Primary root cause Where to investigate Corrective action Asset count is doubled or inflated Duplicate asset records created during manual entry or CSV imports Assets Decommission or merge duplicate asset records, redirecting work history to the primary asset Asset missing from location hierarchy Location record has no parent location specified Location Open the location record and populate the Parent Location field Inventory balance is negative Parts were issued from the storeroom before receipt transactions were processed Inventory Perform a physical count in Count Books and adjust the balance to match physical reality Technical attributes are missing on asset Asset is not linked to a classification structure Classifications Assign the correct classification class to the asset on the Specifications tab Work order shows zero labor cost Assigned labor record has no craft hourly rate defined Labor Open the Labor record and define standard hourly billing rates for the craft Fixing orphan locations and broken hierarchies ¤ When a technician or supervisor cannot locate equipment in the hierarchy tree, the location record is usually missing its parent link. How to reconnect an orphan location ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Location and open it. Search for the affected location , such as Packaging zone . In the Location details view, check the Parent field. If the field is empty, click the detail menu next to Parent and select the parent area, such as Production building . Open the Location Hierarchy tab to verify that the location now sits under the correct plant building. Click Save Location . Resolving duplicate asset records ¤ Duplicate assets distort maintenance histories by splitting work orders and costs across multiple records for the same physical machine. How to remediate duplicate assets ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Assets and open it. Filter by asset description or serial number to identify the duplicate records, such as MTR-101 and MTR-DRIVE-01 . Determine which record holds the primary maintenance history and active preventive maintenance schedule. For the redundant duplicate record: Check for open work orders on the Work tab and reassign them to the primary asset . Update the status of the redundant asset to DECOMMISSIONED or INACTIVE . Add a cross-reference note in the long description directing users to the primary asset ID. Click Save Asset . Correcting inventory balance discrepancies ¤ Negative balances occur when emergency repairs consume parts faster than receiving paperwork is entered. How to reconcile stock balances ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Inventory and open it. Find the item in the target storeroom, such as Main storeroom . In the Inventory Balances table, enter the actual physical count verified on the shelf. Compare the Current Balance with the Physical Count . Save the record, then check that the Reconciled? checkbox is selected on the balance row. Real-world example: Resolving data errors at the ice cream plant ¤ Consider how the system administrator corrected data anomalies affecting the cold storage room and filler FL-02 drive motor. Scenario: Broken reporting metrics ¤ Symptom 1: The supervisor reported that the cold storage room did not appear on the plant hierarchy navigation card. Fix: The administrator opened the Location application, found Cold storage room , and added Ice cream main plant into the Parent field. The room immediately appeared in the site drilldown. Symptom 2: The motor for filler FL-02 showed zero historical maintenance costs despite multiple recent repairs. Fix: The administrator opened the Labor application and found that the mechanical technician labor record lacked an hourly rate on craft MECH-01 . Adding the standard rate immediately corrected labor cost calculations on all future work orders . docs.text: How do I make data reliable? ¤ Reliable data enables accurate maintenance forecasting, automated work order generation, and dependable inventory planning. When data entries contain typos, inconsistent naming conventions, or missing attributes, reports produce misleading results and scheduled maintenance fails to trigger. To make operational data reliable across your organization, replace free text entry with controlled vocabularies, enforce mandatory fields, structure asset classifications, and conduct routine data health audits. Looking to verify data reliability right away? Skip to data reliability checklist ↓ Core principles of reliable data ¤ Reliable maintenance data rests on four structural pillars: Controlled vocabularies: Restrict data entry to defined picklists using the Domains application instead of free-form text fields. Standardized hierarchies: Organize assets , locations , and failure records into structured parent and child relationships. Consistent attribute capture: Apply classifications to categorize equipment specifications, such as motor horsepower or refrigeration refrigerant types. Regular validation audits: Review data exceptions on a recurring schedule to catch orphaned records, duplicate entries, or missing rates before they impact reporting. Table 1: Data standardization mechanisms in Maximo Application Suite Select ¤ Standardization mechanism Application Operational purpose Example implementation ALN domains Domains Provides a fixed list of text values for selection fields Standard work order priority reasons or inspection condition grades Synonym domains Domains Extends internal system statuses with custom business sub-statuses Adding WAITING_PERMIT under internal status WAPPR Numeric and range domains Domains Enforces numeric validation and boundary limits Restricting allowable temperature entries between -30 and 50 degrees Celsius Classifications Classifications Applies uniform attribute templates across equipment families Requiring voltage, frame size, and RPM attributes on all drive motors Failure hierarchies Failure Codes Standardizes failure reporting across Problem, Cause, and Remedy tiers Linking mechanical seal leak failure paths to Filler FL-02 Replacing free text with Domains ¤ Free text entry is the primary cause of data degradation in maintenance management systems. When technicians and planners type freehand notes into categorisation fields, slight variations such as Pump Leak , PMP LK , and Leaking pump prevent automated reporting from aggregating failure history. ALN domains for standard picklists ¤ ALN alphanumeric domains present users with a controlled drop-down list. By attaching ALN domains to user-defined fields, you eliminate spelling discrepancies and enable precise filtering. Creating an ALN domain in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Domains and open it. Click Add New Domain and select Add New ALN Domain . In the Domain field, enter a unique identifier, such as IC_FAIL_REASON . In the Description field, enter a descriptive title, such as Ice Cream Plant Failure Reason Codes . In the ALN Values table, click New Row to add each allowable option: In the Value field, enter the code, such as BEARING_WEAR . In the Description field, enter the full label, such as Mechanical bearing wear or fatigue . Repeat step 5 for all required values. Click OK , then click Save . Synonym domains for status workflows ¤ Synonym domains allow organizations to define business-specific terms that map directly to core system statuses. The internal system logic operates on the base status , while users interact with the familiar synonym value. For example, if the Ice Cream plant requires a specific sub-state for work orders awaiting food safety sign-off before work starts, add a synonym value WFOODSAFE mapped to the system base status Waiting on Approval, WAPPR . Figure 1: Synonym domain mapping to system base status As shown in Figure 1, the core system base status WAPPR branches into multiple user-facing display statuses: Standard Base Status : Waiting on Approval, WAPPR , for general maintenance work orders . Synonym Value WFOODSAFE : Waiting on Food Safety Sign-off for hygiene and sanitation hold points. Synonym Value WENVPERMIT : Waiting on Environmental Permit for environmental compliance hold points. 💡 Tip: Keep domain lists concise and mutually exclusive ¤ Do not overload domains with dozens of overlapping choices. If a picklist exceeds fifteen options, users often pick the first available entry rather than scrolling to find the correct code. Review domain lists quarterly and deactivate obsolete values. Enforcing standardized classifications ¤ Classifications ensure that all assets of the same type store identical technical specifications. Without classifications, one technician records motor power in kilowatts in the description field, while another records horsepower in the remarks section. In the Classifications application, build an equipment hierarchy: Figure 2: Hierarchical asset classification and specification structure As shown in Figure 2, asset classifications organize specifications down a four-level hierarchy: Level 1 ( PRODUCTION ) : Encompasses all plant machinery. Level 2 ( ROTATING ) : Groups dynamic equipment families. Level 3 ( MOTORS ) : Defines electric drive units. Level 4 (Attributes) : Captures standardized technical specifications, including Horsepower or Kilowatts, Voltage or Phase, NEMA Frame, Rated RPM, and Bearing Type. When you classify the drive motor for Filler FL-02 under MOTORS , Maximo Application Suite Select prompts for each defined attribute. This structured capture enables engineers to search for all 50 HP motors across the Ice Cream Main Plant when planning standardized spares. docs.title: Make data reliable

docs.text: Reliable data enables accurate maintenance forecasting, automated work order generation, and dependable inventory planning. When data entries contain typos, inconsistent naming conventions, or missing attributes, reports produce misleading results and scheduled maintenance fails to trigger. To make operational data reliable across your organization, replace free text entry with controlled vocabularies, enforce mandatory fields, structure asset classifications, and conduct routine data health audits. Looking to verify data reliability right away? Skip to data reliability checklist ↓
docs.title: How do I make data reliable?

docs.text: Reliable maintenance data rests on four structural pillars: Controlled vocabularies: Restrict data entry to defined picklists using the Domains application instead of free-form text fields. Standardized hierarchies: Organize assets , locations , and failure records into structured parent and child relationships. Consistent attribute capture: Apply classifications to categorize equipment specifications, such as motor horsepower or refrigeration refrigerant types. Regular validation audits: Review data exceptions on a recurring schedule to catch orphaned records, duplicate entries, or missing rates before they impact reporting.

In the Description field, enter the full label, such as Mechanical bearing wear or fatigue . Repeat step 5 for all required values. Click OK , then click Save .

docs.text: How do I improve completion rates? ¤ A low work order completion rate is a warning signal that operational friction is slowing down your maintenance team. When work orders linger for weeks in unapproved, waiting, or in progress statuses, the maintenance backlog inflates, overdue counts rise, and critical preventive maintenance gets missed. Improving completion rates requires identifying and eliminating the specific bottlenecks that prevent technicians from finishing jobs on time. In Maximo Application Suite Select, this means aligning material readiness, craft qualifications, job plan clarity, and status lifecycle discipline. Looking to verify completion workflows right away? Skip to work order completion checklist ↓ 💡 Tips for success ¤ Review work orders in Waiting on Material status daily. A work order should not be approved or scheduled until all required parts are verified in stock. Match work orders to technician crafts before assigning. Assigning an electrical repair to a general mechanic leads to delays, rework, and incomplete tasks. Attach standardized job plans to recurring work. Work orders with defined step-by-step tasks and estimated hours are completed 40% faster than vague single-line requests. Train technicians to complete work orders on mobile devices before leaving the job site . Delaying data entry until the end of the week creates administrative backlogs and inaccurate actual labor hours. The four major completion blockers ¤ When work orders stall, the cause usually falls into one of four operational categories. Table 1: Common completion blockers and solutions ¤ Blocker System symptom Operational root cause Remediation strategy Material availability Work order stuck in WMATL status Required spare parts are out of stock or not reserved in advance Use the Storerooms application to check balances and reserve parts before approving work Craft mismatch Long duration in INPRG status Technician lacks the specialized certification or tools for the task Check craft and skill requirements in Labor and match assignments accordingly Unclear scope Task marked incomplete or rejected Work order description lacks specific instructions or safety procedures Attach a standardized Job Plan with documented task steps and safety requirements Approval delay Accumulation of WAPPR records Supervisors lack a consolidated daily review routine Use the Work queues card on the supervisor Operational Dashboard to approve work in batches Managing the work order lifecycle ¤ Maintaining disciplined status progression prevents work orders from getting lost between shifts or departments. Table 2: Standard work order status lifecycle ¤ Status Code Meaning Who manages it Waiting on Approval WAPPR Work order created; pending review and resource verification Supervisor Approved APPR Work order approved; ready for scheduling and resource allocation Supervisor Waiting on Material WMATL Work approved but waiting for required inventory parts Inventory Clerk Waiting on Plant Condition WPCOND Work approved but requires equipment shutdown or line clearance Supervisor In Progress INPRG Technician is actively performing the physical work Technician Completed COMP Physical work finished; actual hours, materials, and notes recorded Technician Closed CLOSE Financial and operational review completed; record locked Administrator Pre-job staging: Eliminating parts delays ¤ The single largest cause of stalled work orders in manufacturing and facilities operations is the lack of replacement parts when the technician arrives at the asset . How to verify and reserve parts before work begins ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Work Orders and open it. Open the planned work order and open the Plans tab. Open the Materials subtab and verify that required parts and quantities are listed. Review the Direct Issue and Line Status indicators. If items show insufficient stock, update the status to WMATL and notify the inventory clerk. Once the inventory clerk confirms stock availability in the storeroom, update the status to APPR for assignment. Real-world example: Clearing stalled work on the filling line ¤ Consider how the maintenance supervisor at the ice cream main plant cleared a backlog of overdue work orders on filling line filler FL-02. Scenario: Stalled preventive maintenance ¤ The Problem: Three consecutive monthly PM work orders for filler FL-02 remained in INPRG for over four weeks. The overall plant completion rate had dropped to 62%. Diagnosis: The supervisor opened Operational Dashboard : Supervisor and reviewed the work orders . Two work orders were stalled because the sanitization seal kit was on backorder ( WMATL ). The third was stalled because the assigned technician was an apprentice mechanic who needed a certified electrician to complete the motor drive calibration task. Corrective Action: The supervisor reconfigured the job plan for filler FL-02 into two separate tasks: Task 10 for mechanical seal replacement, and Task 20 for electrical motor calibration. The supervisor worked with the inventory clerk to establish a dedicated kit item in Item Master for filler FL-02 monthly maintenance. The supervisor updated shift assignments so that mechanical and electrical tasks were assigned to the appropriate crafts simultaneously during the planned Tuesday sanitation shutdown. The Outcome: The backlog was cleared in a single shift, and monthly PM completion rates on the packaging line rose to 94%. Daily supervisor completion routine ¤ Supervisors who follow a consistent 15-minute daily triage routine maintain significantly higher completion rates across their teams. Table 3: Daily completion triage workflow ¤ Time Action Application Focus Shift start (10 min) Review WAPPR and WMATL queues Operational Dashboard Approve verified work and allocate to technicians based on craft availability Mid-shift (5 min) Check long-running INPRG records Work Orders Identify technicians who encounter unexpected blockers or scope changes Shift end (10 min) Review COMP work orders Work Orders Verify actual labor hours, materials used, and failure codes before closing Work order completion checklist ¤ Use this checklist to ensure that your organization maintains high work order completion rates. Table 4: Work order completion verification checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Daily queue review Supervisor checks the WAPPR work queue on the dashboard at the start of every shift [ ] Materials confirmed No work order is released to INPRG without confirmed parts availability in Storerooms [ ] Craft alignment Assigned labor craft matches the skill requirements listed on the job plan [ ] Mobile completion Technicians log labor actuals, materials used, and failure codes directly on mobile [ ] Status hygiene Work orders are advanced from COMP to CLOSE within standard accounting timeframes Continue building your skills ¤ Reduce unplanned asset downtime ¤ High completion rates on preventive maintenance directly reduce unscheduled breakdowns. docs.text: How do I reduce downtime ? ¤ Unplanned equipment downtime is one of the most costly disruptions in industrial and facilities operations. When critical machinery stops unexpectedly, production halts, maintenance costs surge, and emergency repairs replace planned work. Reducing downtime requires shifting your maintenance operation from reactive emergency response to proactive defect prevention. In Maximo Application Suite Select, this transformation rests on four core pillars: structured preventive maintenance , standardized failure reporting, condition monitoring, and critical spare parts availability. Looking to verify your downtime reduction program right away? Skip to downtime reduction checklist ↓ 💡 Tips for success ¤ Maintain a preventive maintenance compliance rate of 85% or higher. When PMs are deferred, equipment failure rates increase dramatically within 30 to 60 days. Implement structured failure codes with Problem, Cause, and Remedy levels. Without standardized failure data, reliability teams cannot identify repeat root causes. Report actual downtime hours on every corrective work order . Recording when the breakdown started and ended allows the system to calculate accurate Mean Time to Repair and Mean Time Between Failures. Ensure critical spare parts are linked directly to asset records on the Spare Parts tab. Technicians should never lose hours searching storerooms for routine wear components. The four pillars of downtime reduction ¤ World-class maintenance programs keep unplanned downtime below 10% of total operating hours. Maximo Application Suite Select supports this goal through four integrated capabilities. Table 1: Core capabilities for downtime reduction ¤ Capability What it does Operational impact Where configured Preventive Maintenance (PM) Generates recurring inspections and servicing before equipment degrades Prevents up to 70% of mechanical and electrical wear failures PM Condition Monitoring Triggers corrective work orders when meter readings breach action limits Detects impending failures days or weeks before catastrophic breakdown Condition Monitoring Failure Code Hierarchies Captures structured Problem, Cause, and Remedy data on work orders Reveals recurring defect trends across equipment classes Failure Codes Storeroom Reorder Points Automates reorder notifications when stock falls below safety levels Eliminates repair delays caused by missing replacement parts Storerooms Structuring failure codes to identify root causes ¤ When technicians record failure details in free-form notes, analyzing defect trends is difficult. Structured failure codes convert maintenance history into actionable reliability data. A failure hierarchy follows a three-level parent-child structure headed by a failure class: Failure Class: Identifies the broad asset type, such as PUMP or MOTOR . Problem: Describes the observed symptom, such as HIGH-TEMP or VIBRATION . Cause: Identifies why the problem occurred, such as BEARING-WEAR or LUBRICATION-LOSS . Remedy: Describes the corrective action taken, such as REPLACE-BEARING or GREASE-UNIT . Table 2: Example failure hierarchy for electric drive motors ¤ Level Code Description Operational meaning Failure class MTR-ELEC Electric Motor Top category assigned to all motor asset records Problem OVERHEAT Operating temperature above limit Observed symptom during production Cause FAN-BLOCK Cooling fan blocked with debris Root cause identified upon inspection Remedy CLEAN-FAN Cleaned fan cowl and housing Corrective action executed by technician Tracking asset downtime on work orders ¤ To measure whether downtime is decreasing, maintenance teams must record downtime accurately on corrective work orders . How to report downtime in the Work Orders application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Work Orders and open it. Open the completed corrective work order . Select Report Downtime from the common actions menu. Specify whether the downtime occurred during operational or non-operational production hours. In the Downtime Code field, select the reason code, such as BRKDWN for unscheduled breakdown. In the Start Date and End Date fields, enter the exact timestamps when the asset stopped and returned to service. Click OK to save the downtime record. Real-world example: Eliminating recurring downtime on Filler FL-02 ¤ Consider how the maintenance supervisor at the ice cream main plant used failure data to eliminate repeated stoppages on filling line filler FL-02. Scenario: Chronic packaging line stops ¤ The Problem: Filler FL-02 in the filling line room suffered four unscheduled stops over six weeks, totaling 18 hours of lost ice cream packaging time. Data Analysis: The supervisor reviewed KPI Viewer and filtered work orders by asset Filler FL-02 . The failure reporting tab showed that all four work orders shared the problem code JAM and cause code SEAL-LEAK . Root Cause: Product leakage from worn nozzle seals was contaminating the drive belt track, causing drive slip and safety stops. Corrective Action: The supervisor updated the preventive maintenance schedule for filler FL-02, changing the nozzle seal replacement interval from 90 days to 45 days. The supervisor set up a characteristic condition monitoring point to inspect seal integrity during weekly sanitization rounds. The inventory clerk increased the safety stock level for nozzle seal kits from 2 to 6 units in the main storeroom. The Outcome: Unscheduled downtime on filler FL-02 dropped to zero hours over the following quarter. Downtime reduction roadmap ¤ Follow this progressive roadmap to systematically reduce downtime across your facility. Table 3: Progressive steps to reduce equipment downtime ¤ Stage Focus area Key milestone Target metric Stage 1: Basic control Achieve 85%+ PM compliance All critical production assets have active PM schedules generated on time PM Compliance > 85% Stage 2: Failure tracking Enforce failure code entry Technicians select Problem, Cause, and Remedy on 100% of emergency work Failure Code Capture > 90% Stage 3: Parts alignment Secure critical spare parts All high-risk failure components have active reorder points in Storerooms Stock-Out Rate < 2% Stage 4: Early detection Implement condition monitoring Critical drives and compressors use gauge meters to detect early wear Reactive Work Ratio < 15% Downtime reduction checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm that your downtime reduction processes are operating effectively. Root Cause: Product leakage from worn nozzle seals was contaminating the drive belt track, causing drive slip and safety stops. Corrective Action: The supervisor updated the preventive maintenance schedule for filler FL-02, changing the nozzle seal replacement interval from 90 days to 45 days. The supervisor set up a characteristic condition monitoring point to inspect seal integrity during weekly sanitization rounds. The inventory clerk increased the safety stock level for nozzle seal kits from 2 to 6 units in the main storeroom. The Outcome: Unscheduled downtime on filler FL-02 dropped to zero hours over the following quarter.

docs.text: How do inspections work? ¤ An inspection is a set of questions that you answer about an asset or a location . Inspections use two apps: Inspection Forms . Use it to define the forms that inspections use. Inspections . Use it to conduct inspections and record the results. To open either app, use the Find navigation item field and search for its name. Inspections is also in IBM Maximo Mobile, so you can inspect an asset or location where it is. The app has the same name on the desktop and in IBM Maximo Mobile. [SME confirmation required: Confirm that the inspection behavior in this topic applies to MAS Select. The source is the Maximo Manage documentation. Confirm that Inspection Forms and Inspections are the app names and locations in Select.] How inspections fit together ¤ A form defines the questions for an inspection. When the form is activated, an inspection appears in the Inspections app. An inspector answers the questions and completes the inspection. The results are saved with the asset or location that was inspected. [SME confirmation required: Confirm how inspections are scheduled or generated from a form in Select, and where the results appear for the asset or location.] What you can do in Inspections ¤ Filter your inspections by pending, in progress, and completed. Conduct several inspections at the same time, as a batch. Create an unscheduled inspection when you find something that is not on your schedule, including for several assets or locations at once. Show only the required questions, or only the questions that you have not answered. Review your answers in a summary before you complete the inspection. View the results of completed inspections. Attach photos to an inspection. Create follow-up work from an inspection. The app saves your answers automatically as you go. docs.text: What apps are in IBM Maximo Mobile? ¤ IBM Maximo Mobile provides role-based applications on your mobile device or tablet. You can complete work orders , conduct inspections, manage storeroom inventory , approve work, review reported hours, and update asset and location records while in the field. The apps you see on your home screen depend on your role and the security groups assigned by your administrator. If an app you need is missing, contact your administrator. Note IBM Maximo Mobile is also used with IBM Maximo Manage. If you see references to Maximo Manage, you can ignore them. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Use the search bar or app tiles on your home screen to find the app you need. Work offline when you lose connectivity. Your updates save locally and sync automatically when your device reconnects. If an app is missing from your home screen, ask your administrator to verify your security group permissions. Work execution and supervisor apps ¤ Technician ¤ Use the Technician app to review and complete your assigned work orders . You can view work on a map, follow job plans , log labor , tools, and materials, report failure codes , attach photos, and record meter readings. To get started with completing work orders , see Technician: Complete your first work order . Inspections ¤ Use Inspections to complete inspection forms for assets and locations . You can answer required questions, record measurements, attach photos, and generate follow-up work orders . To learn more about how inspection forms and checklists operate, see How do inspections work? . Approvals ¤ Use Approvals to review, approve, and monitor work orders awaiting supervisor authorization. When notifications are enabled, you receive alerts on your device when a work order requires approval. To learn more about supervisor workflows, see Supervisor: Assign and track work . Service Requests ¤ Use Service Requests to report issues or log maintenance requests directly from your device, and to monitor the status of requests you submitted earlier. Inventory management apps ¤ Issues and Transfers ¤ Use Issues and Transfers to issue parts and tools to work orders , issue items without a reservation, and transfer stock between storerooms. To get started with issuing inventory , see Inventory clerk: Issue a part . Inventory Counting ¤ Use Inventory Counting to perform physical stock counts and cycle counts in storerooms using count books or ad hoc counts. To learn more about stock counts and count books, see What happens if stock is incorrect? . Material Request ¤ Use Material Request to request parts, tools, or services for a work order from the field, and to track previous requests. People and team apps ¤ Timesheet ¤ Use Timesheet to review your personal reported labor transactions. You can check labor entries recorded for today or earlier, including the associated work order , asset , location , and total hours. Crew Manager ¤ Use Crew Manager to manage work orders assigned to a crew . A crew leader or supervisor can start and stop timers for the entire crew , recording labor for all active crew members simultaneously. To set up crews , see How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? . Asset and location management apps ¤ Locations ¤ Use Locations to view, create, and update location records in the field. You can navigate location hierarchies, view locations on a map, and record location meter readings. To learn more about location structures, see How do I plan my location hierarchy? . Assets ¤ Use Assets , also known as Asset Manager, to look up equipment details, specifications, and meter readings, view asset locations on maps, and register new assets found in the field. To learn more about asset structures, see How do I plan my asset hierarchy? . Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Apps in IBM Maximo Mobile ¤ App Primary use Technician View and complete assigned work orders , report labor , materials, tools, and record meter readings. Inspections Conduct scheduled and unscheduled inspections, complete checklists, and log results. Approvals Review and approve work orders requiring supervisor sign-off. Service Requests Create service requests to report issues and track request status . Issues and Transfers Issue reserved or non-reserved parts to work orders and transfer items between storerooms. Inventory Counting Perform physical stock counts and cycle counts. Material Request Request parts, tools, or services for a work order from the field. Timesheet Review reported labor entries and hours. Crew Manager Track work and log collective labor hours for crew -assigned work orders . Locations Review location hierarchies, update location records, and log location meters . Assets Search equipment, view specifications and meters , and register new assets . To find an app on the desktop, use the Find navigation item field at the top of the menu and search for the app name. To return to the desktop applications after you open one of these apps on your computer, see How do I get back to the desktop applications? docs.text: What happens when I'm offline in IBM Maximo Mobile? ¤ IBM Maximo Mobile keeps working when your device loses its connection. The app stores your data on the device, so you can keep working and sync your changes later. How online and offline work ¤ Online: The app is connected to the server. It saves the data it retrieves to your device and keeps that data in sync with the server. You can also sync manually. Offline: The app is not connected to the server. It uses the data that is stored on your device. When the connection returns, the app syncs your changes automatically. When is my device offline? ¤ IBM Maximo Mobile treats your device as offline when any of these conditions apply: The device is in airplane mode. The network adapter of the device is turned off. The network bandwidth is low. The server cannot be reached from the device. Your sign-in session has expired. Signing in and staying signed in ¤ First sign-in: You need a network connection the first time you sign in. You use the same credentials that you use on the desktop. The app then creates a local data store on your device. Opening the app: Each time you open the app, it asks for your device's security credentials before it opens your local data. Session expiry: After your session expires, the app asks you to sign in again. If you do not sign in, you work offline until you do. By default, access expires after 30 minutes and the session can be renewed for up to 12 hours. Signing in again: To sign in at any time, select the cloud icon on the app screen. docs.text: What is an asset ? ¤ An asset is any piece of equipment, machinery, or infrastructure that your organization maintains. Assets are the physical things you work on. Examples of assets ¤ Production equipment : Filler FL-02, Conveyor CV-02, Labeler LB-01 Process equipment : Pumps, motors, compressors, heat exchangers, chillers Facilities : HVAC systems, refrigeration units, lighting systems Vehicles : Trucks, forklifts, pallet jacks Storage : Tanks, silos, cold storage units Why assets matter ¤ Track maintenance history for each piece of equipment Schedule preventive maintenance Monitor asset condition and performance Plan for replacements and upgrades Calculate total cost of ownership Asset hierarchy ¤ Figure 1: Sample asset hierarchy for an ice cream manufacturer An asset is a physical piece of equipment that you maintain. You can organize assets in a parent-child hierarchy to show how equipment connects and to track maintenance at the correct operational level. In Figure 1, the top-level system is the Filling line system, which contains three parent assets : Filler FL-02 : Contains child components Drive motor and Nozzle assembly. The Nozzle assembly breaks down further into Part 1: Nozzle body and Part 2: Shutoff valve. Conveyor CV-02 : Contains child components Belt and Sensor. Labeler LB-01 : Contains child components Printhead and Label sensor. Assets are installed in locations , which show where the equipment operates. Using asset hierarchies has many benefits: Understand how equipment is related Track maintenance for a complete system or a specific component See both what the equipment is and where it is installed Want to see how this connects to locations and work orders ? See How do locations , assets , and work orders work together? To plan your own hierarchy, see How do I plan my asset hierarchy? Naming assets ¤ ✓ Do Use a short alphanumeric asset number Write a clear, specific description Use a consistent description format Identify the parent asset when relevant ✗ Don't Don't use vague descriptions such as PUMP Don't overload the asset number with too much detail Example assets : Filler FL-02, Conveyor CV-02, Labeler LB-01. Example descriptions : Filler FL-02, cone filling station; Labeler LB-01, carton labeling station. Related topics ¤ What are the basic concepts? What is a work order ? What is a location ? How do locations , assets , and work orders work together? How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? How do I plan my asset hierarchy? How do I track asset history? docs.text: What is a location ? ¤ A location is a physical place where work is performed or assets are installed. Locations help you organize and find equipment. Types of locations ¤ Operating locations : Where assets are installed and running Storerooms : Where parts and materials are kept Service locations : Customer sites or service areas Staging areas : Temporary locations for work preparation Why locations matter ¤ Find equipment quickly Organize maintenance by area Assign work by location Track costs by facility or department Plan work routes efficiently Manage access and safety Location hierarchy ¤ Figure 1: Sample location hierarchy for an ice cream manufacturer A location is a place where work happens or where assets are installed. You can organize locations in a parent-child hierarchy to show how areas in a facility connect and to track work in the correct place. In Figure 1, the top-level location is Ice cream main plant, which branches into three main areas: Production building : A parent location containing child locations Mixing room, Filling line room, and Packaging zone. Cold storage : A dedicated refrigerated facility directly under Ice cream main plant. Main storeroom : The primary parts inventory warehouse directly under Ice cream main plant. Want to see how this connects to assets and work orders ? See How do locations , assets , and work orders work together? To plan your own hierarchy, see How do I plan my location hierarchy? Naming locations ¤ ✓ Do Use a unique location identifier Name locations so they make sense in the hierarchy Use location names for places, not equipment ✗ Don't Don't use the location name to represent the asset Don't mix place names and equipment names at the same hierarchy level without a clear reason Example names : Ice Cream Plant A, Production Building, Mixing Room, Filling Line 2, Packaging Zone, Cold Storage, Main Storeroom. Location vs. asset ¤ Location : The place, such as Filling Line 2 Asset : The equipment, such as Filler FL-02 Relationship : Asset is installed at location Some work orders are for locations , such as Clean production floor, rather than specific assets . Locations vs service addresses ¤ Locations and service addresses work together but serve different purposes. A location represents an operational place. A service address provides the physical or geographic details needed to find it. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Location terminology ¤ Term What it is Location An operational place where assets are used, stored, or repaired Service address The physical or geographic details needed to find that place or its associated assets Table 2: Detailed comparison of locations vs service addresses ¤ Aspect Location Service address Primary purpose Represents a place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired Provides detailed physical or geographic information that helps people find an asset or location Role in the data model Supports asset tracking, work management, purchasing, and the history of asset movements and performance at particular sites Provides another way to search for assets and locations and helps direct field crews to where work must be performed Structure Can belong to one or more location systems, which organize locations into logical parent-child hierarchies. See Can I organize the same locations more than one way? Can participate in an address system that establishes address ancestry and determines how addresses apply to child records Information stored Can include location type, status , associated assets , parent and child locations , and an associated service address Can include an address code, street information, coordinates, directions, landmarks, and other detailed location information Relationship to assets Assets can be installed at or associated with the location One service address can represent the position of one or more assets or physical locations Use on work records A location can identify where work is associated operationally When work is created for an asset or location , its service address can be copied to the service request or work order Example ¤ Consider an ice-cream manufacturing plant: Location : Packaging Line 2 : This record represents the operational place where equipment is installed and work is managed. It might be a child of the Packaging Area in the primary location hierarchy. Service address: Building B, south entrance, second floor, coordinates X/Y : This record provides the physical details that help a technician find Packaging Line 2. The service address does not replace the location . It supplements the location with address, navigation, or geographic information. How they work together ¤ A location can have an associated service address. You can add service addresses to assets , locations , work orders , and service requests. When work is created for an asset or location , the service address can be copied to the work order or service request. If an asset or location does not have its own service address, the system can use the address of the closest ancestor in the address hierarchy. A service address provides an additional way to find individual assets and locations , or groups of them. Related topics ¤ What are the basic concepts? What is an asset ? What is a work order ? How do locations , assets , and work orders work together? How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? How do I plan my location hierarchy?

docs.text: What is a work order ? ¤ A work order is a request or instruction to perform maintenance work. It's the central document that tracks everything about a maintenance job. Types of work orders ¤ Corrective maintenance : Fix something that broke Preventive maintenance : Scheduled routine maintenance Predictive maintenance : Work based on condition monitoring Project work : Installations, upgrades, modifications Inspections : Regular checks and assessments Why work orders matter ¤ Assign work to the correct people Track what work was done Record labor hours and costs Document parts used Maintain history of all maintenance Measure performance and productivity Work order lifecycle ¤ A work order progresses through six sequential stages from initial creation to final historical closeout: Created : The requester or the system creates the work order . It captures what needs to be done, where the work happens, how urgent it is, and any instructions the technician needs later. Approved : A supervisor reviews and approves the work. Approval confirms that the job can move ahead, reserves planned items , and records planned cost and rate information. Assigned : A supervisor or planner assigns the work to a technician. Before work starts, the planner checks that the assigned person has the schedule, instructions, parts, and tools needed. In Progress : The technician starts the job and records updates. Labor , materials, services, and tools are recorded as physical work happens so the record stays accurate. Completed : The technician documents labor , parts, and notes upon finishing the physical work. The record can still undergo final review or closeout. Closed : A supervisor or planner reviews completion and closes the work order . Closing finalizes the record, removes unused item reservations, and archives the job into maintenance history. Figure 1: The lifecycle of a work order in Maximo Application Suite Select A work order records maintenance work. It tells you what needs to be done, where the work happens, and which asset the work applies to. In this example, the work order Inspect filler nozzles is linked to Filler FL-02 at Filling Line 2. It also shows the work type and the parts used. This helps you track maintenance clearly and keep a useful history of the work performed. Want to see how this connects to locations and assets ? See How do locations , assets , and work orders work together? Creating a work order ¤ You create a work order when work needs to be done. Start with a clear description of the work. Then add details such as the work type, the priority, and the asset and location . For example, you might create a work order for Inspect filler nozzles and link it to Filler FL-02. Technicians can also create a work order from the field with the add button in the Technician app, for example when they find a problem on site . [SME confirmation required: Confirm the details you can add when you create a work order in Select.] Naming work orders ¤ ✓ Do Let Maximo Application Suite Select create the work order number automatically Write the description as a clear, action-oriented summary ✗ Don't Don't use vague descriptions such as Broken or Need fix Don't treat the description and work type as the same thing Example names : Inspect filler nozzles; Replace seal on Batch Mixer MX-01; Quarterly inspection, Spiral Freezer SF-01. Work order vs. work request ¤ Work request : Someone reports a problem or need Work order : Approved request with assigned resources Not all requests become work orders . Some may be rejected, combined, or deferred. Ready to work with work orders ? See How do I complete a job? for step-by-step guidance.

docs.text: Why can I manage work orders in more than one place? ¤ You can work with work orders in three places: The Work Orders application. The Technician app on the desktop, in your web browser. The Technician app in IBM Maximo Mobile, on your phone or tablet. All three work with the same work orders . This happens because Maximo Application Suite Select includes two kinds of apps: Desktop applications , such as Work Orders, Assets , and Inventory . These are the full applications that match the rest of the interface. Mobile apps , such as Technician, Inspections, and Asset Manager. Each is one application with two versions: a web version that runs in your browser next to the desktop applications, and a mobile version that runs in IBM Maximo Mobile on your phone or tablet. The two versions work the same way. Only the mobile version works offline. The two kinds of apps do not match one for one. For example, Technician combines parts of several desktop applications into one app for completing work. Most of the menu is desktop applications. To tell the two kinds apart, look at the name in the menu: The web version of a mobile app has a label in parentheses after its name, such as Timesheet (Mobile) or My Schedule (Mobile) . In a narrow menu, the label is cut off, as in Inventory Counting (M... . A desktop application has no label, such as Work Orders or Count Books . Some mobile apps are grouped under a name such as Technician or Asset Manager. The group has no label, but the apps inside it do. Which one should I use? ¤ There is no fixed rule. Use the one that suits how you work: If you use IBM Maximo Mobile often, use the web version of apps such as Technician on the desktop too. The app works the same way in both places. If you rarely use IBM Maximo Mobile, you might prefer desktop applications such as Work Orders. They are more consistent with the rest of the interface. How do I get back to the desktop applications? ¤ The web version of a mobile app, such as Technician or Inspections, opens without the desktop menu. To go back to the desktop applications, select the application menu icon at the bottom right of the screen, then select Start Center or Operational Dashboard in the navigator. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Mobile apps and what they do ¤ App Use it to Technician Complete assigned work. Inspections Complete inspections. Inspection Forms Work with inspection forms. Asset Manager Look up and manage assets . Issues and Transfers Issue and transfer inventory . Inventory Counting Count inventory . Service Requests Create and track service requests. To find any app, use the Find navigation item field at the top of the menu and search for the app name. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the purpose of each app in the "Use it to" column.] Which apps can I see? ¤ The apps you see depend on the security group that your administrator assigned to you. For the security groups , see How do I add users? Note Technician is both a security group and an app. The Technician security group is a role that you assign to a user. The Technician app is one of the apps that role can use. What to do next ¤ Technician: Complete your first work order : Complete a work order . How do I get IBM Maximo Mobile? : Get the app that contains Technician, Inspections, and the other apps in Table 1. How do I add users? : Assign the security group that gives a user access to apps. What apps are in IBM Maximo Mobile? : Overview of all the apps in IBM Maximo Mobile. Related topics ¤ What are the basic concepts? What is a work order ? What can I do in my role?
