docs.text: What if I can't complete a task? ¤ Add notes explaining the issue, change the work order status to show it's blocked, and notify your supervisor. The work order stays open until the problem is resolved. Sometimes you can't finish work because parts aren't available, you need help, or you discover a bigger problem. That's normal. The important thing is to document what's blocking you so others can help resolve it. 💡 Tips for handling blocked work ¤ Document issues as soon as you discover them. Don't wait until later. Be specific about exactly what's needed to continue Take photos of problems to make the issue clear Change status immediately so supervisors can see the block Check back periodically on blocked work to see if it can be resumed Update notes if the situation changes or you learn more Common reasons you can't complete work ¤ Missing parts or materials ¤ Problem : You need parts that aren't in stock What to do : Request the parts through the work order Add notes about what's needed Change status to "Waiting on Parts" Notify your supervisor Move to other work while waiting Need additional help or skills ¤ Problem : The job requires expertise you don't have What to do : Add notes describing what's needed Change status to "Waiting on Assignment" Contact your supervisor to assign additional help Document what you've completed so far Equipment or tools not available ¤ Problem : You need special tools or equipment that aren't available What to do : List the required tools in your notes Change status to "On Hold" Notify your supervisor Check if tools can be borrowed or rented Discovered a bigger problem ¤ Problem : You found additional issues that need to be addressed What to do : Document the new problem with photos if possible Add detailed notes about what you found Discuss with your supervisor whether to: Expand the current work order Create a new work order for the additional work Update the work order status appropriately Safety concerns ¤ Problem : Unsafe conditions prevent you from completing work What to do : Stop work immediately Document the safety issue Change status to "On Hold" Notify your supervisor right away Follow your organization's safety procedures Access issues ¤ Problem : You can't access the equipment or location What to do : Note why access is blocked Change status to "Waiting" Contact whoever can provide access Notify your supervisor In practice Technicians often continue working on blocked tasks instead of moving to other work, wasting time Work orders are frequently left in "In Progress" status even when blocked, hiding the real problem Notes are vague or missing, so supervisors cannot help resolve issues quickly Teams sometimes work around problems informally instead of documenting them in the system How to document the issue ¤ When you can't complete work, add clear notes: What to include : What you were trying to do What's blocking you What you've already completed What's still needed Any photos of the problem What good looks like Poor note "Can't finish. Need parts." Good note "Spiral freezer SF-01: Replaced conveyor belt rollers 1-3. Roller 4 bearing is seized and needs to be drilled out. Need drill and bearing puller. Completed 75% of work. Freezer is safe to leave overnight but should not be operated until repair is complete." Changing work order status ¤ Use the correct status to show what's blocking you: On Hold : General hold, waiting for something Waiting on Parts : Specifically waiting for materials Waiting on Assignment : Need additional people or skills Waiting : Other reasons, such as access or approval Your supervisor can see these statuses and help resolve the issue. What happens next ¤ After you update the status and add notes: Your supervisor is notified They can see exactly what's blocking you They work to resolve the issue, such as by ordering parts or assigning help You're notified when you can continue Work order stays in your queue until resolved Common mistakes ¤ Leaving work orders in "In Progress" when they are actually blocked Writing vague notes that don't explain what's needed Not notifying the supervisor, assuming they will check the system Continuing to work on blocked tasks instead of moving to other work Forgetting to update notes when the situation changes Why proper documentation matters ¤ If you do not change status , supervisors cannot see blocked work and delays get worse If notes are vague, resolving the issue takes longer because details are missing If blocked work is not documented, the same problems repeat on future jobs Poor communication leads to wasted time and missed deadlines Preventing future blocks ¤ Help prevent similar issues: Review work orders thoroughly before starting to identify potential issues early Check parts availability before you begin work, not after you need them Verify you have the correct tools and equipment before starting Ask questions if instructions are unclear. Don't guess. Report recurring problems to your supervisor so they can be fixed systematically Continue building your skills ¤ Understand the equipment you're working on ¤ See the full maintenance history of any asset to spot patterns and avoid repeat failures. How do I track asset history? Document what went wrong ¤ Learn how to record failures properly so patterns can be found and fixed. What happens when an asset fails? docs.text: How do I complete a work order ? ¤ New to Maximo Application Suite Select? Start with Technician: Complete your first work order for a guided introduction. Open your work order . Do the work. Record what you did. Mark it complete. The system tracks your time and parts automatically. Good records help everyone. They track costs and provide history for future work. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Start work tracking as soon as you begin. Don't add time later. Record notes and parts as you go, not at the end Use clear, specific language so others can understand what happened Take photos for anything unusual or hard to describe Complete and close work orders promptly to keep queues accurate Steps to complete work ¤ Step 1: Find and open your work order ¤ Go to the Technician app on the desktop or in IBM Maximo Mobile. You can also use the Work Orders application. Look for work assigned to you Open the work order Need help finding your work? See How do I find my work? Step 2: Start the work ¤ Click Start work to track time. You need a labor record to track time. If you cannot start work, ask your administrator to check that you have one. See How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? Read the job plan or instructions Check you have all parts and tools Note any safety requirements Step 3: Do the work ¤ Follow the job plan steps Complete any checklists Take photos of issues or finished work Note any problems you find Step 4: Record what you did ¤ When you finish, you can report the failure, your labor , and the materials and tools that you used. Add work details: Describe what you found and fixed Be specific, which helps the next person Note any follow-up work needed Record materials: Add parts from inventory System tracks costs automatically Request more parts if needed Learn how to issue parts to a job for detailed instructions on recording materials. Confirm time: System tracks time from when you started Adjust for breaks if needed Time is used for costs and planning Your user account must have an active labor record assigned to start and report work In practice Many technicians wait until the end of the job to enter notes, which leads to missing or inaccurate details Parts are often used but not recorded, causing inventory errors later If time tracking isn't started at the beginning, reported labor is usually incorrect Teams sometimes rely on memory instead of updating the work order in real time Common mistakes Writing vague notes such as "fixed issue" instead of describing the actual problem and repair Forgetting to record parts or recording them later from memory Leaving the work order in the wrong status , for example, still "In Progress" Skipping photos or checklists when they are available Not documenting additional problems discovered during the job What good looks like Poor note "Fixed filler" Good note "Filler FL-02: Nozzle seal was worn and causing leaks. Replaced seal, cleaned nozzle assembly, tested operation. No leaks detected." Step 5: Mark it complete ¤ Click Complete work when done System stops tracking time Work order goes to your supervisor Supervisor closes it after review What to include in your notes ¤ Good notes help everyone: What you found : "Seal on Filler FL-02 was worn and leaking" What you did : "Replaced seal, cleaned nozzle assembly" Result : "Filler running smoothly, no leaks" Follow-up : "Monitor for leaks during next production run" Using checklists ¤ For inspections, go to the Inspections app on the desktop or in IBM Maximo Mobile. For more information, see How do inspections work? If your work order has a checklist: Complete each item as you go Mark pass or fail for each point Add notes for any failures Take photos of issues Finish all items before completing work Working offline (mobile) ¤ On the mobile app: Start work without internet Complete tasks and add notes offline Take photos, which are saved on your device Changes sync when you're back online For more detail, see What happens when I'm offline in IBM Maximo Mobile? What happens after you complete work ¤ After you mark complete: Your supervisor gets notified They review your work and notes They close the work order if correct Work order becomes part of equipment history Costs are calculated and recorded Why accurate records matter ¤ If you do not record work details, asset history becomes unreliable If parts are not recorded, inventory levels quickly become inaccurate If time is incorrect, cost tracking and planning are affected Poor data leads to repeated failures and inefficient maintenance Having trouble completing work? Check What if I can't complete a task? for common issues and solutions. Once this feels routine, you'll move through your work queue with confidence and spend less time wondering what to do next. Continue building your skills ¤ Issue parts to a job ¤ Record the materials you use as you go so inventory stays accurate. How do I issue parts to a job? When something gets in the way ¤ Know what to do when you're blocked by missing parts, access issues, or a problem bigger than expected. What if I can't complete a task? Understand the equipment you're working on ¤ See the full maintenance history of any asset to spot patterns and avoid repeat failures. How do I track asset history?

docs.text: How do I find my work? ¤ Use work queues to see all your assigned work in one place. Work queues group similar tasks so you can quickly find what needs to be done. Work queues show only the work that matters to you. No searching through everything. To see your assigned work, open the Technician app and select Assigned work . You can also use the Technician app in IBM Maximo Mobile or the Work Orders application. For the differences, see Why can I manage work orders in more than one place? 💡 Tips for success ¤ Check your work queues at the start of each shift and periodically during the day Always do urgent and overdue items first, then work by priority Update work order status as soon as you start or complete work Add notes immediately if you encounter issues or delays Close completed work promptly so your queue stays accurate When to use work queues ¤ Work queues help you: See all work assigned to you Find urgent or overdue work fast Focus on specific work types, such as inspections or repairs Track work for your team or location Act on multiple items at once How work queues work ¤ Your administrator creates work queues that filter and show relevant work. Common types: My work orders All work orders assigned to you. Overdue work Work that should be done already. High priority Urgent work that needs immediate attention. Team work Work assigned to your crew or department. Pending approval Work waiting for your review. Finding your work ¤ Step 1: Open work queues ¤ Go to the Operational Dashboard Find the Work Queues section Each queue shows how many items it has Step 2: Pick a queue ¤ Click on a work queue See all items with key details: status , priority, and due date Use filters to narrow down more if needed Step 3: Open a work order ¤ Click on any item Read the work description Check what you need Start work when ready In practice Technicians often check work queues only at shift start, missing urgent work added during the day Work orders sometimes sit in queues because no one checks regularly Teams may rely on verbal assignments instead of using the system Mobile users forget to sync, so they miss new assignments Using the mobile app ¤ On your phone or tablet: Open the IBM Maximo Mobile app Open the Technician app and select Assigned work Work orders sync automatically Work offline if needed Changes sync when you're back online If new work does not appear, see Why can't I see new work in IBM Maximo Mobile? Common mistakes ¤ Only checking work queues at the start of the shift Ignoring priority and due dates when choosing work Not refreshing the queue to see new assignments Working on unassigned tasks without updating the system Leaving completed work in your queue instead of closing it What good looks like ¤ Poor approach Check queue once at 8 AM, work on whatever looks easiest, leave completed work open. Good approach Check queue at shift start and periodically throughout the day. Prioritize by urgency and due date. Update status as you progress. Close work promptly. What if I don't see my work? ¤ If work is missing: Check that it's assigned to you Check the work order status , because it might be on hold Refresh your work queue Ask your supervisor if it's still missing Why work queues matter ¤ If you do not check queues regularly, urgent work gets delayed If status is not updated, supervisors cannot track progress accurately If completed work is not closed, queues become cluttered and unreliable Poor queue management leads to missed deadlines and inefficient work distribution Once you know where to look, finding your work takes seconds, and you'll never miss an assignment again. Continue building your skills ¤ Complete a work order ¤ Walk through the full workflow, recording time, parts, and notes the correct way. How do I complete a work order ? When something gets in the way ¤ Know what to do when you're blocked by missing parts, access issues, or a problem bigger than expected. What if I can't complete a task? docs.text: Why can't I complete a work order ? ¤ You might see errors like " Status cannot be changed" or not see the Complete option at all. Looking to troubleshoot completion blockers right away? Skip to work order completion blocker checklist ↓ Common causes ¤ You don't have permission ¤ Your security group might not allow you to change work order status or complete work. What to do : Contact your supervisor or system administrator to verify your permissions. Work order is not in the correct status ¤ You can only complete work orders that are in progress. If the work order is in a different status , such as "Approved" or "On Hold", you need to change it to "In Progress" first. What to do : Check the current status and move it to "In Progress" before trying to complete it. An approval or business rule is controlling status changes ¤ Some organizations configure approval rules and requirements that control which status changes are allowed and when. What to do : Complete any required prerequisite steps, or contact your supervisor if you're unsure what's required. Required data is missing ¤ The system might require certain information before allowing completion: Labor hours must be entered Failure codes must be recorded: problem, cause, and remedy Materials or actuals must be documented What to do : Check what information is required and add it before completing the work order . Why is the Complete status missing? ¤ The Complete (COMP) status might be hidden by your organization's configuration. Status domain conditions ¤ Your organization might have set up rules that hide the Complete status until certain conditions are met, such as: Labor transactions are entered All required fields are filled in Specific approval steps are completed What to do : Enter all required information, or ask your supervisor what conditions must be met. Required prerequisites ¤ Business rules can restrict which status transitions are available based on the current state and data of the work order . What to do : Complete any outstanding prerequisites such as recording labor actuals or failure codes , or contact your supervisor for guidance. Why does completing fail even though work is done? ¤ Completion can fail if required data is missing, even if the physical work is complete. Typical gaps ¤ No labor transactions : You must record the time spent on the work No failure codes : Problem, cause, and remedy codes might be required Missing actuals or costs : Materials used or other costs must be documented What to do : Review the work order to ensure all required information is entered, then try completing again. Document as you go Record labor , materials, and other information while doing the work, not after. This prevents completion delays and ensures accurate records. Why does a work order behave differently for different users? ¤ Differences are usually caused by security groups or roles. What to check ¤ Security permissions : Different users might have different rights to change status , complete work, or initiate tasks Site or application-level access : Some users might have access to certain sites or applications that others don't What to do : If you need different permissions, contact your system administrator. Work order completion blocker checklist ¤ Use this checklist to identify and resolve blockers preventing work order completion: Table 1: Work order completion blocker checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Work order in progress Current work order status is set to INPRG, not WAPPR, WSCHED, or WMATL [ ] Labor actuals entered Actual labor hours with start and finish times are recorded for all assigned technicians [ ] Material actuals recorded Materials and parts used on the job are issued and charged to the work order [ ] Child tasks completed All child task assignments and mandatory inspection forms are marked completed [ ] Failure reporting complete Problem, Cause, and Remedy codes are selected if the asset has a failure class assigned [ ] User security permission User security group permits changing work order status to COMP Related topics ¤ How do I complete a job? What if I can't complete a task? How do I find my work? docs.text: Why can't I see new work in IBM Maximo Mobile? ¤ You were assigned a work order , but it does not appear in IBM Maximo Mobile. In most cases, the app is offline, your session has expired, or the app has not synced yet. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Causes and what to do ¤ Cause What to do The device is offline Check your connection, then wait for the app to sync. Your session has expired Select the cloud icon to sign in again. The app has not synced yet Sync the app manually. The work order is not assigned to you Ask your supervisor to check the assignment. Your administrator turned off data download Ask your administrator to check the sync settings. Likely causes ¤ The device is offline ¤ IBM Maximo Mobile treats your device as offline when it is in airplane mode, the network adapter is turned off, the network bandwidth is low, the server cannot be reached, or your sign-in session has expired. While the device is offline, the app shows the data that is stored on the device and cannot receive new work. What to do : Move to a place with a better connection, or turn off airplane mode. When the connection returns, the app syncs automatically. For more information, see What happens when I'm offline in IBM Maximo Mobile? Your session has expired ¤ After your session expires, the app asks you to sign in again. Until you do, you work offline and new work does not arrive. What to do : Select the cloud icon on the app screen and sign in again. The app has not synced yet ¤ While your device is online, the app syncs automatically. If you were assigned work a moment ago, it might not have arrived yet. What to do : Sync the app manually, then check your assigned work again. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the name and location of the manual sync control in Select.] The work order is not assigned to you ¤ The work order might be assigned to another person, or it might not be in a status that appears in your assigned work. What to do : Check the work order on the desktop, or ask your supervisor. For causes that apply on the desktop too, see Why don't technicians see their assigned work? Your administrator turned off data download ¤ Administrators set which data IBM Maximo Mobile downloads to devices. If the download of work data is turned off, new work does not appear after a sync. What to do : Ask your administrator to check the sync settings. For administrators, see How do I configure IBM Maximo Mobile for my team? Notifications about new work ¤ Push notifications arrive only when you have an active session and have not signed out of the app. If you are not getting notifications, sign in again. For administrators, see When users receive push notifications . What to do next ¤ How do I find my work? : Find your assigned work on the desktop and in IBM Maximo Mobile. How do I get IBM Maximo Mobile? : Sign in and sync. Related topics ¤ What happens when I'm offline in IBM Maximo Mobile? Why don't technicians see their assigned work? docs.text: What happens when an asset fails? ¤ Record the failure using failure codes , create a work order to fix it, and track downtime . Looking to validate failure reporting right away? Skip to failure reporting verification checklist ↓ Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Failure code levels ¤ Failure code level What it describes Example Failure class Type of problem Filling and Packaging Problem What specifically failed Nozzle seal leak Cause Why it failed Normal wear Remedy How it was fixed Replaced seal, cleaned nozzle assembly Figure 1 illustrates the failure reporting workflow: when equipment breaks down, the technician selects the asset failure class, selects the specific problem code, identifies the root cause, records the remedy code, and logs asset downtime . Figure 1: Failure reporting workflow from asset class to remedy 💡 Tips for success ¤ Be specific: Don't just say "broken": describe what failed Use correct failure codes Include relevant details Be consistent: Use the same codes for similar failures Follow your organization's standards This makes trend analysis accurate Be timely: Report failures when they happen Don't wait until work order is closed Fresh details are more accurate Include context: Note operating conditions Mention recent changes Record environmental factors Add photos of damage Why track failures? ¤ When equipment fails, documenting what happened and why helps you understand reliability issues and prevent future problems. Recording failures helps you: Identify patterns: see if the same problem keeps happening Improve maintenance: adjust schedules to prevent failures Track costs: understand the true cost of equipment problems Make decisions: decide when to repair versus replace Analyze trends: report on reliability by equipment type Prevent recurrence: learn from past failures Failure codes provide a standardized way to track problems. This makes it easy to spot patterns and trends. How failure codes work ¤ Failure codes are organized in four levels: 1. Failure class (Problem type) ¤ What kind of problem occurred: Mechanical failure Electrical failure Operational error External cause 2. Problem (Specific issue) ¤ What specifically failed: Nozzle seal leak on Filler FL-02 Agitator not rotating on Batch Mixer MX-01 Compressor not reaching temperature on Spiral Freezer SF-01 Control malfunction 3. Cause (Why it failed) ¤ Root cause of the failure: Normal wear Drive belt worn Refrigerant low Overload 4. Remedy (How it was fixed) ¤ What was done to resolve the failure: Replaced seal, cleaned nozzle assembly Replaced drive belt Topped up refrigerant, checked for leaks Operator retraining Recording the remedy completes the picture. If the same problem keeps recurring with the same cause but different remedies, the data shows which fix actually works and which ones don't. Without remedy codes, pattern analysis stops at "what broke" and never reaches "what actually fixes it." How do I report a failure? ¤ Note The failure class on the work order is copied automatically from the asset record. If the asset has no failure class set, the Failure Reporting tab will be empty and you won't be able to select problem or cause codes. Contact your administrator to set the correct failure class on the asset first. See How do I classify assets ? . What to do: ¤ Create or open a work order : If no work order exists, create one If working on existing work order , use that Record the failure: Go to the Failure Reporting tab Confirm the failure class is correct. It should be pre-filled from the asset Choose the specific problem Identify the cause Select a remedy code to record how the failure was resolved Add details: Describe what happened Note when the failure occurred Record any damage or safety issues Take photos if helpful Track downtime : Record when equipment went down Note when it's back in service System calculates total downtime Complete the repair: Fix the problem Document what you did Close the work order How do I use failure data? ¤ Identify recurring problems ¤ Review failure reports to find: Equipment that fails frequently Common failure modes Patterns by time of year or usage Whether maintenance schedules need adjustment Analyze failure trends ¤ Look for: Increasing failure rates, which can mean equipment is wearing out Seasonal patterns Failures after specific events Cost trends over time Make informed decisions ¤ Use failure data to: Justify equipment replacement Adjust preventive maintenance Improve operating procedures Train operators on common issues Budget for repairs and replacements Figure 2 illustrates how aggregated failure records and downtime metrics feed reliability analysis to optimize preventive maintenance schedules, guide operator training, and justify equipment replacement. Figure 2: Using failure data for reliability decision making Common failure scenarios ¤ Premature failure ¤ Equipment fails before expected: Check if maintenance schedule is adequate Review operating conditions Verify proper installation Consider if equipment is undersized Repeated failures ¤ Same problem keeps happening: Look for root cause, not just symptoms Check if repairs are done correctly Consider if operating conditions changed Evaluate if equipment is right for the application Sudden catastrophic failure ¤ Equipment fails without warning: Review if warning signs were missed Check if inspections are thorough enough Consider adding condition monitoring Evaluate if maintenance frequency is adequate What if I don't know the cause? ¤ If the cause isn't clear: Use "Unknown" or "Under Investigation". Add notes about what you observed. Update the failure code when cause is determined. Don't guess: inaccurate data is worse than incomplete data. Failure reporting verification checklist ¤ Use this checklist to ensure complete and actionable failure reporting on work orders : Table 2: Failure reporting verification checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Failure class assigned Operating equipment record has a valid Failure Class defined on its asset master [ ] Problem code selected Specific failure symptom is chosen on the Failure Reporting tab [ ] Cause code identified Root cause code is selected from the causes linked to the problem [ ] Remedy code recorded Action code describing how the failure was corrected is logged [ ] Downtime recorded Actual equipment downtime hours and timestamps are entered on the work order Continue building your skills ¤ See the full picture ¤ Failures tell you what broke. Asset history tells you the full story: all maintenance, costs, and patterns over time. How do I track asset history? Related topics ¤ How do I reduce equipment downtime ? docs.text: How do I classify assets ? ¤ Use classifications to group similar assets together and add detailed specifications. Looking to verify your asset classification setup right away? Skip to asset classification verification checklist ↓ Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Classification terminology ¤ Term What it means Classification A category that describes what type of equipment you have, such as "Rotary Fillers" or "Spiral Freezers" Attribute A specific detail about the equipment, such as "Manufacturer" or "Fill capacity" Hierarchy How classifications are organized from broad to specific, such as Equipment to Filling and Packaging to Rotary Fillers 💡 Tips for success ¤ Choose the correct classification ¤ Use the most specific classification that fits Don't use overly broad classifications, such as just "Equipment" Be consistent across similar assets Follow your organization's standards Complete all relevant attributes ¤ Fill in as many attributes as possible More detail makes assets easier to find and manage Include manufacturer and model information Add technical specifications for maintenance planning Use consistent values ¤ Use the same format for similar data Example: Always use "HP" for horsepower, not "hp" or "Horsepower" Follow naming conventions This makes searching and reporting more accurate Why classify assets ? ¤ Classifications help you organize equipment and track information consistently. When you classify an asset , you can: Group similar assets together Search for all assets of a specific type Store technical details in a standard way Report on maintenance by equipment type Match vendor or industry standards For example, if you classify all your fillers the same way, you can easily find them, compare their maintenance costs, and track specifications consistently. Attribute search depends on consistent classification ¤ Maximo's attribute search lets you find all assets meeting a specification, for example, all rotary fillers with a fill capacity above 100 units per minute, or all spiral freezers from a specific manufacturer. This only works when assets of the same type share the same classification and attribute structure. Inconsistent classification breaks this capability silently: the search runs, but returns incomplete results with no indication that records are missing. How classifications work ¤ Classification hierarchy ¤ Classifications are organized like a tree, from broad to specific: Top level : Broad categories, such as "Equipment" or "Refrigeration" Mid level : Specific types, such as "Filling and Packaging" or "Freezers" Bottom level : Detailed subtypes, such as "Spiral Freezers" or "Rotary Fillers" Figure 1 illustrates an example classification tree branching from a top-level Equipment category into three distinct branches: Filling and Packaging : branches into Rotary Fillers, with example asset Filler FL-02, and Case Packers. Refrigeration : branches into Freezers, which further branches into Spiral Freezers, with example asset Spiral Freezer SF-01. Processing Equipment : branches into Mixers, with example asset Batch Mixer MX-01. Figure 1: An example classification hierarchy Use the most specific classification that fits your equipment. This makes it easier to find and manage. Attributes and specifications ¤ Each classification can have attributes that define specific details: Manufacturer : Who made it Model number : Specific model Capacity : How much it can handle Voltage : Electrical requirements Serial number : Unique identifier Once you add these details, they become searchable. You can find all fillers from a specific manufacturer or all mixers with a certain capacity. Table 2: Classification attribute data types ¤ Data type What it stores Example attribute ALN Alphanumeric text strings Model number, serial number, or manufacturer name NUMERIC Numerical values with optional unit of measure Horsepower (HP), operating voltage (V), or tank capacity (L) TABLE Values validated against a predefined system lookup table or domain Refrigerant type, frame size, or metallurgy grade DATETIME Calendar dates and timestamps Commissioning date, warranty expiration date How do I classify an asset ? ¤ Before you classify ¤ Set a failure class on the asset record before or at the same time as the classification. The failure class is automatically copied to every work order created for that asset . It controls which failure codes , meaning problem, cause, and remedy, technicians can select during failure reporting. Without it, the Failure Reporting tab on work orders starts empty and structured failure data cannot be captured for this asset . What to do: ¤ Open the Assets application. Find the asset you want to classify. Open the asset record. On the main tab, set the Failure Class field to the appropriate failure hierarchy for this type of equipment. Go to the Specifications tab. Click to add a classification. Browse or search for the correct classification. Fill in the attributes: Complete all required attributes Add optional attributes for more detail Save the asset . The system stores all classification data. The information appears on the asset record and becomes searchable. Common classifications ¤ Typical classifications you might use: Processing Equipment : Mixers, blenders, homogenizers, pasteurizers Filling and Packaging : Filling machines, cappers, labelers, case packers Refrigeration : Chillers, freezers, cold storage units, ice cream hardening tunnels Pumps : Sanitary pumps, transfer pumps, clean-in-place (CIP) pumps Conveyors : Belt conveyors, roller conveyors, spiral freezers Tanks and Vessels : Storage tanks, mixing tanks, fermentation vessels HVAC Systems : Climate control, air handling units Vehicles : Forklifts, pallet jacks, delivery trucks How do I search by classification? ¤ Once assets are classified, you can: Find all assets of a specific type Filter work orders by equipment classification Report on maintenance costs by classification Identify assets needing similar maintenance This makes it easy to analyze maintenance patterns and costs for specific types of equipment. What if the classification doesn't exist? ¤ Select includes some classifications. If you need a classification that doesn't exist: Check if a similar classification works. Contact your administrator to create new classifications. Don't create duplicate classifications. Follow your organization's approval process. Asset classification verification checklist ¤ Use this checklist to ensure complete and standardized asset classification: Table 3: Asset classification verification checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Most specific category Asset is mapped to the lowest applicable branch of the classification hierarchy [ ] Failure class aligned Failure Class is populated on the asset master to enable failure reporting on work orders [ ] Mandatory attributes filled Essential specifications such as manufacturer, model, and serial number are entered [ ] Standardized units of measure Measurement attributes use consistent units, such as HP for horsepower and V for volts [ ] Specification tab saved Added classification and attributes are committed and visible on the Specifications tab Related topics ¤ How do I make data reliable? How do I standardize across teams? How do I manage more assets ? How do I track asset history? What happens when an asset fails? How do I set up failure codes ?

docs.text: How do I track asset history? ¤ View all work orders , meter readings, and maintenance activities for any asset in one place. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Asset history information ¤ What you can see Why it matters All work orders Know what's been done Meter readings Track equipment usage Costs Understand maintenance expenses Downtime See when equipment was unavailable Failures Identify recurring problems TODO: Add visual content A screenshot showing the asset history view with work orders and costs would be useful here. 💡 Tips: Best practices for asset history ¤ For technicians: Complete work orders promptly so history stays current Add detailed notes about what you did Record all parts used Take photos of problems and repairs Enter meter readings regularly For supervisors: Review and close work orders quickly Make sure costs are accurate Verify meter readings are current Use consistent failure codes Keep asset records up to date Why track asset history? ¤ Asset history shows you the complete story of your equipment. You can see what maintenance was done, when it happened, and what it cost. This helps you: Spot problems that keep happening Plan better maintenance schedules Decide whether to repair or replace equipment Estimate future maintenance costs Every completed work order becomes part of the permanent record. This creates a reliable history you can use to make smart decisions. What's included in asset history? ¤ The system automatically tracks these details for each asset : Work orders All maintenance and repairs performed on the equipment. Meter readings Equipment usage over time, such as hours run, cycles completed, or miles driven. Costs Labor , parts, and total maintenance expenses. Downtime When equipment was out of service and for how long. Failures Problems that occurred and how they were fixed. Moves Location changes and transfers. Specifications Technical details and attributes. When should I review asset history? ¤ Check asset history when you need to: Understand why a problem keeps happening Plan preventive maintenance schedules Decide whether to repair or replace equipment Estimate maintenance costs for budgeting Troubleshoot current issues Prepare for audits or compliance reviews How do I view asset history? ¤ What to do: ¤ Open the Assets application. Search for the asset by name, number, or location . Open the asset record. Review the information you need: Work history : See all completed work orders , who did the work, and costs Meter readings : View usage trends and identify unusual patterns Costs : See total maintenance costs and cost breakdown TODO: Add visual content A video showing how to navigate asset history and find specific information would be useful here. How do I use history to make decisions? ¤ Identify recurring problems ¤ If you see the same issue repeatedly: Review failure codes to spot patterns Check if preventive maintenance needs adjustment Consider if the problem indicates a larger issue Evaluate if replacement is more cost-effective than continued repairs Plan preventive maintenance ¤ Use history to: See what maintenance has been done Identify optimal maintenance intervals Adjust schedules based on actual usage Prevent problems before they occur Evaluate equipment performance ¤ Track: How often equipment goes down and for how long Maintenance costs compared to equipment value Reliability trends over time Whether equipment meets performance expectations Figure 1 illustrates how continuous asset history records, including completed work orders , meter readings, downtime logs, and failure reports, feed equipment performance evaluations to drive preventive maintenance adjustments, spare parts planning, and repair versus replacement decisions. Figure 1: Using asset history data for maintenance decisions What if history is incomplete? ¤ If asset history is missing or incomplete: Check if work orders were closed properly. Verify the asset number is correct. Look for work orders under old asset numbers. Contact your administrator if data needs to be corrected. Start maintaining complete records going forward. Understanding an asset 's history turns reactive fixes into informed decisions. That is the difference between guessing and knowing. Continue building your skills ¤ Document what went wrong ¤ Learn how to record failure codes , track downtime , and use failure data to prevent future problems. What happens when an asset fails? docs.text: How do I get a new part into inventory ? ¤ To stock a part, you work in three applications in order: Item Master, Storerooms, and Inventory . You describe the part once, add it to a storeroom, and then manage how much of it you have. For example, to stock a food-grade gasket kit for Filler FL-02, you create the item , add it to Main storeroom, and record the starting balance. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Describe each part once in Item Master. Add it to as many storerooms as you need. Decide the issue unit before you add the item to a storeroom. It is the unit you use when you take the part out, such as each. If you buy a part in a different unit than you issue it, set up the conversion between the two first. For example, you might buy gaskets by the box and issue them one at a time. Make sure the storeroom exists before you add items to it. Quick reference ¤ Figure 1 illustrates the five sequential steps required to get a new part into inventory and ready for work orders : Item Master : create the item record, specify what it is, and indicate whether it is rotating. Storerooms : verify that the target storeroom exists and is active. Item Master : add the item to the storeroom, which creates the inventory record. Inventory : record the physical location such as the bin and enter the quantity on hand. Inventory : issue the stocked part to an approved work order . Figure 1: The steps to get a new part into inventory Table 1: From a new part to a balance you can issue ¤ Order Application What you do there 1 Item Master Create the item . Say what it is and whether it is rotating. 2 Storerooms Make sure the storeroom exists and is active. 3 Item Master Add the item to the storeroom. This creates the inventory record. 4 Inventory Record where the part is kept and how many you have. 5 Inventory Issue the part to a work order . To find any of these applications, use the Find navigation item field at the top of the menu and search for the application name. What is the difference between an item and an inventory record? ¤ An item describes the part. An inventory record describes the part in one storeroom, including how many you have and where they are. If the same gasket kit is in three storerooms, you have one item and three inventory records. Each record has its own balance. How do I create the item ? ¤ In Item Master, you describe the part, including whether it is rotating and the units you order and issue it in. Mark rebuildable parts, such as motors, as rotating. For more about the choice, see How do I plan my storeroom and inventory strategy? How do I add the item to a storeroom? ¤ From Item Master, use the Add Items To Storeroom action. Choose the storeroom, then give the item the details it needs in that storeroom. You can add the item to one storeroom or to several. The issue unit is required because the system needs it to track the balance. You can set up the rest, such as the bin and starting balance, now or later in Inventory . Adding the item to a storeroom creates its inventory record. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the details Select asks for when you add an item to a storeroom, and which of them are required.] How do I set the balance and bin? ¤ In Inventory , open the record for the item and storeroom, and record where the part is kept and how many you have. For example, if you counted 10 gasket kits on the shelf, record 10 as the starting balance. Record a physical count to check the system against the shelf. If they do not match, see What happens if stock is incorrect? What if I cannot issue the part? ¤ Check that the part has a balance in the storeroom. For other causes, see Why can't I issue materials to a work order ? What to do next ¤ How do I issue parts to a job? : Take the part out of the storeroom for a work order . How do I track stock levels? : Watch your balances and reorder needs. How do I plan my storeroom and inventory strategy? : Decide how to organize storerooms and items before you load them. Related topics ¤ What happens if stock is incorrect? Why can't I issue materials to a work order ? Inventory clerk: Issue a part How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part?

docs.text: How do I issue parts to a job? ¤ Take parts from the storeroom and assign them to a work order . Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Issue methods ¤ Method When to use From work order Most common, when you're working on a job From storeroom When managing inventory directly Mobile app When working in the field Figure 1 illustrates the end-to-end parts issue and material transaction workflow across three main stages: 1. Issue entry methods : Technicians or inventory clerks initiate an issue through one of three paths: from an active work order on the Materials tab, directly at the storeroom counter using the Inventory issue action, or in the field using barcode scanning in the Technician mobile app. 2. Validation checks : The system validates the transaction by confirming a valid storeroom and item number, verifying that the work order is in a chargeable status , checking that sufficient available storeroom balance exists, and confirming all required accounting fields are populated. 3. Simultaneous updates : Upon successful validation, the system executes three updates simultaneously: deducting the physical balance from the storeroom and logging an audit transaction, charging actual material costs directly to the work order , and evaluating reorder thresholds to trigger inventory replenishment if stock drops below minimum levels. Figure 1: Parts issue and material transaction workflow 💡 Tips: Best practices for issuing parts ¤ Before you start work: Check the job plan for required materials Verify parts are in stock Reserve parts if needed for later Request parts that aren't available During the job: Issue parts as you use them Record actual quantities used Return unused parts promptly Note if you used different parts than planned After completing work: Verify all materials are recorded Return any unused parts Add notes about part usage Close the work order Why issue parts properly? ¤ When you issue parts correctly, the system: Updates inventory levels automatically Records costs to the work order Tracks what materials were used Helps with reordering decisions This ensures accurate inventory counts and a complete record of what each job cost. When should I issue parts? ¤ Issue parts when: You're starting a job and need materials You use parts during a repair You want costs recorded to the work order How do I issue parts? ¤ Method 1: Issue from work order ¤ This is the most common way to issue parts. What to do: Open your assigned work order . Go to the Materials or Actuals tab. Click to add a material. Search for the item by number or description. Select the correct item . Enter how many you need. Choose the storeroom location . Click Issue . The system checks if parts are available, deducts from inventory , adds cost to the work order , and records the transaction. TODO: Add visual content A video showing how to issue parts from a work order would be useful here. Method 2: Issue from storeroom ¤ Use this when managing inventory directly. What to do: Open the Inventory application. Search for the item you need. Open the inventory record. Click Issue Current Item . Enter the work order number. Specify quantity. Confirm the issue. The system updates inventory balance, shows the material on the work order , and records the cost. Inventory clerks can also use the Issues and Transfers app on the desktop or in IBM Maximo Mobile. Use it to issue items that are reserved for approved work orders , issue items that are not reserved, and transfer items between storerooms or between bins. Method 3: Use mobile app ¤ On mobile devices: Open your work order Add materials as you use them Scan barcodes if available Changes sync automatically TODO: Add visual content A screenshot showing the mobile parts issue screen would be useful here. What happens when I issue parts? ¤ The system automatically: Reduces inventory : storeroom balance goes down Records cost: material cost is added to the work order Tracks usage: creates transaction history Updates reorder: triggers reorder if below minimum Logs who and when: records who issued and when Common scenarios ¤ Part not in stock ¤ If the part you need isn't available: Check other storeroom locations . Request a purchase. Use an alternate part if approved. Update work order status to "Waiting on Parts". Used wrong quantity ¤ If you issued too many or too few parts: Issue additional parts if you need more. Return unused parts to storeroom. System adjusts inventory and costs. Add notes explaining the change. Emergency issue ¤ For urgent repairs: Issue parts immediately. Add to work order as soon as possible. Don't skip recording: it affects inventory . Explain urgency in notes. Figure 2 outlines the sequential resolution workflows for three common parts issue scenarios: Scenario 1 (Part not in stock) : First check other storerooms across plant sites for available stock, then initiate a purchase requisition or storeroom transfer, and finally update the work order status to Waiting on Material. Scenario 2 (Quantity mismatch) : For an under-issue where additional parts are needed, create an extra issue line for the difference. For an over-issue where too many parts were taken, use the Return action on the actuals tab to return extra parts to the storeroom. The system automatically adjusts storeroom balance and work order cost. Scenario 3 (Emergency repair) : For urgent breakdowns, issue parts immediately to perform the repair, record the material actuals on the work order once the equipment is safe, and add explanatory documentation notes to the work log. Figure 2: Decision tree for handling common parts issue scenarios How do I return unused parts? ¤ If you have leftover parts: What to do: Go to the work order . Find the issued material. Click Return action. Enter quantity to return. The system increases inventory balance, adjusts cost on work order , and records the transaction. Why accurate parts tracking matters ¤ For your organization: Correct inventory counts Accurate cost tracking Better reorder planning Reliable stock levels For you: Parts are available when needed No delays waiting for materials Clear record of what was used Easier to find parts next time Issuing parts accurately keeps inventory reliable for everyone and makes it easier to plan future work. Continue building your skills ¤ When an issue fails ¤ Learn what to check when the system won't let you issue a part to a work order . Why can't I issue materials to a work order ? Know what you have ¤ Monitor stock levels so you can see what's running low before it causes a delay. How do I track stock levels? Fix a discrepancy ¤ When the system and the shelf don't match, learn how to investigate and correct it. What happens if stock is incorrect? Related topics ¤ How do I track stock levels? docs.text: What happens if stock is incorrect? ¤ When physical inventory doesn't match system records, you need to investigate and correct it. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Common causes of stock discrepancies ¤ Common cause What to check Transaction errors Parts issued but not recorded, returns not processed Physical issues Items misplaced, wrong bin locations , damaged items System issues Data entry mistakes, incomplete transactions Figure 1 outlines the sequential six-step inventory correction process: Verify the count : recount the item to confirm physical quantities. Review transactions : look at recent activity for missed entries. Check related records : inspect work orders and receipts. Get approval if needed : obtain supervisor sign-off for large adjustments. Adjust the balance : update records by using Inventory Adjustments. Follow up : resolve underlying causes to prevent recurrence. Figure 1: The inventory correction process 💡 Tips: Best practices for inventory accuracy ¤ Daily habits: Record transactions immediately Verify before confirming Return items promptly Keep storeroom organized Report issues quickly Weekly tasks: Review high-value items Check reorder items Spot check locations Investigate variances Update procedures Monthly activities: Analyze error patterns Review adjustment reports Conduct cycle counts Train as needed Improve processes Why fix inventory errors quickly? ¤ Inventory discrepancies can cause stockouts, excess inventory , and inaccurate costs. Fixing errors quickly ensures: Accurate records No work delays Reliable stock levels Correct cost tracking Regular counting and prompt adjustments keep your inventory data trustworthy. What causes inventory errors? ¤ Transaction errors ¤ Parts issued but not recorded Returns not processed Wrong quantities entered Duplicate transactions Missing receipts Physical issues ¤ Items misplaced in storeroom Wrong bin locations Damaged or lost items Theft or shrinkage Items in wrong storeroom System issues ¤ Data entry mistakes Timing differences Incomplete transactions System errors Integration problems Figure 2 shows how three distinct sources of error result in a stock discrepancy: Transaction errors : parts issued but not recorded, returns not processed, or wrong quantities entered. Physical issues : items misplaced in the storeroom, wrong bin locations , or damaged and lost items . System issues : data entry mistakes, timing differences, or incomplete transactions. Figure 2: Common sources of inventory errors How do I identify discrepancies? ¤ During work ¤ You might notice: Item shows in stock but can't find it Physical count doesn't match system Bin is empty but system shows quantity Wrong item in labeled bin Unexpected items in storeroom Through cycle counts ¤ Regular counting reveals: Quantity differences Location errors Missing items Extra items Condition issues From reports ¤ System reports show: Negative balances, which are physically impossible Unusually high balances No movement for long periods Frequent adjustments Cost variances TODO: Add visual content A screenshot showing an inventory discrepancy report would be useful here. How do I investigate discrepancies? ¤ Step 1: Verify the physical count ¤ Before adjusting the system: Recount the item : Check all bins for this item Look in nearby locations Verify item number matches Check for similar items Check for reserved items : Items in pick lists Parts allocated to work orders Items being transferred Staged materials Look for recent transactions: Issues not yet processed Returns in progress Receipts being entered Transfers pending TODO: Add visual content A checklist for investigating discrepancies would be useful here. Step 2: Review transaction history ¤ Check recent activity: Issue transactions : Were parts recorded? Receipts : Did everything get entered? Returns : Were returns processed? Transfers : Did transfers complete? Adjustments : Previous corrections made? Look for patterns: Repeated errors with same item Specific user or storeroom Particular transaction type Time of day issues occur Step 3: Check related records ¤ Verify: Work orders : Materials recorded correctly? Receipts : All delivered stock entered? Inventory transfers : Transfers completed properly? Issues : Items picked and issued from storeroom? Figure 3 maps the four related records to check when a stock discrepancy is identified: Work orders : verify whether materials were recorded correctly against work tasks. Receipts : confirm whether all delivered stock was entered into the system. Inventory transfers : check whether transfers completed properly across locations . Issues : verify whether items were picked and issued from the storeroom. Figure 3: Related records to check when stock is incorrect How do I correct inventory ? ¤ Make adjustments ¤ Once you've verified the error: What to do: Open the Inventory application. Find the item . Go to the storeroom with error. Use Inventory Adjustments . Enter correct physical quantity. System calculates difference. Add reason for adjustment. Include detailed notes. The system updates balance, adjusts cost, records transaction, and creates audit trail. TODO: Add visual content A video showing how to adjust inventory would be useful here. Adjustment best practices ¤ Always document: What you found What you expected Why the error occurred Who discovered it When it was found Corrective action taken Get approval if needed: Large adjustments High-value items Frequent corrections Unusual circumstances Follow up: Prevent recurrence Train if needed Improve processes Monitor for patterns Types of adjustments ¤ Quantity adjustments ¤ Increase balance: Found items not recorded Receipt was missed Return not processed Transfer not completed Decrease balance: Items issued but not recorded Damaged or lost items Theft or shrinkage Items moved to another location Location adjustments ¤ Moving items : Wrong bin recorded Reorganizing storeroom Consolidating locations Correcting bin assignments Cost adjustments ¤ Correcting costs: Wrong price entered Cost method changed Vendor price correction Currency adjustments TODO: Add visual content A table comparing adjustment types would be useful here. How do I prevent inventory errors? ¤ Good practices ¤ At issue time: Record transactions immediately Verify quantities Check item numbers Confirm locations Complete transactions fully At receipt time: Count carefully Match to purchase order Verify item numbers Put in correct location Record promptly During returns: Process immediately Verify condition Return to correct bin Update system Note any issues Regular cycle counting ¤ Count frequently: High-value items weekly Fast-moving items monthly All items quarterly Random spot checks Count systematically: Follow schedule Use count books Verify before adjusting Document findings Analyze patterns TODO: Add visual content A sample cycle count schedule would be useful here. Storeroom organization ¤ Keep organized: Clear bin labels Logical layout Similar items separated Regular housekeeping Defined locations Control access: Authorized personnel only Proper training Clear procedures Accountability Security measures Handling specific scenarios ¤ Negative balance ¤ If system shows negative quantity: This shouldn't happen physically. Indicates transaction error. Review recent issues. Check for duplicate transactions. Correct immediately. Investigate cause. Large discrepancy ¤ For significant differences: Don't adjust immediately. Investigate thoroughly. Get supervisor approval. Document extensively. Implement prevention. Monitor closely. Recurring errors ¤ If same item has frequent issues: Analyze error pattern. Identify root cause. Fix process problem. Retrain if needed. Consider item changes. Monitor improvement. Figure 4 outlines the decision paths and corrective actions for three inventory discrepancy situations: Negative balance : when the system shows a negative quantity, correct it immediately by reviewing recent issues and looking for duplicate entries, then investigate the root cause. Large discrepancy : when the difference is significant, do not adjust immediately; investigate thoroughly, obtain supervisor approval, and document the findings. Recurring errors : when the same item has frequent issues, fix the process by analyzing the error pattern, identifying the root cause, and retraining staff if needed. Figure 4: How to handle different types of inventory error What's the impact of inventory errors? ¤ On operations ¤ Stockouts: Work delays Emergency orders Higher costs Service issues Excess inventory : Wasted space Tied-up cash Obsolescence risk Carrying costs On costs ¤ Direct costs: Incorrect work order costs Wrong inventory valuation Budget variances Financial reporting errors Indirect costs: Time investigating Emergency purchases Lost productivity Customer dissatisfaction On planning ¤ Poor decisions: Wrong reorder quantities Incorrect stock levels Bad purchasing decisions Inefficient operations TODO: Add visual content An infographic showing error impacts would be useful here. When should I perform physical inventory ? ¤ Full physical count ¤ Do complete inventory when: Annual audit required Major discrepancies found System implementation Storeroom reorganization Change in responsibility Cycle counting ¤ Regular partial counts: Less disruptive Continuous accuracy Catches errors early Maintains reliability Spreads workload How do I use count books? ¤ Count books help organize counting: Group items logically Schedule counts Assign counters Track completion Record results Analyze variances The system can: Generate count books Assign to users Track progress Record counts Calculate differences Create adjustments You create count books in the Count Books application. You count items in the Inventory Counting app on the desktop or in IBM Maximo Mobile. In Inventory Counting, you can: Count the items in a count book. Count items that are not in a count book. Count items and rotating assets . Set tolerances that allow for small differences between the system balance and the physical count. See alerts for differences that need a recount. Count in batches as part of a cycle count. After you count, the Reconciled? checkbox on the inventory balance shows whether the count is reconciled. [SME confirmation required: Confirm that you can open Inventory Counting in a desktop browser in Select as well as in IBM Maximo Mobile, and confirm where counts are reconciled.] TODO: Add visual content A screenshot showing a count book would be useful here. Continue building your skills ¤ Understand what your numbers mean ¤ Learn which inventory metrics matter and how to use them to keep parts available when work demands them. What metrics matter? Related topics ¤ How do I track stock levels? How do I issue parts to a job? How do I complete a job? What if I can't complete a task? docs.text: How do I track stock levels? ¤ Monitor what's in your storerooms so you know what's available, what needs reordering, and where items are located. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Stock balance types ¤ Balance type What it means Current balance Total quantity in storeroom (includes reserved items ) Available balance What you can actually use (current minus reserved) Reserved quantity Parts allocated to work orders Reorder point Minimum level before reordering 💡 Tips for success ¤ Regular monitoring: Check stock levels daily Review reorder needs weekly Analyze usage monthly Audit inventory quarterly Maintain accuracy: Issue parts promptly Return unused items Perform cycle counts Investigate discrepancies Optimize levels: Adjust reorder points based on usage Reduce slow-moving inventory Increase stock of critical items Balance cost versus availability Use reports: Stock status reports Reorder reports Usage analysis Cost reports ABC analysis: prioritize high-value items Why track stock levels? ¤ Good inventory tracking prevents stockouts and ensures parts are available when you need them. When you track stock levels, you can: Know what's available right now See what needs reordering Find where items are located Control costs Optimize storeroom space The system tracks quantities, costs, and locations automatically as items move in and out. What can I track? ¤ The Inventory application shows: Current balance How many items are in stock. Location Which storeroom and bin. Cost Current value of inventory . Reorder status Items below minimum levels. Reserved items Parts allocated to work orders . Usage history How items are being consumed. How do I view inventory levels? ¤ Check a specific item ¤ What to do: Open the Inventory application. Search by item number or description. Select the item . View the information you need: Current quantity on hand Available balance: not reserved Cost information Reorder point and minimum stock level If the item is in multiple storerooms, you can view all locations on one screen and compare quantities across sites . Check storeroom contents ¤ What to do: Open the Storerooms application. Select your storeroom. View all items stocked there: Current quantities Items below reorder point Reserved quantities Items in pick lists View by bin or lot ¤ For detailed tracking: Bin level : See exactly where items are stored Lot level : Track specific batches Condition : Monitor item condition changes Rotating assets : Track individual asset items Figure 1 illustrates the storeroom inventory hierarchy across three connected columns representing physical location , item tracking levels, and real-time balance calculations: Physical location : Navigates from Main storeroom as the primary inventory site , down through aisle and shelf coordinates such as Row A, Shelf 03, to a specific storage compartment, BIN-04. Item tracking level : From the physical bin, items branch into three tracking modes: standard inventory items tracked by item number, lot and batch tracking recording batch numbers and expiration dates, and rotating serialized assets tracking unique serial numbers. Balance calculation : Tracks inventory availability across records, where a current physical balance of 25 items minus a reserved quantity of 5 items allocated to work orders yields an available balance of 20 items ready for issue. Figure 1: Storeroom hierarchy for bin, lot, and rotating asset tracking How do I understand inventory balances? ¤ Key balance types ¤ Current balance Total quantity in storeroom Includes reserved items Shows what you physically have Available balance Current balance minus reserved What you can actually use Updates as items are reserved Reserved quantity Parts allocated to work orders Not available for other use Released when work order closes Reservations are either hard or soft. A hard reservation immediately reduces available balance and requires sufficient stock to exist. If stock is insufficient, the reservation cannot be created and work order approval may fail. A soft reservation records demand without locking stock. If your storeroom uses hard reservations and a critical spare such as a nozzle seal for Filler FL-02 runs out, technicians will not be able to reserve it at approval time, causing delays. Check which reservation type is configured for critical items . Picked quantity Items in active pick lists Being prepared for issue Not yet issued to work order How do I monitor reorder needs? ¤ Reorder point system ¤ The system tracks: Table 2: Reorder settings and when each is required ¤ Setting Required when Reorder point You want the system to flag items for reordering automatically Lead time The reorder calculation should account for procurement time. Without it, items may be flagged too late Order quantity (EOQ) You want the system to recommend how much to order, not just flag that an order is needed Safety stock Only when demand is unpredictable and you need a buffer above the reorder point When balance drops below reorder point, the system flags the item so you can replenish stock. How the reorder calculation works ¤ The system uses this formula: Order quantity = Reorder point + 1, minus quantity on order, minus available balance. The +1 means a reorder point of 0 still triggers an order when balance hits zero. Setting your reorder point equal to your minimum-on-hand target is a common misconfiguration that causes reorders to trigger one unit too early and leads to excess stock over time. Check items to reorder ¤ What to do: Filter for items below reorder point. See recommended order quantities. Check vendor information. Review lead times. Take action: Order parts from supplier or request replenishment Transfer from another storeroom Adjust reorder settings if needed How do I track item costs? ¤ Cost information available ¤ For each item , see: Average cost : Current average unit cost Last cost : Most recent purchase price Standard cost : Planned or budgeted cost Total value : Quantity × cost How costs are calculated ¤ Average cost method Weighted average of all purchases Updates with each receipt Smooths price fluctuations Most common method If a high-value emergency purchase is received, it raises the average cost for all future issues of that item until the balance normalises. This can distort maintenance cost reports for that period. For frequently used spare parts such as nozzle seals for Filler FL-02, average cost is usually appropriate. For low-volume, high-value items , consider whether standard cost gives you more predictable reporting. Standard cost method Fixed cost set in advance Doesn't change with purchases Variances tracked separately Used for budgeting How do I monitor inventory usage? ¤ Usage tracking ¤ The system records: When parts are used, from issue transactions What jobs used items , from work orders How often items are needed Usage patterns over time Analyze usage ¤ Use this information to: Identify fast-moving items Spot slow-moving inventory Adjust stock levels Improve reorder quantities Reduce excess inventory Special inventory types ¤ Rotating items ¤ For serialized assets : Track individual items Monitor asset condition See installation history Manage asset rotation Item kits ¤ For grouped items : Issue multiple items together Track kit components Maintain kit integrity Simplify common issues Table 3: Special item types comparison ¤ Item type How it works Typical example Rotating items Rebuildable units tracked by inventory balance and individual asset serial number 50 HP slurry pumps, electric drive motors, and gearboxes Item kits Pre-assembled collections of items issued together under a single kit identifier PM overhaul seal kits, filter replacement bundles Condition-enabled items Items tracked and valued by distinct physical condition rates Reconditioned spare valves, refurbished circuit breakers Lotted items Batches tracked by unique lot identifiers for expiration and manufacturer traceability Food-grade lubricants, chemical sanitizers, and specialty adhesives Common scenarios ¤ Item running low ¤ When stock is getting low: Check reorder settings. Verify lead time. Order replacement stock or transfer from another storeroom. Update reorder point if needed. Excess inventory ¤ If you have too much: Review usage history. Check for obsolete items . Transfer to other locations . Adjust reorder quantities. Consider disposal if appropriate. Can't find item ¤ If item shows in stock but you can't find it: Check bin location . Verify storeroom. Look for reserved quantity. Check pick lists. Perform physical count. Adjust if necessary. Figure 2 illustrates the diagnostic workflow when an item shows a positive stock balance in the system but cannot be found on the storeroom shelf: Diagnostic trigger : Starts when the system balance shows stock on hand, but the item is missing from its primary shelf location . Step 1 (Verify bin locations ) : Check primary, secondary, and staging bins. If found in an alternate bin, pick the item and update the bin assignment in the system. If still missing, proceed to Step 2. Step 2 (Check transfers and receipts) : Verify in-transit transfers between storerooms and recent receiving staging areas. If located in receiving or transit, complete the pending transaction. If still missing, proceed to Step 3. Step 3 (Check reservations and kits) : Inspect active work orders and staged item kits. If the item was allocated to an active work order , it is already staged for maintenance. If still missing, proceed to Step 4. Step 4 (Conduct physical count) : Count physical shelf stock across the storeroom. If a true variance is confirmed, enter an inventory adjustment in the Inventory application to reconcile the balance. Figure 2: Missing inventory item troubleshooting workflow Why accurate tracking matters ¤ Prevents stockouts: Parts available when needed No work delays Better service levels Fewer emergency orders Controls costs: Reduces excess inventory Optimizes stock levels Improves cash flow Lowers carrying costs Improves planning: Better reorder decisions Accurate budgeting Informed purchasing Efficient operations Good stock visibility means fewer surprises when jobs need parts and fewer delays when it matters most. Continue building your skills ¤ Fix a discrepancy ¤ When the system and the shelf don't match, learn how to investigate and correct it. What happens if stock is incorrect? Understand what your numbers mean ¤ Learn which inventory metrics matter and how to use them to keep parts available when work demands them. What metrics matter? docs.text: Why can't I issue materials to a work order ? ¤ Material issues fail when required fields or relationships are missing. Looking to troubleshoot material issues right away? Skip to material issue troubleshooting checklist ↓ What to check first ¤ Storeroom, item , and quantity are valid ¤ The system needs to know: Which storeroom the part is coming from Which item you're issuing, using the correct item number How many you're issuing, as a valid quantity What to do : Verify all three pieces of information are correct and the item exists in that storeroom. Work order exists and is chargeable ¤ You can only issue materials to work orders that: Exist in the system Are in a status that allows charging Haven't been closed or completed What to do : Check the work order status . If it's closed or in a non-chargeable status , you'll need to reopen it or change the status first. Required fields are populated ¤ Some organizations require additional information: Bin location : Where in the storeroom the part is stored Unit of measure : The unit you're issuing, such as each, box, or meter GL account : For cost tracking What to do : Fill in all required fields. If you're not sure what's required, check with your supervisor or system administrator. Why didn't inventory update after issuing? ¤ Material issues should trigger inventory and cost updates simultaneously. If they didn't, something went wrong. Figure 1 illustrates the parts issue validation and update workflow: 1. Issue entry methods : Work begins from an active work order , at the storeroom counter, or via the mobile app. 2. Validation checks : The system checks four conditions: valid storeroom and item number, chargeable work order status , sufficient available storeroom balance, and populated required fields. 3. Simultaneous updates : When all validation checks pass, the system performs three actions at the same time: deducts the physical balance from the storeroom, records actual material costs on the work order , and evaluates whether remaining stock breaches the reorder point. If any validation check fails, none of these updates occur. Figure 1: Parts issue and material transaction workflow Transaction didn't complete ¤ The issue might have failed partway through. What to check : Look for error messages you might have missed Verify the transaction appears in the work order 's materials list Check if inventory balance changed What to do : If the transaction didn't complete, try issuing again. If it appears to have worked but inventory didn't update, contact your system administrator. Wrong storeroom or item used ¤ If you issued from the wrong storeroom or selected the wrong item , the inventory update happened in the wrong place. What to do : Return the incorrectly issued material Issue the correct item from the correct storeroom Add notes explaining the correction Issue not confirmed ¤ Some systems require confirmation after issuing. What to do : Check if there's a confirmation step you need to complete, or verify the issue was saved properly. Why do users issue parts incorrectly? ¤ Common causes of issuing errors: Confusion between planned vs unplanned materials ¤ Planned materials : Already listed on the work order , just need to be issued Unplanned materials : Need to be added and issued What to do : Check if the material is already planned on the work order . If so, issue it directly. If not, add it first, then issue. Multiple ways to issue ¤ You can issue materials from: The work order , which is the most common The inventory application Mobile apps Each method works slightly differently. What to do : Use the method your organization prefers, typically issuing directly from the work order . Missing understanding of cost tracking ¤ When you issue materials, costs are automatically recorded against the work order . Why it matters : Incorrect issues lead to: Wrong costs on work orders Inaccurate inventory balances Poor cost reporting What to do : Always issue materials to the correct work order and verify quantities are accurate. Why are costs or usage incorrect? ¤ Issues are often caused by: Issuing to the wrong work order ¤ If you issue materials to the wrong work order , costs are charged incorrectly. What to do : Return the material from the wrong work order Issue it to the correct work order Add notes explaining the correction Using incorrect quantities or units ¤ Issuing the wrong quantity or using the wrong unit of measure causes cost and inventory errors. What to do : Double-check quantities before issuing Verify the unit of measure is correct Return excess materials if you issued too much Skipping planned reservations ¤ If materials were reserved for a work order , issuing different materials can cause confusion. What to do : Issue the reserved materials when possible, or update the reservation if you need to use different materials. Material issue troubleshooting checklist ¤ Use this checklist to identify why a material transaction failed to record: Table 1: Material issue troubleshooting checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Chargeable work order status Work order is in an approved or in-progress status (APPR, WSCHED, or INPRG), not WAPPR, CAN, or CLOSE [ ] Active storeroom Selected storeroom record exists and is set to ACTIVE status [ ] Inventory item record Item is linked to the storeroom with an established inventory record [ ] Bin balance availability Storeroom bin has sufficient quantity on hand, or the storeroom allows negative balance [ ] Unit of measure alignment Issue unit on the transaction matches the inventory issue unit defined for the item [ ] Storeroom user authorization User account has security authorization to issue materials from the selected storeroom Continue building your skills ¤ Know what you have before you issue ¤ Monitor stock levels so you can see what's available in each storeroom before you start a job. How do I track stock levels? Fix a discrepancy ¤ When the system and the shelf don't match, learn how to investigate and correct it. What happens if stock is incorrect? Related topics ¤ How do I issue parts to a job? What happens if stock is incorrect? How do I track stock levels? What if I can't complete a task? Still stuck? ¤ If this page did not answer your question: Browse all Q&A: Get answers In the product: Click the help icon (?) in the top right For a specific field: Click the field name or press Alt+F1
