docs.text: How do I configure IBM Maximo Mobile for my team? ¤ IBM Maximo Mobile lets technicians, supervisors, and inventory clerks view and complete work, manage inventory , and update records from their mobile device. As an administrator, you configure the defaults that control how mobile devices sync data, which map app your team uses for navigation, and how service requests and work orders behave in the app. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Configure mobile settings before your team downloads and signs in to IBM Maximo Mobile. Changes to defaults apply to all users. Set up Map Manager before configuring mobile map settings. The map app you choose here opens the map that Map Manager provides. Start with the defaults and adjust after your team has used the app in the field. Most settings can be changed at any time. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Data sync options ¤ Each data category offers the same three options. Choose the option that balances data freshness against bandwidth and device storage for your team. Option What it does Reload all data Downloads the full data set each time a sync runs. Use when you need your team to have complete, current data regardless of what changed. Update recent changes Downloads only data that changed since the last sync. Faster and lighter on bandwidth. Suitable for most teams. Do not download data Skips this data category during sync. Use when the data is not needed on the device. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the option labels and where you set them in Select. The Maximo Manage documentation calls the options "Complete", "Only delta", and "Do not download", and lists them under "Worklist data" and "Supporting data" in the Mobile administration app. This page uses "Record data" and "Supporting data".] Before you start ¤ Confirm that your role has permission to update mobile configuration settings in Maximo Application Suite Select. Confirm that Map Manager is configured if you plan to use map navigation. See How do I set up maps? . Confirm that labor records and security groups are set up so technicians can be assigned work. See How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? . [SME confirmation required: Identify which Maximo Application Suite Select roles can update mobile configuration settings.] Open the mobile configuration ¤ Open the Mobile properties application. Choose how mobile data is synchronized ¤ The Default data sync settings section controls what data mobile devices download when a user syncs the app. Configure each category separately. Record data ¤ Record data controls how work orders and service requests are synced to the device. Select one of the three options described in Table 1 . Supporting data ¤ Supporting data controls how lookup data, such as asset records and location lists, is synced to the device. Select one of the three options described in Table 1 . Map data ¤ Map data controls whether map data is downloaded to the device. Select Update recent changes or Reload all data to download map data to devices. Select Do not download data to skip map data during sync. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the exact option labels for map data in the Maximo Application Suite Select design. The Maximo Manage equivalent is a single "Download map data" toggle rather than the three-option model.] Choose the map app ¤ The Map settings section controls which map application IBM Maximo Mobile opens when a user navigates to a location . The available options are: Apple Maps Google Maps Waze Select the map app that your team uses. [SME confirmation required: Confirm whether map app options are platform-specific (for example, Apple Maps on iOS only) or available on all supported platforms. Confirm whether a browser fallback option appears in the final Maximo Application Suite Select design.] Configure service request behavior ¤ The SR mobile settings section controls how the service request experience works in IBM Maximo Mobile. Enable follow similar requests ¤ Enable follow similar requests allows technicians to see service requests that are similar to the one they are creating or viewing. Turn this setting on or off depending on whether your team uses this feature. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the exact effect of enabling or disabling this setting, and whether "similar requests" is defined by a matching location, asset, description, or another criterion.] Service address priority ¤ Service address priority determines which address IBM Maximo Mobile uses when a service request has more than one address associated with it. Select the priority value that reflects how your organization resolves address conflicts. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the available priority values and their order of precedence in the final Maximo Application Suite Select design.] Enable show all systems ¤ A system is a hierarchy of locations . Enable show all systems controls whether users can select locations outside their primary system when they create service requests. For more about systems, see Can I organize the same locations more than one way? Turn this setting on if your team reports problems at locations outside their own primary system. Configure work order behavior ¤ Two sections control how work orders behave in IBM Maximo Mobile: Work order status and Miscellaneous settings . Work order status ¤ Work order status controls which status values are available to technicians when they update a work order in the app. Complete status sets the status value that IBM Maximo Mobile applies when a technician marks a work order as complete. [SME confirmation required: Confirm whether COMP is the default complete status value in the Maximo Application Suite Select design, and whether technicians see the status code or a plain-language label.] Allow go to report work ¤ Allow go to report work controls whether technicians see an option to navigate to the report work view from the work order . Turn this on if your team records labor , materials, or other actuals directly against work orders in the mobile app. [SME confirmation required: Confirm the exact label used in the Maximo Application Suite Select interface for the report work view. Do not use "Report Works" or "Actuals" unless those terms appear in the final product interface.] Date attributes ¤ The Miscellaneous settings section includes settings that control which date attributes are visible in the app. [SME confirmation required: Confirm which date attributes are exposed in the Maximo Application Suite Select design (for example, scheduled start, scheduled finish, target start) and whether the SCHEDULE default selection is confirmed in the final design.] Configure travel guidance ¤ The Travel settings section includes Enable travel prompt and Travel radius . Use these settings if your team tracks travel time to a work location . What to do next ¤ After you configure IBM Maximo Mobile, prepare your team to use it: How do I automate communication? : Set up real-time push notifications so field technicians receive alerts on their mobile devices when work is assigned. How do I complete a work order ? : Understand what technicians experience when completing work in the app. How do I find my work? : See how technicians and supervisors access their work queue in IBM Maximo Mobile. Share with your team ¤ Send technicians, supervisors, and inventory clerks to How do I get IBM Maximo Mobile? for download and sign-in instructions. Continue building your skills ¤ Load your existing data ¤ With your system configured, bring in your locations , assets , and inventory records. How do I prepare data for import? Related topics ¤ How do I set up maps? How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? How do I automate communication? Administrator: Add users

docs.text: What is the correct load order? ¤ Import order matters. Referenced records must exist before records that use them, and parent records must exist before child records. Figure 1 outlines the five sequential steps of the data onboarding pathway: Understand the correct load order : review dependency rules so supporting data and parent records load first. Plan your location and asset hierarchies : design physical places and equipment breakdown structures top-down. Prepare data for import : download CSV templates from Data Management, format columns as text, and validate fields. Get data into the system : upload files, run preview validation, and commit the import. Fix import errors : diagnose rejected records in error logs and re-import corrected rows. Figure 1: The five-step data onboarding pathway Why does load order matter? ¤ Child records reference parent records. If the parent does not exist yet, the child import fails. Similarly, if a record references supporting data that does not exist, the import fails. Example : You cannot create Ice cream main plant > Production building > Filling line room if Ice cream main plant and Production building do not exist. Recommended import order ¤ 1. Reference data used by locations and assets ¤ Import supporting records before importing locations or assets that reference them. What to import first : GL accounts Service addresses Calendars and shifts Failure classes Vendors and manufacturers Asset type values Classifications and specifications Addresses, including bill-to and ship-to addresses Why this matters : Locations and assets reference these records. If the referenced data does not exist, the import fails. 2. Locations in hierarchy order ¤ Import locations from top to bottom of the hierarchy: Top-level locations first , such as Ice cream main plant Second-level locations next , such as Production building Lowest-level locations last , such as Filling line room What to check : Verify the location hierarchy before importing Import parent locations before child locations Confirm that system location references use valid values Confirm that each child location references the correct parent Import hierarchies sequentially Hierarchies require sequential loading from the top down. Import parent locations first, then their children. 3. Assets and asset relationships ¤ Import assets after their locations exist. What to check : Location references are valid Parent assets exist, if you use asset hierarchies. Learn how to structure equipment packages in How do I plan my asset hierarchy? . For asset hierarchies : Import parent assets before child assets or subassemblies Verify that each child asset references the correct parent asset Verify that the parent asset exists and is at the expected location 4. Other records that reference locations or assets ¤ Import other records that depend on locations and assets : Work orders , which reference assets and locations Inventory and storerooms, which reference locations Common hierarchy patterns ¤ Location hierarchies ¤ Correct order : Top-level location , such as Ice cream main plant Second-level location , such as Production building Lower-level location , such as Filling line room Further sub- locations , if applicable What happens if you import in the wrong order : Child locations fail because their parent does not exist. What to do : Sort your import file so parent records come before child records. Asset hierarchies ¤ If you use parent-child asset relationships: Correct order : Parent assets Child assets or subassemblies What to check : Parent asset IDs are correct Each child asset references the correct parent Parent assets exist at the expected location Parent-child relationships ¤ General rule : Always import parents before children. What to check : Parent location IDs are correct Hierarchy levels are properly defined System location references are valid What to do : Verify all parent records exist before importing child records. Data onboarding roadmap ¤ Follow these five steps in sequence to load your facility data: Table 1: The five steps of data onboarding and the guide for each ¤ Step Action Guide 1 Understand load order Review dependencies and ensure referenced records and parent locations exist first. What is the correct load order? 2 Plan your location and asset hierarchies Map your locations and equipment top-down on paper before creating records. How do I plan my location hierarchy? How do I plan my asset hierarchy? 3 Prepare data for import Download CSV templates from Data Management, format ID columns as text, and clean fields. How do I prepare data for import? 4 Get data into the system Upload CSV files in Data Management, validate rows in preview mode, and commit the import. How do I get data into the system? 5 Fix import errors Diagnose preview errors, correct source CSV rows, and re-import failed records. How do I fix import errors? Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Plan your hierarchies ¤ Before preparing spreadsheet files, sketch your locations and equipment top-down to avoid orphan records and grouping errors. How do I plan my location hierarchy? How do I plan my asset hierarchy? Related skills ¤ How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? : Classify every facility entity, machine, and consumable wear item accurately. How do I plan my asset hierarchy? : Structure equipment packages, subassemblies, and maintainable components. How do I prepare data for import? : Format and clean your CSV files and prevent spreadsheet corruption. How do I get data into the system? : Upload and preview your records in the Data Management application. How do I fix import errors? : Troubleshoot missing parents and referenced record failures. Related topics ¤ Locations What is an asset ? How do locations , assets , and work orders work together? Which object structure do I use for each data type?

docs.text: How do I create inspection forms? ¤ Digital inspection forms replace paper clipboards with structured, interactive checklists on mobile devices. Technicians and inspectors use inspection forms to execute safety audits, hygiene checklists, equipment condition assessments, and routine operator rounds. In Maximo Application Suite Select, you design forms in the Inspection Forms application. Technicians and inspectors complete them in the Inspections role-based app or directly within mobile work orders . Looking to verify your inspection form setup right away? Skip to inspection form verification checklist ↓ What you can capture on an inspection form ¤ The Inspection Forms application gives you flexible ways to capture exact field observations. You can create questions such as: A pass or fail check, for example, whether the sanitary seal on Filler FL-02 is intact. A choice from a standard list of values, for example, lubricant condition rated as clear, cloudy, or dark. A meter reading that updates the asset meter , for example, discharge pressure on the cold storage compressor. A number that you track without updating a meter , for example, ambient warehouse temperature. A photo or file, for example, a photo of a scored drive shaft. A signature, for example, sanitation supervisor sign-off after a clean-in-place flush. The application offers more ways to capture answers than these examples. Use them as a starting point, and explore the options when you design a question. Figure 1 illustrates the inspection form lifecycle from initial authoring to field execution: Step 1 (Design) : build the form using three core question types: Single or domain choice : pass or fail checks and domain picklist selections. Meter or numeric entry : readings that update asset meters or track standalone values. Media or signature : photo attachments and digital sign-offs. Step 2 (Activate and link) : activate the draft template and attach it to PM schedules, route stops, or work orders . Step 3 (Field execution) : technicians complete the interactive checklist in the Inspections role-based app or on mobile work orders . Figure 1: Inspection form design, configuration, and field execution lifecycle Step 1: Create a form template ¤ You create and revise inspection forms in the Inspection Forms application. To open it, use the Find navigation item field and search for Inspection Forms. When you design a form, you can: Give the form a clear, descriptive name, such as Filler FL-02 Daily Sanitation & Mechanical Inspection . Choose the purpose of the form, such as an inspection, an audit, or a round. Add instructions, such as safety lockout procedures or required personal protective equipment. Add the questions that make up your checklist. Mark critical questions as required, so that technicians cannot complete the form without answering them. For a meter reading question, you also choose the meter that the answer updates, such as DISCH_PSI . 💡 Tip: Use conditional logic for failed steps ¤ Configure conditional questions so that when a technician marks an item as a failure, the form reveals follow-up questions. For example, require a photo and an explanatory note. This guarantees complete failure documentation. Step 2: Configure conditional response logic ¤ Conditional rules keep inspection checklists compact while capturing detailed evidence when problems occur. For example, you can set up a pass or fail question so that a failed answer asks the technician to take a photo of the defect and describe the observed damage. Step 3: Activate the form template ¤ Inspection forms start in draft status . Activate a form before you assign it to work orders or preventive maintenance schedules. When updates are needed later, create a revision of the active form. The existing version remains active for in-progress work until you activate the new revision. Step 4: Link inspection forms to maintenance workflows ¤ Once a form is active, you can attach it to automate field checklists: PM schedules: Attach the form to a PM so that every generated work order includes the digital checklist. Route stops: Attach specific forms to individual route stops to guide technicians through multi-room plant rounds. Work orders : Add a form to a work order or to a specific task on the work order . Inspection form verification checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm your inspection forms are configured for reliable field execution. Table 1: Inspection form setup checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Clear title and instructions Form specifies safety precautions and required tools in the header [ ] Mandatory flags configured Critical regulatory and safety questions are marked as required [ ] Meter bindings verified Meter reading questions connect to valid continuous or gauge meters [ ] Conditional logic tested Marking failure options reveals required photo and description prompts [ ] Status set to Active Form is promoted from draft to active for work order selection [ ] PM or Route associations Recurring maintenance schedules have the approved form template attached Related topics ¤ How inspections work How do I plan recurring maintenance? How do I set up meters and meter groups? How do I standardize across teams?

docs.text: How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? ¤ When setting up Maximo Application Suite Select, every physical entity in your plant or facility must be classified as one of three primary record types: a location , an asset , or a spare part. Making the right classification before importing data ensures accurate maintenance history, simplified storeroom operations, and clean drilldown navigation in Maximo Mobile and desktop applications. Misclassifying entities leads to cluttered asset registers and duplicate data entry. For more about planning equipment structures, see How do I plan my asset hierarchy? Looking to verify your record classification right away? Skip to classification decision checklist ↓ As outlined in What is the correct load order? , locations and items are loaded before maintainable assets are established. Video 1: Deciding between locations, assets, and spare parts (about 2 minutes). [Video in production, placeholder preview for design review] The three-way classification model ¤ Maximo Application Suite Select uses three distinct record types to track facilities, machinery, and replacement materials. Figure 1 illustrates the three-tier classification hierarchy: Location : a physical place where work happens, such as Filling line room , which stays in place and retains room-level history. Asset : maintainable equipment operating within the location , such as Filler FL-02 , including serialized child subassemblies such as drive motor MTR-DRV-01 . Spare part : consumable replacement items cataloged in Item Master and referenced on the asset 's Spare Parts tab, such as flange gaskets, o-rings, mechanical seals, and fuses. Figure 1: The three-way classification model in Maximo Application Suite Select 1. Location : A place where work happens ¤ A location represents a place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired. A location can be a building or room, but it can also be a section of a map grid or a telephone pole: Primary purpose : Tracks the place, accumulates its maintenance history, and provides the structure for your plant. Key characteristic : A location stays in place when the machinery in it is replaced or moved, so its history stays with the location . Examples : Production building , Filling line room , Mixing room , Main storeroom . Application : Locations application. 2. Asset : Maintainable equipment ¤ An asset represents a specific piece of serialized equipment or subassembly that operates at a location : Primary purpose : Tracks the lifecycle, maintenance costs, runtime meters , failure history, and work orders for a specific machine. Key characteristic : Assets can move between locations , go into a storeroom for repair, or transfer to another line while retaining their complete work history. Examples : Filler FL-02 , Syrup Pump P-101 , Drive motor MTR-01 . Application : Assets application. 3. Spare part: Consumable replacement item ¤ A spare part represents a stocked or non-stocked replacement material cataloged in the Item Master: Primary purpose : Manages inventory balances in storerooms and allows parts to be issued and charged directly to work orders . Key characteristic : Spare parts are consumed or discarded during maintenance. They do not track individual serial numbers, separate runtime meters , or independent work histories. Examples : Flange gaskets, o-rings, mechanical seals, replacement filters, fuses, drive belts. Applications : Item Master, Storerooms, and the Spare Parts tab on asset records. The four-question decision framework ¤ To classify any physical item or facility entity, follow these four sequential decision questions: Figure 2 outlines the decision pathway through the four classification questions: Question 1 (Place) : if the entity is a place where work happens, create a location in the Locations application. Otherwise, proceed to Question 2. Question 2 (Maintainable equipment) : if it is maintainable equipment with a serial number or nameplate, create an asset in the Assets application anchored to its location . Otherwise, proceed to Question 3. Question 3 (Rebuildable storeroom unit) : if it is a rebuildable unit cycling through storeroom inventory , create a rotating asset using Item Master and Assets . Otherwise, proceed to Question 4. Question 4 (Consumable wear part) : if it is a consumable wear part replaced during repairs, catalog it as a spare part in Item Master and link it to the asset 's Spare Parts tab. Figure 2: The four-question classification decision framework Question 1: Is it a place where work happens? ¤ Ask: "Does this record represent a room, building, bay, outdoor area, or other place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired?" If yes , create a location . If no , proceed to Question 2. Question 2: Is it maintainable equipment that retains its own history? ¤ Ask: "Does this equipment carry a unique serial number or manufacturer nameplate, undergo regular overhauls or preventive maintenance , track runtime meters , or move between locations ?" If yes , create an asset and anchor it to its operating location . If no , proceed to Question 3. Question 3: Is it a rebuildable unit that moves through storeroom inventory ? ¤ Ask: "Is this a standard motor, pump, or gearbox that is stocked in the storeroom as inventory , issued to a machine, pulled for overhaul when it fails, and returned to stock?" If yes , create a rotating item in Item Master and track the serialized unit as an asset . If no , proceed to Question 4. Question 4: Is it a consumable part replaced and discarded during servicing? ¤ Ask: "When this item fails, is it thrown away and replaced with a new one from the storeroom without tracking individual overhaul history?" If yes , catalog the spare part in Item Master and link it to the parent asset 's Spare Parts tab. Boundary cases: How to classify tricky items ¤ Some physical items sit on the boundary between locations , assets , and spare parts. Use these real-world examples from the ice cream plant to guide your decisions. Table 1: Boundary cases for classifying tricky items ¤ Equipment or item Correct record type Why it is classified this way Conveyor line routing Location The path through the building is a place that stays the same when the conveyor equipment changes. Conveyor drive package Asset The motorized mechanical drive has a nameplate, PM schedule, and runtime meter . Conveyor belt and rollers Spare part Consumable wear components issued from storerooms and replaced during repairs. 50 HP rebuildable drive motor Asset Serialized rotating equipment that undergoes shop overhauls and bearing replacements. Fractional throwaway fan motor Spare part Inexpensive non-rebuildable unit; replaced and scrapped upon failure. Calibrated safety relief valve Asset Requires mandatory inspection certification, calibration records, and test history. Manual isolation ball valve Spare part Standard pipe fitting; replaced and discarded upon failure without dedicated history. Main electrical switchgear cabinet Asset High-voltage distribution cabinet installed in an electrical room location . Cabinet power circuit breaker Child asset Maintainable subassembly with its own trip testing and maintenance history. Cabinet fuses and terminal blocks Spare part Consumables cataloged in Item Master and issued to electrical repair work orders . Figure 3: Boundary classification example for a conveyor system In Figure 3, a conveyor line illustrates how to divide complex equipment across the three classification tiers: Location : Packaging zone provides the route where the conveyor operates. Parent asset : Conveyor CV-01 is the main maintainable equipment package with its own operating history and PM schedule. Child asset : Drive motor MTR-DRV-02 is a serialized rotating subassembly tracked for shop overhauls and rewinds. Spare parts : Wear items like modular belt sections, drive rollers, and guide bearings live on the Spare Parts tab and are issued directly to repair work orders . 💡 Tip: Using the Spare Parts tab for consumable parts ¤ Never create asset records for wear parts like gaskets, o-rings, bearings, or filters. Instead, add these stocked items to the Spare Parts tab of the parent asset in the Assets application. Technicians can view the approved bill of materials directly on active work orders and reserve parts from storeroom inventory with one click. Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your understanding before building your records. Problem 1: The 1:1 Location -to- Asset trap ¤ A maintenance planner creates a separate location record for every pump, motor, and machine in the plant, such as creating Filler FL-02 Operating Location to hold Filler FL-02 . Figure 4 illustrates the anti-pattern where artificial location records are created for individual machines, showing Filling line room divided into duplicate locations Filler FL-02 Operating Location for asset Filler FL-02 and Syrup Pump P-101 Operating Location for asset Syrup Pump P-101 . Figure 4: Problem 1: The 1:1 location-to-asset anti-pattern What goes wrong when equipment is replaced or when technicians navigate in Maximo Mobile? Show the answer Creating a 1:1 location for every asset doubles data entry, clutters navigation trees, and destroys asset mobility. When Filler FL-02 is moved or overhauled, planners must rename or reconfigure the location record. Technicians also lose the ability to see all equipment operating inside a single room. What to do instead: Create one location for the room, such as Filling line room , and place multiple assets directly inside that room location . Figure 5 shows the correct structure where the single room location Filling line room contains three independent assets : Filler FL-02 , Syrup Pump P-101 , and Feed Conveyor CV-01 . Figure 5: Solution 1: One location containing multiple assets Problem 2: The over-assetization trap ¤ To help technicians find every part during repairs, a team creates asset records for all internal o-rings, flange bolts, and fuses under Filler FL-02 . What happens to storeroom operations and asset drilldown trees? Show the answer The database becomes flooded with thousands of static records that never receive individual work orders . Asset searches become cluttered, and storeroom clerks cannot issue replacement parts through normal inventory stock balances because the items were modeled as assets instead of inventory materials. What to do instead: Catalog replacement materials in the Item Master and link them to Filler FL-02 through the Spare Parts tab. When work is performed, technicians select items from the spare parts list and charge them directly to the work order . Problem 3: Modeling a building or room as an asset ¤ A data team imports Production building and Cold storage as asset records so they can attach equipment as child assets . What happens when supervisors look for work across a facility? Show the answer Buildings and rooms are places, not maintainable equipment. Modeling places as assets breaks filtering by location in Maximo Mobile and prevents accurate tracking of room and building maintenance. What to do instead: Model buildings, floors, and rooms in the location hierarchy under the Locations application. Anchor equipment records into their respective operating location records. Follow the layout guidelines in How do I plan my location hierarchy? . Problem 4: Throwaway vs rebuildable motors ¤ The ice cream plant uses two types of motors: large 50 HP homogenizer drive motors that cost thousands of dollars to rewind and rebuild, and small fractional horsepower exhaust fan motors that cost fifty dollars and are scrapped when they fail. How should each motor type be classified? Show the answer 50 HP Homogenizer drive motor : Model as an asset using a rotating item record. It carries a unique serial number, tracks operating hours, moves between the machine, storeroom, and repair shop, and accumulates overhaul costs across its lifecycle. Fractional exhaust fan motor : Model as a spare part in Item Master. When a fan motor fails, a replacement is issued from the storeroom to the work order , and the failed motor is discarded. Common classification mistakes ¤ When classifying facility records, avoid these common mistakes: Creating a matching location for every asset record. Modeling consumable wear parts, bolts, or gaskets as asset records. Creating asset records for rooms, buildings, or outdoor areas. Failing to use the Spare Parts tab for approved equipment bills of materials. Treating throwaway non-rebuildable items as serialized assets . A clean classification model keeps your asset register concise, your storeroom inventory accurate, and your hierarchy trees easy to navigate. Classification decision checklist ¤ Before loading records into Maximo Application Suite Select, verify each classification decision: Table 2: Classification checklist ¤ Check Classification item What to verify [ ] Places as locations Buildings, rooms, and storerooms are created in the Locations application. [ ] Maintainable machines as assets Equipment with serial numbers, PM schedules, or runtime meters is created in the Assets application. [ ] One location holds multiple assets Rooms contain multiple assets rather than creating artificial 1:1 location records. [ ] Consumables in Item Master Wear parts, gaskets, seals, and fuses are cataloged in Item Master, not the Assets application. [ ] Spare Parts tabs populated Replacement parts are linked to parent assets on the Spare Parts tab for fast work order selection. [ ] Rotating items identified Rebuildable motors and pumps that cycle through storerooms are configured as rotating items . TODO: Confirm with a subject matter expert [SME confirmation required: Confirm whether an item can be both an asset and a location , such as an air conditioning compressor in an HVAC system, and how to describe it here. Confirm whether Rotating Items and Item Assembly Structures are fully supported in Maximo Application Suite Select data loader templates, and verify the maximum recommended spare parts per asset tab.] Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next steps: Plan your hierarchies ¤ With your classification decisions established, plan the location and equipment hierarchies for your facility. How do I plan my asset hierarchy? : Build your equipment breakdown structure and configure parent machines and subassemblies. docs.text: How do I get data into the system? ¤ Use Data Management to import your existing records into IBM Maximo Application Suite Select from a CSV file. This is how you bring in locations , assets , items , and other data in bulk during setup, or any time you need to add or update a large number of records. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Always download the export template first. The template shows you the exact column names and format the system expects. Keep your CSV file under 500 KB. Larger files need to be split into smaller batches. Import one data type at a time, in the correct sequence. See What is the correct load order? for the import sequence. Format ID columns as text in your spreadsheet application before entering data. Spreadsheet applications such as Microsoft Excel can silently reformat IDs as numbers, which breaks the import. Run a small test batch of 5 to 10 records before importing hundreds. This lets you catch format problems quickly. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: What you can import ¤ Data type When to import Locations Sites , buildings, areas, and functional locations where assets are installed Assets Equipment and infrastructure your organization maintains Items Inventory parts and materials stocked in your storeroom GL accounts Cost codes and account structures How to get the correct template ¤ Before filling in your data, use the Data Management application to download a template or export sample records with the correct column names and structure. What to do: In the Find navigation item field, search for Data Management and open it. Select the data type or object structure you want to import, such as locations or assets . Click Export data or download the template for that data type. Open the downloaded CSV file in a spreadsheet application to review the required columns and format. Note If you need a breakdown of the specific column fields for each data type, see Which object structure do I use for each data type? and How do I prepare data for import? . How to import your data ¤ Once your CSV file is prepared and validated: What to do: In the Find navigation item field, search for Data Management and open it. Select the data type or object structure that matches your file. Click Import data . Click Browse and select your prepared CSV file. Select Import preview to check for errors before committing the import. Review any errors flagged in the preview. Fix any issues in your CSV file and upload again if needed. Once the preview is clean, clear Import preview and click Import to run the full import. Review the import summary and row counts to confirm that all records were created successfully. [SME confirmation required: confirm exact UI labels for Import data button, template downloads, and Import preview checkbox in the MAS Select Data Management application — these may differ from Maximo Manage] What happens during import ¤ When you import a file, the system: Reads each row in your CSV Validates each field against system rules Creates or updates the records Reports any rows that failed, with the reason Failed rows do not stop the rest of the import. The system processes every row and reports failures at the end. How to fix import errors ¤ After importing, review the error report: Missing required field : A column that the system requires was blank. Fill in the value and re-import that row. Invalid value : A field contained a value that doesn't match the system's valid values. For example, a status code that doesn't exist, or a site ID that isn't set up yet. Record already exists : You are trying to create a record with an ID that already exists. Either update the existing record instead, or use a different ID. Parent record not found : A referenced record doesn't exist yet. Import the parent record first. See What is the correct load order? . For a full list of import error causes and fixes, see How do I fix import errors? . File size limits ¤ The maximum file size for a single import is 500 KB. If your data exceeds 500 KB: Split the file into smaller batches. Import each batch separately, in the same order. Wait for each batch to complete before importing the next. Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Fix errors when an import fails ¤ Not every import goes smoothly. Learn how to diagnose preview errors, correct source CSV rows, and re-import failed records. How do I fix import errors? Related skills ¤ What metrics matter? : Once your data is loaded, check whether the system is performing as expected. How do I plan my location hierarchy? : Review location structure rules and parent-child best practices. How do I plan my asset hierarchy? : Structure equipment packages, subassemblies, and maintainable components. What is the correct load order? : Review the full five-step data onboarding roadmap. docs.text: Which object structure do I use for each data type? ¤ When you import data into Maximo Application Suite Select, you use an object structure to define what you're loading. Think of an object structure as a spreadsheet template that defines the columns available for a particular type of data, such as assets or locations . You pick the template that matches what you're loading, then fill it with your data. Use this reference to find the correct object structure for each data type. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Object structure by data type ¤ [SME confirmation required: Verify all object structure names against the Maximo Application Suite Select Data Management application before publishing. Names noted with * are unconfirmed and may differ from standard Maximo Manage names.] Data type Object structure Notes Asset MXAPIASSET Use for importing asset records, including asset numbers, descriptions, locations , and classifications. Inventory MXAPIINVENTORY [SME confirmation required: Confirm the correct object structure name and usage for inventory imports in Maximo Application Suite Select.] Item MXAPIITEM Use for importing item records. Job plan MXAPIJOBPLAN [SME confirmation required: Confirm the correct object structure name and usage for job plan imports in Maximo Application Suite Select.] Labor MXAPILABOR [SME confirmation required: Confirm the correct object structure name and usage for labor imports in Maximo Application Suite Select.] Location MXAPIOPERLOC Use for importing operating locations and location hierarchies. Meter MXAPIMETER [SME confirmation required: Confirm the correct object structure name and usage for meter imports in Maximo Application Suite Select.] PM/Master PM MXAPIPM [SME confirmation required: Confirm the correct object structure name and usage for PM and Master PM imports in Maximo Application Suite Select.] Service Item MXAPISERVITEM [SME confirmation required: Confirm the correct object structure name and usage for service item imports in Maximo Application Suite Select.] Common fields by data type ¤ Assets ( MXAPIASSET ) ¤ [SME confirmation required: Confirm the required and commonly used fields for asset imports in Maximo Application Suite Select. The following are common fields in standard Maximo Manage and require validation.] Table 2: Location fields by object structure ¤ Field Description Required ASSETNUM Unique identifier for the asset Yes SITEID The site the asset belongs to Yes DESCRIPTION Short description of the asset Recommended LOCATION The operating location of the asset No ASSETTYPE The asset type classification No STATUS Asset status , such as OPERATING or DECOMMISSIONED No SERIALNUM Serial number of the asset No VENDOR Vendor or manufacturer name No Locations ( MXAPIOPERLOC ) ¤ [SME confirmation required: Confirm the required and commonly used fields for location imports in Maximo Application Suite Select. The following are common fields in standard Maximo Manage and require validation.] Table 3: Asset fields by object structure ¤ Field Description Required LOCATION Unique identifier for the location Yes SITEID The site the location belongs to Yes DESCRIPTION Short description of the location Recommended TYPE Location type, such as OPERATING Yes PARENT Parent location identifier for hierarchy No STATUS Location status , such as OPERATING No What to do next ¤ How do I prepare data for import? : Format your import file correctly before loading data. What is the correct load order? : Import data in the correct sequence to avoid reference errors. How do I fix import errors? : Troubleshoot common import failures. docs.text: How do I plan my asset hierarchy? ¤ Your asset hierarchy is the equipment breakdown structure of your facility. It organizes machinery, subassemblies, and critical maintainable components into a parent-child relationship operating within your locations . When onboarding data into Maximo Application Suite Select, planning your asset hierarchy follows the creation of your location hierarchy, as outlined in What is the correct load order? and How do I plan my location hierarchy? . Looking to verify your asset hierarchy structure right away? Skip to asset hierarchy planning checklist ↓ An asset hierarchy organizes equipment into parent machines and their components. It allows maintenance teams to track the lifecycle of serialized equipment, schedule overhauls at the machine or component level, and move subassemblies across the plant without losing work history. A small operation can keep it simple. Avoid adding consumable parts, which clutter drilldown trees. Video 1: Building an effective asset hierarchy (about 2 minutes). [Video in production, placeholder preview for design review] Core principles for planning your hierarchy ¤ Before loading equipment records into the system, apply these five best practices with your maintenance planners, reliability engineers, and storeroom managers. 1. Distinguish maintainable equipment from consumable spare parts ¤ The most critical decision in asset hierarchy design is separating serialized, maintainable equipment from consumable replacement parts. Apply the nameplate and overhaul test to every item : Asset : A piece of equipment that carries a unique serial number or manufacturer nameplate, undergoes preventive maintenance or repair, and tracks its own cost and operating history over time. Examples include Filler FL-02 , a drive motor, or a centrifugal pump. Spare part : A consumable or non-serialized item that is issued to a work order and replaced during maintenance. Examples include gaskets, o-rings, mechanical seals, bearings, filters, and fuses. Creating asset records for consumable wear parts creates thousands of unnecessary records that clutter search results and navigation trees. Keep consumable wear parts in the Item Master and associate them directly with the parent asset . Quick test: Should this be a child asset ? ¤ Create a child asset only if one or more of the following are true: It is maintained independently. It has its own maintenance history. It can be replaced, rebuilt, or transferred separately. It needs its own inspections, meters , or work orders . If the component is simply replaced when it fails and does not require separate tracking, it is probably a spare part rather than an asset . 2. Keep the hierarchy shallow ¤ While the database supports deep nesting, asset hierarchies work best when they stop at units that are maintained independently. Many organizations need only two or three levels: Parent machine package → Subassembly → Maintainable component For example, a packaging machine package contains a drive motor subassembly, which contains a gearbox component. Do not attempt to model every bolt, bracket, or hose in the asset tree. If an item is not independently maintained, tracked with a meter , or transferred between machines as a complete unit, stop at the subassembly level. 💡 Tip: Managing spare parts with the Spare Parts tab ¤ To make replacement parts easy for technicians to find without turning them into child assets , add stocked items from the Item Master to the Spare Parts tab of the parent asset . Technicians can view approved part numbers, verify storeroom availability, and reserve parts directly on active work orders . 3. Anchor every parent asset to a valid location ¤ Every top-level parent asset must be assigned to an operating location in your location hierarchy, such as Filling line room . When a parent asset is assigned to a location , child subassemblies inherit that location context automatically. When you move a parent asset to a new room or send it to the storeroom for rebuild, child components move along with the parent. 4. Standardize naming and import from the top down ¤ Establish consistent, descriptive naming conventions that combine an equipment code with an operational description, such as ASSET-FL02 / Filler FL-02 and MTR-DRV-01 / Filler FL-02 drive motor . When preparing spreadsheet files for data loading: Locations first : Ensure all operating locations exist in the system before importing assets . Top-level parent assets second : Load main equipment packages with their location references. Child subassemblies third : Load child records referencing their parent asset identifiers. Spare parts lists fourth : Attach stocked item records to assets after asset records exist. What a good asset hierarchy looks like ¤ In this sample ice cream plant equipment model, the asset hierarchy represents the filling line machinery installed inside Filling line room : Filler FL-02 is the top-level parent asset anchored to the operating location Filling line room . Drive motor is a critical serialized subassembly under Filler FL-02 with its own runtime meter and overhaul schedule. Nozzle assembly is a mechanical subassembly under Filler FL-02 that receives regular rebuilds. Nozzle body and Shutoff valve are maintainable child components under Nozzle assembly. Consumable seals, o-rings, and gaskets for the nozzle assembly live on the Spare Parts tab from Item Master, not as child asset records. Figure 1: Sample asset hierarchy for the Filling line system Why this structure works ¤ This equipment structure delivers clean maintenance history and streamlined navigation for everyday operations: Targeted work order history : Technicians can raise a repair work order against Drive motor to log electrical diagnostics, or against Filler FL-02 for general line servicing. Fast drilldown navigation : Technicians navigating in Maximo Mobile or the desktop applications find any maintainable component in two to three clicks from the main filler record. Clean separation of wear parts : Because o-rings and gaskets are cataloged on the Spare Parts tab, storeroom clerks issue parts against the work order without generating orphaned asset records. Independent equipment tracking : If the Drive motor is swapped out during a breakdown, the motor asset record retains its full rebuild history as it moves to the repair shop, while the replacement motor links to Filler FL-02 . Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your understanding before building your equipment hierarchy. Problem 1: Are wear parts and consumables child assets ? ¤ Your maintenance planner wants to create child asset records under Filler FL-02 for mechanical seals, o-rings, and flange gaskets so technicians can select them during repairs. Figure 2 shows the over-assetized hierarchy where consumable wear parts, including o-rings, mechanical seals, and flange gaskets, are incorrectly modeled as individual child asset records underneath Nozzle assembly . Figure 2: Problem 1: Over-assetized hierarchy with consumable parts modeled as child assets What happens if you model these consumable items as child assets ? Show the answer Creating asset records for consumables results in severe over-assetization. The asset register becomes bloated with thousands of static parts that do not undergo individual preventive maintenance or carry serial numbers. Technicians face cluttered drilldown trees, and storeroom inventory counts cannot sync properly with asset records. What to do instead: Keep consumable wear parts in the Item Master and link them to the parent asset using the Spare Parts tab. Technicians can view the approved bill of materials, check storeroom stock, and charge items directly to work orders . Figure 3 shows the corrected asset structure where maintainable child assets Nozzle body and Shutoff valve remain under Nozzle assembly , while consumable o-rings and gaskets are cataloged in Item Master and linked through the Spare Parts tab. Figure 3: Solution 1: Correct asset hierarchy with consumable wear parts managed on the Spare Parts tab Problem 2: What happens when Filler FL-02 moves to a new line? ¤ Filler FL-02 is moved from Filling line room to a newly constructed packaging suite in another building. How do child subassemblies, such as Drive motor and Nozzle assembly , handle the move? Show the answer When a parent asset moves to a new operating location , all child assets in its hierarchy automatically move with it to the new location . The parent-child relationship remains intact, and historical work orders remain linked to both the equipment and the previous location . Figure 4 illustrates moving parent asset Filler FL-02 from location Filling line room to location Packaging suite , showing how child subassemblies Drive motor and Nozzle assembly as well as child components Nozzle body and Shutoff valve automatically inherit the new location . Figure 4: Problem 2: Child subassemblies automatically inherit parent asset relocation What to do instead: Move the top-level parent asset record to the new location . The system updates the location reference across all child subassemblies in a single operation. Problem 3: Should a building or room be modeled as an asset ? ¤ A team member creates an asset record named Production building and places all equipment inside that asset record instead of creating a location record. What goes wrong when supervisors run building maintenance reports? Show the answer Buildings, rooms, and areas are places, not movable equipment. Modeling rooms as assets disables filtering by location in Maximo Mobile and prevents accurate tracking when equipment moves between rooms. Figure 5 contrasts the incorrect model where Production building is created as an asset record holding Filler FL-02 against the correct model where Production building is created as a location record holding asset Filler FL-02 . Figure 5: Problem 3: Comparison of modeling places as locations versus assets What to do instead: Model buildings, floors, and rooms in the location hierarchy under the Locations application. Anchor equipment records, such as Filler FL-02 , into their respective operating location records. Problem 4: In what order do you load parent and child asset records? ¤ You are importing equipment data from a spreadsheet with rows sorted in the following order: Nozzle body : Child component Nozzle assembly : Subassembly Filler FL-02 : Parent machine Filling line room : Operating location What happens when you run the import in this sequence? Show the answer The import fails. Nozzle body fails because its parent Nozzle assembly does not exist yet. Nozzle assembly fails because Filler FL-02 is missing. Filler FL-02 fails because its operating location Filling line room has not been loaded into the database. What to do instead: Sort import rows top-down: Filling line room : Location Filler FL-02 : Top-level parent asset Drive motor , Nozzle assembly : Subassemblies Nozzle body , Shutoff valve : Child components Always verify your import count against the number of rows in your source spreadsheet. Follow data formatting guidelines in How do I prepare data for import? and review sequencing in What is the correct load order? . Common planning mistakes ¤ When designing an asset hierarchy, avoid these common mistakes: Creating assets for every component, no matter how small. Tracking spare parts as assets . Adding hierarchy levels that provide no maintenance or reporting value. Creating separate assets that will never have their own work history. Building a hierarchy that is difficult to navigate or maintain. A good asset hierarchy reflects how equipment is maintained, inspected, and reported on. Focus on maintainable equipment rather than trying to model every physical component. Asset hierarchy planning checklist ¤ Before loading your asset hierarchy into Maximo Application Suite Select, verify each planning requirement: Table 1: Asset hierarchy planning checklist ¤ Check Planning item What to verify [ ] Maintainable equipment only Every asset record represents serialized, maintainable equipment, not consumable wear parts. [ ] Spare parts cataloged Consumables, o-rings, and gaskets are organized in Item Master for use on the Spare Parts tab. [ ] Valid operating locations Every top-level parent asset is assigned to an existing location record. [ ] Shallow hierarchy depth The equipment structure stops at maintainable units. Many organizations need only two or three levels. [ ] Standardized naming Equipment identifiers and asset tags follow consistent naming conventions. [ ] Top-down import sequence Spreadsheet records are ordered so parent assets and locations exist before child records load. TODO: Confirm with a subject matter expert [SME confirmation required: Confirm whether the Maintain Hierarchy setting is exposed on the Asset details view in Maximo Application Suite Select, and whether Item Assembly Structures are available for template-based asset generation.] Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Prepare data for import ¤ With your location and asset hierarchies planned, download CSV templates from Data Management and format your data files. How do I prepare data for import? Related skills ¤ How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? : Classify every facility entity, machine, and consumable wear item accurately. What is the correct load order? : Review the full five-step data onboarding roadmap. How do I get data into the system? : Learn the upload, preview, and commit steps in Data Management. How do I fix import errors? : Troubleshoot missing parent records or invalid fields. Related topics ¤ What is an asset ? Locations How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? docs.text: How do I plan my location hierarchy? ¤ Your location hierarchy is the map of the places where your assets are operated, stored, or repaired. It organizes those places into a clear parent-child structure. A place can be a building, a room, a section of a map grid, or a telephone pole. When loading data into Maximo Application Suite Select, locations must be established before you load equipment, inventory , or work orders , as outlined in What is the correct load order? . Looking to verify your location hierarchy structure right away? Skip to location hierarchy planning checklist ↓ A location hierarchy lets you find work across an entire building or drill down to a single room. How much structure you need depends on your operation. A plant with a few rooms needs far less than a site with many buildings and floors. Video 1: Building an effective location hierarchy (about 2 minutes). [Video in production, placeholder preview for design review] Core principles for planning your hierarchy ¤ Before loading records into the system, follow these five best practices with your maintenance planners, supervisors, and operations team. 1. Map your layout on paper first ¤ Before creating records in the system, sketch the facility on paper or a whiteboard. Distinguish clearly between locations , assets , and storerooms: Location : A place where work happens or where equipment is operated, stored, or repaired, such as Production building or Filling line room . A location accumulates the long-term history of that place. Asset : Maintainable equipment operating at a location , such as Filler FL-02 or a motor. Assets can move between locations or into a storeroom, retaining their own lifecycle history wherever they go. Storeroom : A specialized location used specifically to receive, store, and issue inventory items , such as Main storeroom . Ask yourself: "Is this a place where work occurs, or a piece of equipment that could be moved, replaced, or overhauled?" 2. Choose one clear primary structure, usually based on place ¤ The primary location hierarchy usually follows the places where work happens, for example: Top-level location → Building or area → Floor or zone → Room or position A location does not have to be a building with floors and rooms. It can be a section of a map grid or a telephone pole. Choose levels that fit how your operation is laid out. When you search for work in a building, the results include the locations under it. If you group locations by what they are used for, such as all restrooms or all compressor rooms across multiple buildings under one branch, a search for Production building will miss any rooms placed outside that building's branch. Can I organize the same locations more than one way? ¤ Yes. Maximo Application Suite Select lets you organize locations into more than one system. A system is a hierarchy of locations . The same location can belong to more than one system. Primary system : The physical layout of your operation, such as plant, building, and room. You can have only one primary system. Secondary systems : Other groupings of the same locations , based on how equipment works together, such as refrigeration, heating and cooling, or electrical. For example, in the ice cream plant, the primary system follows the physical layout. A secondary Refrigeration system can group Cold storage and Freezer Tunnel , so a supervisor can see everything that keeps product cold in one view. The primary system is not affected, and a search for Production building still covers every room in that building's branch. Keep your primary system based on place. Use secondary systems for functional views, so you do not have to change the physical layout to get them. TODO: Confirm with a subject matter expert [SME confirmation required: confirm whether Maximo Application Suite Select also supports network systems, and how an administrator creates a secondary system. The previous version of this page mentioned network systems.] 💡 Tip: Grouping by function ¤ If you want to view locations by how equipment works together, such as everything that keeps product cold, add a secondary system instead of changing the primary hierarchy. See Can I organize the same locations more than one way? If you want to find locations by type, such as all restrooms or all electrical closets across a facility, use Classifications or location attributes. Some organizations also define locations by function, so that history stays with the location as the assets in it are swapped. For example, an air conditioning compressor can be both an asset and a location in an HVAC system. For more about items that are both, see How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? . TODO: Confirm with a subject matter expert [SME confirmation required: confirm how functional locations work in Maximo Application Suite Select, and how to describe an item that is both an asset and a location .] Quick test: Should this be a location ? ¤ Create a location only if all of the following are true: It is a place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired, or a functional position that keeps its history when equipment is swapped. Maintenance work might be planned, performed, or reported for it. It needs its own maintenance history, costs, or operational context. If the item moves with the equipment when it is repaired, replaced, or transferred, it is probably an asset rather than a location . 3. Decide how deep to go: stop at the maintainable level ¤ More levels are not always better. Extra levels make drilldown navigation slower for technicians in the field. For every level you consider adding, ask this rule-of-thumb question: "Will someone plan, assign, or report maintenance work at this specific level?" If yes , create the location record. If no , stop at the parent level. For example, if maintenance is scheduled for Cold storage as an entire room, do not create sub- locations for every individual shelf or rack. Start with only the levels you need. A small operation might need only two or three levels, and a site with many buildings and floors might need more. You can add sub- locations later as your maintenance processes mature. Do I need a deep hierarchy? ¤ Not always. A hierarchy helps most when you can use it to find things, such as picking a building and drilling down to a floor or room. If your locations do not nest, a flat list is fine. For example, a series of telephone poles does not need levels above or below them. Add structure only where it helps people find or group their work. 4. Connect every child location to a valid parent ¤ Except for the top-level location , every operational location in your hierarchy must have an assigned parent location . Locations created without a parent become orphaned records. They do not appear in hierarchy drilldown navigation trees and are not included when you search for a parent facility. 5. Standardize naming and import from the top down ¤ Establish consistent, descriptive naming conventions across the facility. Combine a clear code with an easily recognized name, such as BLD-PROD / Production building and RM-MIX / Mixing room . When importing data from spreadsheets: Sort your records top-down : Parents must exist before child records are added. Import order : Top-level location , then parent locations , then child locations , then assets . If child rows appear before their parents in an import file, the database cannot resolve the parent reference, leading to import errors and orphaned records. What a good location hierarchy looks like ¤ In this sample ice cream plant, the structure follows the layout of the plant from the top-level location down to individual rooms: Ice cream main plant is the top-level location that all other locations sit under. Production building is a primary parent location that groups related production spaces. Mixing room , Filling line room , and Packaging zone are child locations under Production building. Cold storage and Main storeroom are separate operating locations directly under Ice cream main plant . Figure 1: Sample location hierarchy for Ice cream main plant Why this structure works ¤ This layout succeeds because it mirrors the physical layout of the plant while meeting everyday operational and reporting needs: Work found by building : Work orders assigned to Mixing room , Filling line room , or Packaging zone appear when you search for Production building . Supervisors can review work for the whole building or drill down into a single room. Targeted context for technicians : When technicians open Filling line room in Maximo Mobile or the desktop application, they see only the equipment, safety requirements, and open work orders relevant to that specific room, without clutter from other areas. Clear separation of storerooms and production areas : Main storeroom is designated as an inventory location for receiving, storing, and issuing parts. Keeping storerooms separate from operating production rooms prevents inventory transactions from mixing with equipment maintenance history. Independent tracking for standalone facilities : Cold storage sits directly under Ice cream main plant because it is a separate physical structure with its own refrigeration systems and temperature controls, allowing its costs and work to be tracked independently of the main production building. Fast, shallow drilldown : Technicians reach any room in only two navigation steps from Ice cream main plant . This shallow depth keeps navigation fast in the field while providing all the detail required for work management. Equipment mobility : When assets such as fillers, motors, or pumps are replaced, moved to another room, or sent for overhaul, the location hierarchy remains stable while the asset records track their own movement history. Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your understanding before building your own hierarchy. Problem 1: Which place is each restroom in? ¤ The plant has two restrooms. In the hierarchy below, both are placed under a separate parent location named Restrooms . Figure 2 illustrates the flawed functional grouping where restrooms across different areas, Production building restroom and Packaging zone restroom , are grouped together under a separate Restrooms parent instead of within their respective physical buildings. Figure 2: Problem 1: Restrooms grouped by functional use instead of physical location A supervisor searches for the work orders for Production building for the past quarter. What goes wrong? Show the answer The Production building restroom is omitted from the results because it sits under Restrooms , not under Production building . The hierarchy was grouped by functional use rather than physical location . What to do instead: Place each restroom under the physical area where it is located. Production building restroom belongs under Production building . Packaging zone restroom belongs under Packaging zone . Figure 3 shows the corrected physical structure where Production building restroom sits directly under Production building , and Packaging zone restroom sits under Packaging zone . Figure 3: Solution 1: Restrooms placed within their physical parent locations If you need to find all restrooms across the plant, assign a common Classification or type rather than creating a functional branch in your primary location hierarchy. Problem 2: Where is the Packaging zone? ¤ In the hierarchy below, Packaging zone was added without selecting a parent location . Figure 4 shows an orphaned record condition where Packaging zone is created without a parent connection, leaving it disconnected from Production building . Figure 4: Problem 2: Packaging zone created as an orphaned record without a parent What happens when a planner opens Production building in the drilldown tree? Show the answer Production building displays only Mixing room and Filling line room . Packaging zone is missing from the tree view and from searches for the building. Because Packaging zone has no parent, it exists as an orphaned record with no connection to Production building . What to do instead: Assign Production building as the parent location for Packaging zone . Figure 5 shows the resolved hierarchy where Packaging zone is properly connected to parent location Production building . Figure 5: Solution 2: Packaging zone connected to Production building parent location Problem 3: How many levels should the plant have? ¤ Your maintenance team wants to add sub- locations under Cold storage for every rack, shelf, and bin. A colleague argues that more detail is always better. What question should you ask before creating these sub- locations ? Show the answer Ask: "Will anyone plan, perform, or report maintenance work at an individual shelf level?" If maintenance is performed on the refrigeration units, doors, and ambient room space, not individual storage shelves, stop at Cold storage . Adding unnecessary levels makes the hierarchy harder to navigate without providing actionable maintenance data. The right depth depends on your operation, so a small plant often needs fewer levels than a large site . If parts or items need shelf-level tracking, that is handled through inventory bins in storerooms, not operational location records. Problem 4: In what order do you load location records? ¤ You are importing location records from a spreadsheet with rows in the following sequence: Packaging zone Mixing room Production building Ice cream main plant What happens when you run the import in this order? Show the answer Packaging zone and Mixing room fail to import because their parent, Production building , does not exist in the database yet. Production building then fails because Ice cream main plant has not been loaded yet. What to do instead: Sort import rows top-down: Ice cream main plant : Top-level location Production building : Parent location Mixing room , Filling line room , Packaging zone : Child locations Always verify your import count against the number of rows in your source spreadsheet. Prepare your spreadsheet formatting by following How do I prepare data for import? . For details on sequencing, see What is the correct load order? , and see How do I fix import errors? if rows fail to load. Common planning mistakes ¤ When designing a location hierarchy, avoid these common mistakes: Grouping locations by function in your primary hierarchy when you need reports by building or area. Use a secondary system for functional views. Creating a location for every movable piece of equipment. Adding levels that nobody will maintain, report on, or navigate to. Designing only for today's facility without considering future expansion. Creating orphan locations that are not connected to a parent location . A simple hierarchy that reflects the layout of your operation is easier to maintain than a highly detailed one. Location hierarchy planning checklist ¤ Before loading your location hierarchy into Maximo Application Suite Select, verify each requirement: Table 1: Location hierarchy planning checklist ¤ Check Planning item What to verify [ ] Places and positions Every location record represents a place where assets are operated, stored, or repaired, or a functional position, not a movable piece of equipment. [ ] One clear primary structure The primary system follows one consistent structure, usually from the top-level location to building to room. Functional views use secondary systems, and groupings by type use classifications. [ ] Valid parent connections Every child location connects to an existing parent location to prevent orphan records. [ ] Maintainable depth The structure stops at the level where work is planned, assigned, or reported. A small operation might need only a few levels. [ ] Standardized naming Location codes and identifiers follow consistent naming conventions across the hierarchy. [ ] Top-down import sequence Spreadsheet rows are sorted so that parent locations exist before child records are imported. The answers above use sources about Maximo Manage.] Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Plan your asset hierarchy ¤ With your location hierarchy planned, organize your machinery, subassemblies, and maintainable components operating within those locations .
