docs.text: How do I plan my preventive maintenance strategy? ¤ A successful preventive maintenance strategy prevents equipment breakdowns, stabilizes labor schedules, and ensures replacement parts are staged before work begins. Creating maintenance records without a strategic design leads to work order overload, missed service dates, or unnecessary teardown inspections that cause equipment defects. Planning your preventive maintenance strategy in Maximo Application Suite Select involves selecting between time-based and usage-based frequencies, choosing fixed versus floating schedules, buffering lead times for parts staging, and organizing multi-stop routes. Looking to verify your PM strategy right away? Skip to PM strategy planning checklist ↓ Core principles for designing a PM strategy ¤ Before configuring schedules in the PM application, establish your maintenance strategy with your reliability engineers, planners, and operations team. 1. Balance time-based and usage-based triggers ¤ Equipment operating under constant loads benefits from calendar schedules, while machinery with fluctuating production cycles requires usage-based runtime triggers. Figure 1 outlines the decision framework for selecting maintenance frequencies based on operating patterns: 24/7 continuous operation : time-based schedule using fixed calendar days, weeks, or months. Variable batch production : usage-based schedule driven by continuous run hours or cycles. Intermittent seasonal operation : combined schedule triggered by whichever threshold occurs first, calendar elapsed time or meter run hours. Figure 1: Decision framework for preventive maintenance frequency Table 1: Matching equipment types to maintenance triggers ¤ Schedule type How interval is calculated Best suited for Ice Cream Plant example Time-based Fixed calendar days, weeks, or months Continuously running utility systems Monthly emergency lighting and safety valve inspections Usage-based Cumulative continuous meter run hours or cycles High-wear production machinery with fluctuating shift schedules 500-hour bearing lubrication on Filler FL-02 drive motor Combined Elapsed calendar time or accumulated run hours, whichever occurs first Standby machinery or seasonal backup systems Cold Storage backup compressor serviced every 6 months or 250 run hours 2. Choose fixed versus floating intervals carefully ¤ Understanding the difference between fixed and floating schedules is one of the most critical decisions in maintenance planning: Fixed schedule: Calculates the next due date based on the Target Start Date of the previous work order . A monthly PM scheduled for the first of the month always generates on the first of the month, regardless of when technicians complete the physical work. Floating schedule: Calculates the next due date based on the Actual Completion Date of the previous work order . If a monthly PM due on January 1 is finished late on January 15, the next work order is scheduled for February 15. 💡 Tip: Beware of the floating PM halting trap ¤ While a floating PM work order remains open in In Progress or Waiting on Material status , the system cannot calculate the next due date. If a technician forgets to close a floating work order , future preventive maintenance on that machine stops generating entirely without warning. Use fixed schedules for regulatory inspections and reserve floating schedules for usage-based overhauls. 3. Buffer work generation with realistic lead times ¤ Lead time specifies how many days before the maintenance due date Maximo Application Suite Select generates the work order . Set lead times based on your physical storeroom procurement cycles and shift planning routines: Standard lead time: 7 to 14 days: Gives supervisors time to verify parts availability in the storeroom, assign qualified crafts , and coordinate equipment downtime with production supervisors. Zero lead time penalty: If lead time is left at zero, work orders appear on their due date, leaving zero preparation time and causing immediate parts shortages. What a good PM strategy looks like ¤ In our sample ice cream plant, the maintenance strategy combines calendar routines, usage-based triggers, and consolidated routes. Figure 2 illustrates the three maintenance streams that feed into the automated generation engine: Fixed calendar PMs : recurring safety and facility audits scheduled on fixed calendar intervals. Meter run-hour PMs : usage-based servicing for production machines like Filler FL-02 and pumps. Multi-stop routes : consolidated inspection rounds, such as the daily Cold storage walk-through. Automated cron processing : background tasks evaluate lead times and generate work orders 7 days in advance for supervisor assignment. Figure 2: Architecture of an integrated plant preventive maintenance strategy Why this strategy works ¤ Prevents over-maintenance: Variable-speed production machinery triggers maintenance only after true operating wear, saving labor and consumable seal costs. Guarantees regulatory compliance: Hygiene, sanitation, and safety inspections run on fixed calendar dates that cannot drift over time. Eliminates parts delays: A mandatory 7-day lead time ensures replacement gaskets and food-grade lubricants are staged before technicians open equipment panels. Reduces work order volume: Low-risk walk-through checks across 45 cold storage valves are bundled into a single routed work order rather than 45 separate tickets . Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your strategy before creating PM records. Problem 1: The silent halting trap on a floating schedule ¤ A maintenance planner creates a floating monthly preventive maintenance schedule for Filler FL-02 . A technician completes the physical lubrication on January 10 but forgets to advance the work order status from In Progress to Completed. What happens to scheduled maintenance for February and March? Show the answer No work orders are generated for February, March, or any subsequent month. Because floating schedules calculate next due dates from the completion timestamp of the previous work order , the open ticket blocks all future generation. Maintenance halts silently until someone investigates the backlog. What to do instead: Use fixed schedules for recurring time-based servicing, or establish a daily supervisor dashboard triage routine to close completed work orders promptly. Problem 2: The premature calendar PM on idle equipment ¤ A plant sets a fixed 30-day lubrication PM on the packaging room conveyor drive motor. Due to seasonal supply constraints, the filling line was shut down for three weeks during the month and only operated for 20 hours. What happens when the calendar PM generates on schedule? Show the answer Technicians perform an unnecessary lubrication service on a machine that experienced almost zero mechanical wear. Over-lubricating bearings can blow out grease seals and introduce particulate contamination. What to do instead: Switch the conveyor motor from a calendar frequency to a meter -based schedule triggered every 300 continuous operating run hours. Problem 3: The zero lead time material bottleneck ¤ A planner configures quarterly pump rebuild schedules with zero days lead time. When work orders generate on the first day of the quarter, technicians immediately open the tickets and walk to the storeroom. What happens at the storeroom counter? Show the answer The required mechanical seal kits are out of stock. Because the work order generated on its due date, the inventory clerk had zero advance notice to reorder parts. The work order stalls in Waiting on Material status for two weeks, turning a planned PM into an overdue compliance failure. What to do instead: Configure a 14-day lead time on the PM record. When the work order generates two weeks early, the system reserves storeroom stock and alerts the inventory clerk to replenish low balances before work starts. Problem 4: Work order clutter from individual minor inspections ¤ A facility creates 60 separate monthly PM records to inspect each individual fire extinguisher and emergency eyewash station across the production building. What happens to technician productivity and supervisor assignment queues? Show the answer Technicians spend more time opening, logging labor on, and closing 60 individual records than performing the actual physical checks. Supervisor work queues become overwhelmed with dozens of trivial tickets . What to do instead: Group all 60 inspection points into a single multi-stop Route attached to one monthly PM schedule. The system generates one consolidated work order with 60 sequential room stops. Common PM planning mistakes ¤ When planning preventive maintenance schedules, avoid these frequent pitfalls: Creating separate standalone PMs for every minor component instead of using Master PMs and Routes. Setting floating schedules on compliance-critical assets where dates must not drift. Leaving lead time at zero, which causes parts shortages on the scheduled start date. Scheduling invasive teardown inspections on sealed components when non-destructive condition monitoring is more effective. Activating dozens of new PM schedules simultaneously on day one, which overwhelms the maintenance team with sudden work spikes. PM strategy planning checklist ¤ Use this checklist to verify your maintenance strategy before activating schedules. Table 2: PM strategy verification checklist ¤ Check Planning item What to verify [ ] Schedule type alignment Continuous machines use meter run hours; fixed facilities use calendar intervals [ ] Fixed vs floating validation Regulatory and safety checks use fixed intervals to prevent schedule drift [ ] Lead time buffering All PM records have a lead time of 7 to 14 days for material verification [ ] Standardized job plans linked Every PM record references an active Job Plan with task steps and material lists [ ] Route consolidation Minor walk-through checks are bundled into multi-stop routes [ ] Meter configuration verified Usage-based PMs connect to continuous meters with active daily run rates Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next steps: Setup and execution ¤ How do I set up meters and meter groups? : Configure continuous run-hour meters and rollover limits. How do I plan recurring maintenance? : Build time-based and meter -based PM records in the desktop application. How do I manage more assets ? : Scale maintenance across multiple lines with Master PM templates. Related topics ¤ How do I plan recurring maintenance? How do I set up meters and meter groups? docs.text: How do I plan my storeroom and inventory strategy? ¤ An effective storeroom and inventory strategy ensures critical spare parts are on hand when machines break down, prevents expensive stockouts, and eliminates excess capital tied up in slow-moving materials. Without structured storeroom management, maintenance teams suffer frequent job delays and inventory counts drift into inaccurate negative balances. Planning your storeroom and inventory strategy in Maximo Application Suite Select involves designing physical storeroom layouts, classifying consumable versus rebuildable rotating items , establishing dynamic reorder points, and implementing regular cycle counts. Looking to verify your storeroom and inventory strategy right away? Skip to storeroom strategy planning checklist ↓ Core principles for designing a storeroom strategy ¤ Before cataloging items in the Item Master or creating warehouses in the Storerooms application, establish your inventory strategy with your maintenance, procurement, and warehouse teams. 1. Separate physical storerooms from operational locations ¤ In Maximo Application Suite Select, a storeroom is a specialized location record designated for inventory control. Keep storeroom records strictly distinct from operating rooms: Operating location : Where production occurs and machinery operates, such as Filling line room . Work orders and downtime are tracked against operating locations . Storeroom location : Where items and spare parts are securely held, received, and issued, such as Main storeroom . Inventory transactions, stock balances, and unit costs are tracked at storerooms. Figure 1 maps the material and financial flow from storeroom inventory to work orders and physical locations : Storeroom location : Main storeroom holds stocked spare parts. Material issue : items are issued and charged directly to an active work order , such as Filler FL-02 . Operating location : Filling line room provides the physical space where the equipment operates. Cost tracking : maintenance and material expenses are tracked against both the asset and the location . Figure 1: Financial and material flow between storeroom, work order, and operating location 2. Distinguish consumable materials from rotating rebuildable assets ¤ Every item stocked in inventory must be categorized as either a consumable item or a rotating item : Consumable item , non-rotating: Standard wear parts, such as flange gaskets, o-rings, drive belts, and filters. Tracked as physical stock quantities in storeroom bins. When issued, the part is consumed by the work order and discarded upon replacement. Rotating item : Expensive, rebuildable serialized equipment, such as 50 HP drive motors, sanitary pumps, and gearboxes. Tracked simultaneously as an inventory item in storerooms and as an individual asset in the Assets application. When pulled from a machine, the failed unit returns to the storeroom for repair rather than being scrapped. Table 1: Consumable items versus rotating items comparison ¤ Item classification Tracking method Financial impact upon issue Repair handling Ice Cream Plant example Consumable item Quantity balance in storeroom bin Material cost charged directly to work order Discarded and replaced with new stock Food-grade silicone gasket kit for Filler FL-02 Rotating item Quantity balance plus serialized asset record Material usage and asset location transfer recorded Sent to rebuild shop and returned to storeroom stock Rebuildable 50 HP homogenizer pump drive motor 💡 Tip: Use the Attach to Parent Asset on Issue toggle ¤ For rotating items that operate as subassemblies on parent machines, enable Attach to Parent Asset on Issue in the Item Master. When a storeroom clerk issues the replacement motor to Filler FL-02 , Maximo Application Suite Select automatically links the new motor as a child asset to the filler in a single transaction. 3. Establish automated reorder points and safety stock ¤ Automating inventory replenishment prevents emergency stockouts while avoiding over-purchasing. Configure reorder parameters on the Inventory record for each stocked item : Safety stock: Minimum buffer held to protect against supplier shipping delays or unexpected breakdown spikes. Reorder point: Threshold that triggers reordering when the calculation Current Balance + On Order - Reserved drops to or below this level. Economic order quantity: Minimum cost-effective batch size to purchase from vendors. What a good storeroom strategy looks like ¤ In our sample ice cream plant, the inventory strategy combines a secure central storeroom, satellite staging cribs, and structured rotating pools. Figure 2 illustrates the storeroom topology and replenishment architecture: Central storeroom : Main storeroom securely stores high-value spares and rotating items . Issue counter : handles rapid barcode checkout for major jobs like Filler FL-02 overhaul . Satellite crib : receives bulk restocks from the main storeroom to hold consumable parts close to active areas like Cold storage for jobs like Refrigeration routine . Automated replenishment : system calculations monitor stock buffers to trigger timely reorders before stockouts occur. Figure 2: Sample storeroom topology and inventory replenishment flow Why this strategy works ¤ Secures high-value rotating spares: Rebuildable motors and expensive sanitary valves remain controlled in the central warehouse until officially reserved on approved work orders . Minimizes technician transit time: High-frequency consumables like sanitizing lubricants and cold-temperature seals live in an unlocked satellite cabinet near the cold storage facility. Maintains 100% stock accuracy: Storeroom staff conduct weekly cycle counts using Count Books, preventing inventory balance discrepancies before scheduled PMs run. Prevents stockouts on critical lines: Automated reorder calculations alert procurement two weeks before packaging line consumables deplete. Spot the problem: test your plan ¤ Review these common planning scenarios to test your inventory strategy before adding items . Problem 1: The ghost stockout from unrecorded counter withdrawals ¤ Technicians frequently grab mechanical seals from storeroom shelves during emergency repairs without logging an issue transaction on their work orders . What happens when the scheduled monthly PM work order for Filler FL-02 generates two weeks later? Show the answer The system shows 4 seals in stock, so the work order is approved. However, when the technician arrives at the storeroom bin, the shelf is completely empty. The job stalls in Waiting on Material status , and the plant faces unexpected downtime because unrecorded withdrawals created ghost inventory . What to do instead: Require all item checkouts to be recorded at the counter using the Issues and Transfers role-based app, and perform weekly cycle counts in Count Books to catch discrepancies early. Problem 2: Over-stocking low-cost bolts while stocking out of critical seals ¤ A facility stocks $40,000 worth of standard hardware bolts that can be purchased locally in 2 hours, but holds zero custom mechanical seal kits for Filler FL-02 that have an 8-week supplier lead time. What happens when Filler FL-02 suffers an unexpected seal failure? Show the answer The filling line is shut down for weeks waiting for international replacement shipments, costing tens of thousands of dollars in lost production, while valuable working capital sits locked up in excess hardware bolts. What to do instead: Conduct an inventory criticality review. Set high safety stock and automated reorder points on long-lead critical spares, and maintain lean just-in-time minimums for locally available commercial hardware. Problem 3: The throwaway motor trap ¤ A maintenance team purchases ten 50 HP drive motors for production pumps. In Item Master, the planner forgets to check the Rotating? box and catalogs the motors as standard consumable items . What happens when the first motor fails and is replaced? Show the answer The technician issues the replacement motor as a consumable material. The old motor is removed, but because it has no serialized asset record, its lifetime overhaul history, rewind dates, and run-hour meter logs are permanently lost. The repair shop cannot track whether this specific motor has failed multiple times. What to do instead: Mark rebuildable equipment as Rotating in the Item Master before creating inventory balances, and track the individual units as serialized assets . Problem 4: Creating a storeroom as an asset record ¤ A data entry clerk creates Main storeroom as an asset record in the Assets application so that equipment can be linked to it. What happens when inventory clerks attempt to receive purchase orders or issue parts? Show the answer Inventory applications like Inventory , Count Books, and Issues and Transfers store items in storerooms, so parts cannot be stocked inside asset records. What to do instead: Create Main storeroom in the Storerooms application. Common storeroom planning mistakes ¤ When planning your storerooms and inventory catalogs, avoid these frequent mistakes: Allowing open, unmonitored access to storeroom bins without barcode issue logging. Failing to mark rebuildable motors and pumps as Rotating items in Item Master. Setting reorder points to zero, disabling automated stock replenishment calculations. Neglecting to link stocked items to the Spare Parts tab of parent asset records. Skipping periodic cycle counts, which allows physical stock and database balances to drift. Storeroom strategy planning checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm your inventory strategy is ready for operations. Table 2: Storeroom strategy verification checklist ¤ Check Planning item What to verify [ ] Dedicated storerooms Storerooms are created in the Storerooms application, separate from operating locations and assets [ ] Rotating items classified Rebuildable motors and pumps have the Rotating checkbox enabled in Item Master [ ] Critical spares identified Long-lead replacement parts have defined safety stock and reorder points in Inventory [ ] Spare Parts tabs linked Consumable gaskets and seals are linked to parent machines for fast technician lookup [ ] Barcode issue process ready Storeroom counter staff use Issues and Transfers for rapid material checkout [ ] Cycle counting schedule set Periodic physical inventory audits are planned using Count Books Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next steps: Setup and execution ¤ How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? : Master the four-question classification framework. How do I issue parts? : Execute fast counter checkouts using the Issues and Transfers app. How do I track stock levels? : Monitor minimum balances, reservations, and reorder triggers. Related topics ¤ How do I decide: location , asset , or spare part? How do I get a new part into inventory ? How do I track stock levels? How do I issue parts? Why does my data look wrong? How do I reduce downtime ? How do I simplify workflows?

docs.text: How do I prepare data for import? ¤ Data Management is the primary application used to import records into IBM Maximo Application Suite Select. Use this guide to clean, format, and structure your spreadsheets or legacy CSV files before uploading them into Data Management. Looking to validate your CSV file right away? Skip to pre-import data validation checklist ↓ 💡 Tips: Best practices for data preparation ¤ Start with a template : Download official templates or export existing records directly from Data Management to see the required column names and structure. Validate data first : Check all values against system data such as site IDs and failure classes before uploading. Use text format : Prevent spreadsheet software from corrupting leading zeros or converting numbers to scientific notation. Test with small batches : Verify format with a small batch of 5 to 10 records before importing thousands. Keep error logs : Document preview errors to correct source files efficiently. Common preparation steps ¤ Use the correct file format ¤ What to do : Save files as CSV format, using comma delimiters Use UTF-8 encoding for special characters Format ID columns as text in Excel before entering data Validate field names and structure ¤ What to check : Column names match system field names exactly All required fields are included Field names are correct, which are case-sensitive What to do : Use a template or export an existing record to see the correct structure. Prevent Excel from corrupting data ¤ Excel can corrupt data in several ways: Dates : Converts text to dates, such as converting 01-02 to Jan 2 IDs : Removes leading zeros, such as converting 001 to 1 Long numbers : Converts long numbers to scientific notation What to do : Format all columns as text in Excel before entering data, or use a plain text editor to create the CSV. Clean your data ¤ What to check : Remove extra spaces from all fields Ensure consistent formatting Validate data against system values, such as status codes and site IDs Check for duplicate IDs Check referenced data before importing ¤ Verify that supporting records exist before importing locations or assets . Missing referenced data is a common cause of import failures. For location imports ¤ What to check : Table 1: Location fields to check before import ¤ Field Required when GL accounts Your organization tracks maintenance costs by cost centre Service addresses Locations need to appear on maps or work order dispatch Calendars and shifts Scheduling work or calculating availability at this location Failure classes You want structured failure reporting on work orders for this location Classifications and specifications You want to search or report on locations by equipment type What to do : Create missing referenced records before importing locations , or update the import file to use existing values. For asset imports ¤ What to check : Table 2: Asset fields to check before import ¤ Field Required when GL accounts Tracking maintenance costs by cost centre Service addresses Assets need to appear on maps or work order dispatch Failure classes Technicians need to select failure codes on work orders for this asset . Without this, the Failure Reporting tab is empty Rotating items Only when the asset is a rotating, serialised item tracked by individual asset record Vendors and manufacturers Tracking warranty, procurement, or service history by supplier Classifications and specifications You want to search, filter, or report on assets by type or specification What to do : Verify all referenced records exist before importing assets . Create missing records or correct values in the import file. Use consistent date formats ¤ Date formats are a common source of import errors. Follow these guidelines to prevent date-related failures. What to do : Use one accepted date format consistently throughout the file Do not mix regional date formats, such as MM/DD/YYYY and DD/MM/YYYY Avoid ambiguous dates such as 01/02/2026 unless the accepted format is clear Format date columns as text in Excel before entering values Test a small batch that includes date values before importing the full file Common date format issues : Excel automatically converts dates to its default format Mixed formats cause some records to fail while others succeed Ambiguous dates are interpreted incorrectly What to do : Verify the expected date format for your system and apply it consistently to all date fields. Import hierarchies in the correct order ¤ For locations and parent-child relationships: What to do : Import in order: Top-level records first: parent locations Second-level records next Lowest-level records last: child locations Break large imports into batches ¤ What to do : Break files into smaller batches of 1,000 to 5,000 records at a time This prevents timeouts and makes troubleshooting easier Preview before importing ¤ Use preview/import validation : Always preview your import before committing it. This shows: Which records will succeed Which records will fail What errors need to be fixed Without validation If you skip validation, errors are only discovered after processing. This can result in: Partial imports with missing records Incorrect data in the system Time wasted troubleshooting after the fact What happens next? ¤ After preparing your data: Preview the import to validate Fix any errors identified Process the import Verify records were created successfully Pre-import data validation checklist ¤ Before uploading your file into Data Management, verify each data preparation step: Table 3: Pre-import data validation checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] CSV file encoding File is saved in CSV format with UTF-8 encoding [ ] Text column formatting ID, code, and date columns are formatted as Text in spreadsheet software [ ] Leading zeros preserved Asset numbers, location codes, and part identifiers retain leading zeros [ ] Header row alignment Column names match system attribute names and case sensitivity [ ] Mandatory site and org keys Every row contains valid SITEID and ORGID values [ ] Top-down hierarchical sort Parent locations and parent assets appear in rows before their child records [ ] Hierarchy plan agreed Your location and asset hierarchies are planned and agreed with your planners and supervisors before you load [ ] Referenced data verified Status codes, failure classes, crafts , and vendors exist in the system [ ] Batch size limit Large datasets are split into batches of 1,000 to 5,000 rows Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Get data into the system ¤ With your CSV files prepared and validated, upload them into Data Management and preview your records before importing. How do I fix import errors? : Learn how to read import preview reports and fix validation or dependency errors. What is the correct load order? : Review the full five-step data onboarding roadmap. docs.text: How do I set up failure codes ? ¤ Structured failure codes convert subjective technician remarks into standardized reliability data. When technicians record repairs using consistent failure codes , maintenance engineers can track defect trends, identify recurring root causes, and justify equipment redesigns or warranty claims. In Maximo Application Suite Select, failure codes are organized into a four-tier hierarchy headed by a Failure Class, followed by Problem, Cause, and Remedy codes configured in the Failure Codes application. Select includes some failure codes . You can use them as they are, or add your own to match your equipment. Looking to verify your failure code configuration right away? Skip to failure code setup verification checklist ↓ The four-tier failure hierarchy architecture ¤ A failure hierarchy structures failure reporting from initial symptom down to corrective action. Figure 1 illustrates the four-tier failure hierarchy architecture: Tier 1 (Failure Class) : broad equipment category, such as PUMPS . Tier 2 (Problem) : observed operational symptom, such as LEAK for fluid leaks or HIGH_TEMP for heat issues. Tier 3 (Cause) : underlying mechanical defect, such as SEAL_WEAR . Tier 4 (Remedy) : corrective action taken, such as REPLACE_SEAL . Figure 1: Four-tier failure code hierarchy architecture Table 1: Four-tier failure code hierarchy with plant examples ¤ Level Code type What it describes Ice Cream Plant example Level 1 Failure Class Broad equipment family or machine type PUMPS (Sanitary and utility pumps) Level 2 Problem The observed failure symptom or operational defect LEAK (Fluid leaking from pump casing) Level 3 Cause The underlying mechanical or operational root cause SEAL_WEAR (Carbon seal face worn beyond tolerance) Level 4 Remedy The specific corrective action that resolved the failure REPLACE_SEAL (Installed new food-grade mechanical seal kit) Step 1: Create a failure hierarchy in Failure Codes ¤ Failure codes and hierarchies are created at the Organization level in the Failure Codes application. Building a failure tree in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Failure Codes and open it. Click New Failure Code . In the Failure Class field, enter a clear identifier, such as PUMPS . In the Description field, enter Sanitary and Utility Pumps Failure Class . In the Problems table, click New Row to add failure symptoms: In the Problem field, enter LEAK . In the Description field, enter Liquid product or lubricant leak . With the LEAK problem row selected, go to the Causes table below and click New Row : In the Cause field, enter SEAL_WEAR . In the Description field, enter Mechanical seal wear or face scoring . With the SEAL_WEAR cause row selected, go to the Remedies table and click New Row : In the Remedy field, enter REPLACE_SEAL . In the Description field, enter Replaced mechanical seal assembly . Repeat steps 5 through 7 to add remaining problems, causes, and remedies. Click Save . 💡 Tip: Reuse branches with Copy Failure Hierarchy ¤ Many equipment types share identical mechanical failure paths. Instead of retyping problem, cause, and remedy trees for every machine class, use the Copy Failure Hierarchy action in the Failure Codes application to duplicate branches from existing failure classes in seconds. Step 2: Assign Failure Classes to assets ¤ For technicians to select failure codes on work orders , the asset must have an assigned Failure Class. Linking a failure class to an asset record ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Assets and open it. Open the target equipment record, such as Filler FL-02 . On the main Asset tab, locate the Failure Class field. Select the matching failure class, such as FILLERS or ROTATING_PUMP . Click Save . Figure 2 outlines the failure class inheritance and field reporting workflow: Asset record : equipment record Filler FL-02 holds configured failure class PUMPS . Work order header : when the asset is added to a corrective work order , PUMPS is inherited automatically. Field closure : during job completion, the technician accesses the Failure Reporting tab. Cascading selection : the technician navigates the filtered PUMPS hierarchy to log Problem LEAK , Cause SEAL_WEAR , and Remedy REPLACE_SEAL . Figure 2: Failure class inheritance and field reporting flow How failure codes behave on work orders ¤ Understanding how failure codes transfer to work orders ensures smooth field reporting: Automatic inheritance: When an asset is added to a work order , its Failure Class copies automatically to the work order header. Precedence rule: If both an asset and a location are specified on a work order and each has a different failure class, the asset failure class takes precedence. Mandatory reporting: For emergency and breakdown work types, configure work order rules to require Problem, Cause, and Remedy selection before advancing status to Completed. Common failure code design mistakes ¤ To maintain clean reliability analytics, avoid these common design traps: Creating too many failure classes: Keep your initial failure class list focused on 5 to 10 major equipment families, such as Pumps, Motors, Conveyors, Refrigeration, and Electrical. Avoid creating a unique failure class for every individual machine model. Using vague problem descriptions: Do not create codes named Broken , Damaged , or Failed . Use specific physical symptoms, such as High Vibration , Overheating , Jammed , or Leaking . Omitting remedy codes: Recording only what broke without recording which remedy succeeded prevents reliability teams from knowing which repair procedures are most effective. Failure code setup verification checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm your failure hierarchies are ready for operational use. Table 2: Failure code configuration checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Core failure classes established Top-level classes exist for all major plant equipment families [ ] 4-tier depth completed Each problem branch has linked cause codes and associated remedies [ ] Descriptive naming applied Codes use clear alphanumeric identifiers with concise plain-language descriptions [ ] Asset records populated Operating equipment records have a valid Failure Class assigned on their main tab [ ] Mobile visibility verified Technicians can view and navigate the failure hierarchy on mobile work order cards [ ] Mandatory on corrective work Failure reporting is required before closing emergency or unscheduled repair work orders Related topics ¤ What happens when an asset fails? docs.text: How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? ¤ Set up your workforce resources before you start assigning work. Crafts define the skills in your organization. Labor records represent the people. Crews group people together so you can assign a whole team to a job in one step. These records work together. You need to set them up in the correct order. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Set up crafts before labor . A labor record must reference a valid craft . Set up a calendar before creating a crew . The crew 's calendar controls when its members show as available. Match the calendar and shift on each labor record to the crew they belong to. A mismatch is the most common reason crew members show as unavailable when you try to assign work. Leave the End Date blank on labor assignments to a crew unless the assignment has a fixed end. This keeps the member permanently assigned until you need to change it. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Labor and crew terminology ¤ Term What it means Craft A skill or trade, such as Electrician or Mechanic, used to match the correct person to the correct job Calendar Defines working days and shifts. Must be assigned to both the crew and each member. Labor A person who performs work or records time Crew type A template that defines the positions and crafts a crew requires, such as Leader and Helper Crew A named group of people assembled to work together, built from a crew type Setup order ¤ Set these up in sequence. Each step depends on the one before it. Crafts → Calendar → Labor → Crew type → Crew Step 1: Create crafts ¤ Crafts represent the skills in your workforce. Select includes some crafts and skill levels. You can use them as they are, or add your own. In the Find navigation item field, search for Crafts and open it. Create a new craft record. Enter a craft ID and description, for example, MECH, Mechanic or REFRIG, Refrigeration technician . Set the default rate if applicable. Save. Repeat for each skill type in your organization. Step 2: Set up a calendar ¤ Crews need a calendar to define when their members are available. If you have not already created a calendar for your workforce, do this before creating crew types. See How do I schedule work? for steps to create shifts and calendars. Step 3: Create labor records ¤ Labor records represent the individuals who perform work. Select creates a labor record for a person when you create their user, so you usually update the existing record instead of creating a new one. [SME confirmation required: Confirm that Select creates a labor record automatically when you create a user, and when you need to create a labor record yourself.] In the Find navigation item field, search for Labor and open it. Open the person's labor record. In the Crafts section, add the person's craft and set it as their default craft . The Available Labor dialog filters by default craft only. A person with the correct skill listed as a secondary craft will not appear when supervisors search for available people. Set the same calendar and shift you plan to use for the crew they will join. If these differ from the crew 's calendar, the person will show as unavailable every time a supervisor or scheduler tries to assign them, even when they are physically at work. Save. Repeat for each person in your workforce. Step 4: Create a crew type ¤ A crew type is the template for a crew . It defines the positions and crafts required. [SME confirmation required: Confirm whether MAS Select uses crew types, and where you define the positions and crafts that a crew requires.] In the Find navigation item field, search for Crews and open it. Create a new crew type. In the Required Crafts section, add each position with its craft : Add a Leader position and assign the relevant craft Add any Helper or other positions required Save. Step 5: Create a crew ¤ With the crew type, crafts , calendar, and labor records in place, you can now create a crew . In the Find navigation item field, search for Crews and open it. Create a new crew . Select the crew type you created. Assign the calendar the crew will work to. Go to the Labor Assignments tab. Add each team member: Select the position, for example, Leader Select the labor record The Effective Date defaults to the start of today's shift. Adjust if needed. Leave End Date blank for a permanent assignment. If an End Date lapses, the crew member is silently dropped from availability, and work can no longer be assigned to that crew , with no system warning. Save. Common issues ¤ Crew members showing as "Not available" ¤ The most common cause is a mismatch between the crew 's calendar and the calendar assigned to the individual labor records. The system calculates availability from the labor record's calendar and shift , not the crew 's. Even if the crew calendar is correct, a technician will appear unavailable if their personal labor record uses a different calendar. Check that both use the same calendar and shift. " Craft mismatch" warning when adding labor to a crew ¤ The labor record does not have the craft required for that crew position. Go to the labor record, add the correct craft in the Crafts section, then return to the crew assignment. Work can't be assigned to a crew ¤ The crew must have at least one labor member assigned with a valid Effective Date and no expired End Date. Check the Labor Assignments tab for any assignments where the End Date has passed. What to do next ¤ Once labor , crafts , and crews are set up: How do I assign the correct people? : Assign labor or crews to work orders . How do I plan recurring maintenance? : Add labor requirements to job plans . How do I schedule work? : Use calendars and routes to organize your team's work. What apps are in IBM Maximo Mobile? : Learn how field teams use Timesheet and Crew Manager on mobile devices. Continue building your skills ¤ Customize your dropdown values ¤ Add your organization's terminology to status fields and dropdowns so the system uses your team's language. How do I customize dropdown values? Set up maps ¤ Once your workforce is configured, set up a map so field teams can see asset and work order locations visually. How do I set up maps? Related topics ¤ How do I schedule work? How do I assign the correct people? How do I standardize data?

docs.text: How do I set up maps? ¤ Map Manager lets you configure a map so that users can see the location of assets , work orders , and service addresses on a visual map inside the application. Once a map is configured and enabled, it appears in spatially enabled applications for all users. 💡 Tips for success ¤ Keep your first map simple. One basemap service is enough to get started. You can add more map services later. Use a descriptive name for each map service so it is easy to identify if you add more later. If users will be viewing maps on mobile devices, use the same map configuration. Mobile users see the same map as desktop users. Quick reference ¤ Table 1: Map terminology ¤ Term What it means Map Manager The application where you create and configure maps Map provider The mapping service that supplies the background map, such as OpenMap Basemap The background map layer that shows geography, streets, or satellite imagery Map service A URL that points to a map tile or layer from your map provider Initial extent The default view that opens when a user first opens the map What you need before you start ¤ A basemap URL from your map provider. OpenMap supports public ArcGIS basemap URLs, which do not require an account or license to use. The name of the applications you want maps to appear in. How to set up a map ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Map Manager and open it. Click New Map . Enter a unique name and a short description for the map. Select Enable Map to activate this configuration. Set the Map Provider to OpenMap . In the Map Services table, click Add Row . Enter a name for the map service, for example, Basemap . Enter the basemap URL. For example, to use a public ArcGIS basemap : https://services.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/World_Street_Map/MapServer Set the Order value. The basemap should have the highest order value in the list. Set the Initial Extent for the map. Pan and zoom to the geographic area your organization works in, then save the extent. Save the map record. Confirm the map is working ¤ After saving, open the Locations or Assets application and open a record that has a location or address. A map panel should appear on the record showing your configured basemap . If the map does not appear, check that: The map record has Enable Map selected. The basemap URL is accessible from the application. If your map does not load In some environments, the application's security policy may block external map tile servers. If the map panel appears but the map does not load, contact IBM support. In Maximo Application Suite Select, system-level security settings are managed by IBM. Continue building your skills ¤ Automate your notifications ¤ With your map in place, keep your team informed. Set up email and push notifications so people know when work is assigned or updated. How do I automate communication? Configure Maximo Mobile for field teams ¤ Let technicians, supervisors, and inventory clerks use a mobile app to access their work from anywhere. How do I configure IBM Maximo Mobile for my team? Related topics ¤ How do I set up labor , crafts , and crews ? How do I automate communication? How do I configure IBM Maximo Mobile for my team? docs.text: How do I set up meters and meter groups? ¤ Meters track equipment usage, operating conditions, and physical measurements. In Maximo Application Suite Select, meter readings drive automated preventive maintenance schedules based on run hours and trigger corrective work orders when readings breach safety limits. You enter meter readings manually. Select does not receive readings automatically from sensors or IoT devices. Setting up meters involves defining meter definitions at the system level, grouping related meters into reusable templates, and attaching those meters to assets and locations . Looking to verify your meter setup right away? Skip to meter setup verification checklist ↓ The three meter types in Maximo Application Suite Select ¤ Before creating meters , select the appropriate meter type based on how the measurement behaves. Figure 1 outlines the decision framework for selecting meter types: Continuous meter : for cumulative values that always increment, such as run hours or cycles, driving usage-based preventive maintenance . Gauge meter : for numeric values that fluctuate up and down, such as temperature or pressure, driving condition monitoring limits. Characteristic meter : for qualitative observations, such as fluid clarity or physical wear, evaluating values from an ALN domain . Figure 1: Decision framework for selecting meter types and operational applications Table 1: Comparison of meter types and operational applications ¤ Meter type Measurement behavior Allowable values Operational application Ice Cream Plant example Continuous Always increments upward until hardware rollover Positive numbers only Drives usage-based PM generation Run hours on the Filler FL-02 drive motor Gauge Fluctuates up and down Numeric values, including negative numbers Triggers Condition Monitoring alerts Ambient temperature in Cold Storage Room Characteristic Qualitative visual or physical observations Alphanumeric values defined in an ALN domain Triggers Condition Monitoring alerts Lubricant clarity rated as Clear, Cloudy, or Dark Step 1: Define meters in the Meter application ¤ Meters are created once at the system level and can then be applied across multiple assets and locations . Creating a meter in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Meter and open it. Click New Meter . In the Meter field, enter a unique identifier, such as RUNHOURS . In the Description field, enter Operating Run Hours . In the Meter Type field, select CONTINUOUS , GAUGE , or CHARACTERISTIC . Configure type-specific settings: For Continuous meters : In the Reading Type field, select ACTUAL if workers log the total odometer reading, or DELTA if workers log only hours run during the shift. Enter the Unit of Measure , such as HOURS . For Gauge meters : Enter the Unit of Measure , such as CELSIUS or PSI . For Characteristic meters : In the Domain field, select the ALN domain containing allowable inspection values. Click Save . Step 2: Bundle meters into Meter Groups ¤ If your facility operates multiple machines that share the same set of meters , group them into a Meter Group. When you assign the group to an asset , all bundled meters attach automatically in a single step. Creating a meter group in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Meter Groups and open it. Click New Meter Group . In the Meter Group field, enter an identifier, such as ROTATING_PUMP . In the Description field, enter Rotating Pump Standard Meter Package . Check Apply New Meters Where Group Is Used? so that any future meters added to this group cascade to existing assets automatically. In the Meters in Meter Group table, click New Row to add individual meters : In the Meter field, select RUNHOURS . In the Sequence field, enter 10 . Click New Row , select VIB_VELOCITY , and enter 20 . Click New Row , select OIL_COND , and enter 30 . Click Save . 💡 Tip: Order meters by inspection sequence ¤ Use the Sequence field in Meter Groups to arrange meters in the order a technician reads physical gauges on the machine. This layout matches field data entry on mobile devices and eliminates scrolling. Step 3: Attach meters to assets ¤ Once meters and meter groups exist, attach them to equipment records on the Meters tab in the Assets application. Configuring an asset meter in the desktop application ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Assets and open it. Open the target equipment record, such as Filler FL-02 . Open the Meters tab. If attaching a group: In the Meter Group field, select ROTATING_PUMP . All bundled meters populate the table. If attaching a single meter : In the Meters table, click New Row and select the meter . For Continuous meters , configure calculation parameters in the details section: In the Average Calculation Method field, select STATIC to manually set daily consumption, or select ALL to let the system calculate rolling daily usage from entered readings. In the Average Units / Day field, enter the expected daily run rate, such as 16.0 hours per day. In the Rollover Point field, enter the physical dial limit, such as 999999 . Click Save . Figure 2 illustrates the continuous meter projection workflow across five stages: Attach meter to asset : assign the continuous meter to the equipment record. Configure daily average : establish the expected daily operating rate, such as 16 hours per day. Log meter reading : enter cumulative runtime observations, such as 1,200 operating hours. Link to PM schedule : define maintenance trigger intervals, such as every 500 runtime hours. Project due date : background processes calculate when thresholds will be reached and forecast work order generation. Figure 2: Continuous meter setup and automated preventive maintenance projection Step 4: Record and manage meter readings ¤ Technicians enter readings during daily inspections, on work orders , or directly in the Assets application. Entering a meter reading ¤ In the Assets application, open the equipment record. In the Select Action menu, click Enter Meter Readings . In the New Reading field for each active meter , enter the observed value. If a continuous meter hardware dial rolled over past its limit, check the Rollover box to allow a lower numeric entry. Click OK . Resetting or replacing broken meters ¤ If a physical gauge or runtime meter fails and is replaced with a new unit: Open the equipment record in the Assets application. In the Select Action menu, click Reset/Replace Meters . Select the continuous meter row. In the Last Reading field, enter the starting value on the replacement meter . If resetting overhaul counters, update Since Last Overhaul or Since Last Repair to zero. Click OK . Common meter setup pitfalls ¤ Avoid these common configuration errors that disrupt automated maintenance: Missing Average Units per Day: If this field is zero or blank on a continuous meter , background cron tasks cannot project future maintenance dates, and PM work orders will fail to generate ahead of time. Using Continuous type for fluctuating values: Never select Continuous for temperatures or pressure levels. If a temperature drops from 40 to 35 degrees, the system treats the drop as an error or rollover. Use Gauge instead. Forgetting the Rollover point: Leaving the rollover limit blank causes the system to reject readings when mechanical dials cycle from 999999 back to 0. Meter setup verification checklist ¤ Use this checklist to confirm your meters are configured properly. Table 2: Meter setup verification checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Proper meter type Continuous meters are used for cumulative run hours; Gauge meters are used for fluctuating levels [ ] ALN domains on characteristics Characteristic meters have an active ALN domain linked for picklist selections [ ] Daily run rate configured All continuous asset meters have a positive Average Units / Day value populated [ ] Rollover point defined Mechanical meters have their hardware maximum rollover value specified [ ] Meter group cascade toggle Meter groups have the auto-apply toggle checked to simplify future fleet updates [ ] Condition monitoring links Gauge meters on critical equipment are linked to active measurement points Related topics ¤ How do I detect issues early? docs.text: How do I fix import errors? ¤ Import errors can occur with locations or assets . This guide helps you troubleshoot and fix common import problems. Quick navigation ¤ Jump to the section you need: Location import errors Location hierarchy errors Location referenced data errors Asset import errors Asset hierarchy errors Asset referenced data errors Common issues across all import types Date and CSV formatting errors Location import errors ¤ Location imports are error-prone because of parent-child relationships and hierarchies. Location hierarchy errors ¤ Hierarchy imports require careful attention to parent-child relationships. Parent locations not created first ¤ Child locations can't be created if their parent doesn't exist yet. Example : You can't create "Ice Cream Plant A > Production Building > Filling Line 2" if "Ice Cream Plant A" and "Production Building" don't exist. What to do : Import locations in order: Top-level locations first : load facilities with no parent, such as Ice cream main plant . Second-level locations next : load buildings that reference the top-level plant, such as Production building . Lowest-level locations last : load rooms that reference the building, such as Filling line room . Figure 1 contrasts the correct top-down import sequence with a missing-parent validation error: Correct top-down load sequence : top-level location Ice cream main plant loads first with no parent, followed by second-level location Production building referencing the plant, followed by lower-level location Filling line room referencing the building. Hierarchy import error condition : attempting to import child record Filling line room before its parent Production building exists causes the data loader to reject the child record with a validation failure. To fix this, import Production building first, then re-import Filling line room . Figure 1: Location hierarchy import sequence and parent validation Incorrect object structure ¤ Location hierarchies require specific object structure in the import file. What to do : Use the system's location hierarchy template or export an existing hierarchy to see the correct format. Incorrect hierarchy relationships ¤ Parent-child relationships must be defined correctly in the import file. What to check : Parent location IDs are correct Hierarchy levels are properly defined System location references are valid What to do : Verify all parent locations exist before importing child locations . Import hierarchies sequentially Hierarchies require sequential loading from the top down. Import parent locations first, then their children. Location referenced data does not exist ¤ Location imports fail when they reference supporting records that don't exist in the system. What to check : GL account exists and is valid Service address is defined Calendar and shift are configured Failure class is set up Bill-to or ship-to address for the site is correct Classification or specification is available What to do : Create or correct the referenced record, or update the import file to use an existing value Make sure values in the import file match system values exactly, which are case-sensitive Verify spelling and IDs are correct 💡 Tips for successful location imports ¤ Import hierarchies in order : Parents before children Verify referenced data : Check that supporting records exist Start with a template : Export existing records to see correct format Validate data first : Check all values against system data Use text format : Prevent Excel from corrupting data Test with small batches : Verify format before importing thousands of records Asset import errors ¤ Asset imports fail due to object structure , data issues, or missing referenced records. Common asset import problems and solutions ¤ Table 1: Common asset import problems and solutions ¤ Problem What happens Solution Parent doesn't exist Child asset fails Import parents first Excel corrupts IDs Leading zeros removed Format as text in Excel Missing required fields Record skipped Validate all required fields Invalid status codes Import fails Use valid status values File too large Timeout or failure Break into smaller batches Asset hierarchy errors ¤ If using parent-child asset relationships, hierarchy errors can cause import failures. What to check : Parent asset exists before importing child assets Parent asset ID is correct in the import file Parent asset exists at the expected site and location What to do : Import parent assets before child assets or subassemblies Verify that each child asset references the correct parent asset Confirm the parent asset location matches expectations Asset referenced data does not exist ¤ Asset imports fail when they reference supporting records that don't exist in the system. What to check : GL account exists and is valid Service address is defined Calendar and shift are configured Failure class is set up Rotating item is created, if applicable Vendor or manufacturer exists Type value is valid Classification or specification is available What to do : Verify that referenced records exist in the system Correct spelling, IDs, and values in the import file Create missing referenced records before importing assets Revalidate the file before importing again 💡 Tips for successful asset imports ¤ Verify referenced data : Check that supporting records exist Start with a template : Export existing records to see correct format Validate data first : Check all values against system data Use text format : Prevent Excel from corrupting data Test with small batches : Verify format before importing thousands of records Common causes of asset import failures ¤ Wrong object structure ¤ The import file must match the expected object structure exactly. What to check : File structure matches ASSET object All required fields are included Field names are correct What to do : Use a template or export an existing asset to see the correct structure. Missing mandatory fields ¤ Assets have required fields that must be populated. Common required fields : Asset ID Description Site Status What to do : Review the import file to ensure all mandatory fields have values. Data errors in file ¤ Problems with the data itself cause import failures. Common data errors : Invalid status codes Non-existent site references Incorrect data types, such as text in number fields Invalid dates What to do : Validate data against system values before importing. Table 2: Common data import error messages and solutions ¤ Error message or symptom Cause Corrective action Parent record not found Child location or asset is listed before its parent record Sort spreadsheet rows top-down so parent records load before child records Invalid site identifier SITEID column is blank or contains a site code that does not exist Verify the exact SITEID code in the Organizations application Leading zero truncated Spreadsheet software converted numerical ID columns to numbers Format ID columns as Text before populating data or editing CSV files Invalid status code Status column uses unapproved status values or non-standard synonyms Use valid initial statuses such as NOT READY , OPERATING , or DRAFT Referenced record does not exist Supporting failure class, craft , or GL account is missing Create the supporting record in its respective application first Why are only some asset records imported? ¤ Partial imports happen when some records pass validation and others don't. Import limits are exceeded : Some systems have limits on: Number of records per import File size Processing time What to do : Break large imports into smaller batches of 1,000 to 5,000 records at a time. Errors stop processing mid-file : If a critical error occurs, the import might stop processing remaining records. What to do : Review error logs to identify where processing stopped, fix the error, and re-import remaining records. Validation failures block individual records : Each record is validated independently. Invalid records are skipped while valid ones are imported. What to do : Review the error file, fix failed records, and import them separately. Common issues across all import types ¤ Date values are invalid or reformatted ¤ Date formatting is a common source of import errors across all record types. Common causes : Excel changed the date format automatically The file uses mixed date formats, such as MM/DD/YYYY and DD/MM/YYYY The date format is ambiguous, such as 01/02/2026 Date values do not match the expected import format What to do : Format date columns as text in Excel before entering values Use one consistent date format throughout the file Re-export or use a template to confirm the expected format Test a small import that includes date values before importing the full file Excel formatting corrupts data ¤ Excel can corrupt data in several ways: Dates : Converts text to dates, such as converting 01-02 to Jan 2 IDs : Removes leading zeros, such as converting 001 to 1 Long numbers : Converts long numbers to scientific notation What to do : Format all columns as text in Excel before entering data, or use a plain text editor to create the CSV. Lack of pre-validation leads to late errors ¤ Without validation, errors aren't discovered until after processing starts. What to do : Always use the preview/validation function before committing the import. Parent-child relationships missing or loaded in wrong order ¤ Importing child records before parents causes failures. What to do : Sort your import file so parent records come before child records. Why shouldn't I load very large datasets in a single file? ¤ Bulk imports have constraints when loading very large volumes in a single batch. Constraints ¤ UI session timeouts : Long-running imports can time out in the web interface. Not designed for massive single-file batches : CSV imports work best with manageable batch sizes, typically under 5,000 records per file. Better suited for smaller datasets : For large imports, consider: Breaking into smaller batches of under 5,000 records Loading parent records before child records in separate files Using Data Management to monitor and track import status What happens next? ¤ To resolve import failures: Review error logs and error file Fix data issues in source file Ensure parent records exist for hierarchies Verify referenced data exists Preview/validate before importing Process the corrected import Verify records were created successfully Continue building your skills ¤ Recommended next step: Verify the system is working ¤ Once your data is successfully loaded, track work orders , costs, and equipment health across your facility. What metrics matter? Related skills ¤ What is the correct load order? : Review dependencies and ensure parent records exist before children. How do I plan my location hierarchy? : Map physical places and prevent orphan records. How do I plan my asset hierarchy? : Structure equipment packages and avoid over-assetization. How do I get data into the system? : Return to Data Management to re-import corrected rows. Related topics ¤ Which object structure do I use for each data type? How do I prepare data for import? How do I standardize data? What is an asset ? Still stuck? ¤ If this page did not answer your question: Browse all Q&A: Get answers In the product: Click the help icon (?) in the top right For a specific field: Click the field name or press Alt+F1

docs.text: How do I simplify workflows? ¤ Complex maintenance workflows with unnecessary approval stages, redundant data entry, and cluttered application screens create bottlenecks that delay repairs. When a process requires ten clicks where three would suffice, staff bypass the system or delay administrative handoffs. Simplifying workflows involves matching user roles to purpose-built apps, configuring default profile values, automating routine notifications, and removing approval hurdles for low-risk work. Looking to verify workflow simplification right away? Skip to workflow simplification checklist ↓ Core strategies for workflow simplification ¤ To streamline maintenance operations across your plant, focus on four key areas: Role-based routing: Direct field technicians and inventory clerks to streamlined role-based apps while reserving comprehensive desktop applications for planners and system administrators. Default profile values: Configure user defaults for site and storeroom so staff do not manually populate repetitive fields on every transaction. Automated notifications: Use Communication Templates to alert stakeholders automatically when work orders change status . Fast-track approvals: Allow routine preventive maintenance and minor repairs below set financial thresholds to approve automatically upon creation. Table 1: Workflow simplification opportunities across operational areas ¤ Operational area Common complexity bottleneck Simplified approach Work execution Technicians opening multi-tab desktop forms on mobile devices Use the Technician role-based app for fast card-based labor and material logging Storeroom issues Storeroom clerks navigating full inventory master records for daily counter issues Use the Issues and Transfers role-based app for rapid barcode scanning and item checkout Material requests Field staff waiting for manual supervisor approvals on standard consumables Pre-approve stocked gasket and lubricant requests attached to active Job Plans Status updates Senders phoning maintenance planners to check repair progress Trigger automated email notifications via Communication Templates at status changes Matching roles to the right applications ¤ Maximo Application Suite Select provides both comprehensive desktop applications and focused role-based apps. Routing users to the appropriate tool reduces training overhead and accelerates data entry. Table 2: Application routing matrix by operational role ¤ Operational role Recommended role-based app Primary desktop application Key daily responsibilities Field Technician Technician app None required for daily tasks View assigned work orders , record meter readings, log labor time, complete job steps Quality Inspector Inspections app None required for daily tasks Complete safety, hygiene, and environmental condition check sheets Inventory Clerk Issues and Transfers app, Inventory Counting app Inventory , Count Books Issue parts at the counter, transfer stock between storerooms, conduct cycle counts Maintenance Planner Work orders Job Plans, PM, Routes Build multi-step maintenance plans, schedule recurring PMs, coordinate craft routes Reliability Engineer Asset Manager Assets , Condition Monitoring, Failure Codes Manage asset registries, configure upper and lower meter limits, analyze failure trends Figure 1: Simplified work order routing and execution workflow As shown in Figure 1, a simplified routing model processes maintenance work across four distinct stages: Work ingestion : The system or a requester generates a work order . Triage and approval routing : Work splits according to urgency: Emergency and critical work : Routes to the supervisor queue for direct supervisor review. Routine PM and minor repairs : Auto-approves to bypass administrative delays and routes directly to craft assignment. Execution : Both streams converge in the Technician app, where technicians view assigned work orders and execute tasks in the field. Completion : Technicians log labor hours, parts, and notes in the mobile interface, automatically triggering completion notifications to stakeholders. Configuring user profile defaults ¤ When technicians, supervisors, or storeroom clerks create records, having the system auto-populate their home Site and default Storeroom eliminates repetitive keystrokes. Setting default Insert Site in the desktop application ¤ In the navigation bar, click the Profile icon in the upper right header and select Default Information . In the Insert Site field, select your active plant site , such as PLANT01 . In the Default Storeroom field, select your primary physical warehouse, such as CENTRAL . Click OK to save your profile preferences. Future transactions, including work orders and inventory issues, will automatically default to these locations . 💡 Tip: Standardize defaults across security groups ¤ Rather than asking every technician to configure profile defaults individually, system administrators can apply default site and storeroom settings at the security group level during initial user onboarding. Automating status notifications ¤ Instead of requiring maintenance planners to send manual emails to production managers when equipment repairs finish, set up automated email notifications using Communication Templates. Creating an automated notification template ¤ In the Find navigation item field, search for Communication Templates and open it. Click New Communication Template . In the Template field, enter an identifier, such as WO_COMPLETED_NOTIFY . In the Applies to field, enter WORKORDER . In the Subject field, enter a clear title: Work Order :WONUM Completed for Asset :ASSETNUM . In the Message body, enter standard text with substitution variables: Work order :WONUM for asset :ASSETNUM at location :LOCATION has been marked complete by :CHANGEBY. In the Recipients tab, add the requestor role or specific supervisor distribution list. In the Select Action menu, change status to Active , then click Save . docs.text: Why aren't technicians using the system? ¤ Low system adoption by maintenance technicians leads to delayed work order reporting, incomplete labor tracking, and missing failure records. When technicians avoid logging into the system, organizations revert to informal paper notes, spreadsheet logs, and verbal handoffs, which makes maintenance tracking unreliable. Technicians generally bypass software not out of reluctance, but because of workflow friction: excessive required fields, confusing desktop interfaces on mobile tablets, slow network synchronization in shielded plant areas, or missing job instructions. Looking to verify field adoption readiness right away? Skip to technician adoption checklist ↓ Identifying adoption friction points ¤ To resolve low adoption, diagnose where field workers encounter resistance in their daily maintenance routine. Table 1: Common adoption barriers and operational remedies ¤ Observed symptom Root cause Corrective action End of shift batch logging Work entry forms require too many clicks during active work Deploy the Technician role-based app with streamlined card views instead of desktop forms Data loss complaints in shielded areas Wireless drops in refrigerated or concrete structures Enable offline data caching in Mobile Properties so data queues locally and syncs automatically Vague work descriptions Free text fields with no structured checklist guidance Attach standardized Job Plans with numbered task steps to preventive maintenance records Incomplete parts recording Finding storeroom item numbers is slow or difficult Pre-load expected materials on job plans so technicians select staged items with a single tap Work orders left in progress Technicians forget to record stop times or final failure codes Set up operational dashboard Work Queue cards that highlight open assignments directly to the team Figure 1: Streamlined mobile workflow overcoming adoption barriers As shown in Figure 1, the streamlined mobile pathway overcomes adoption barriers across four connected elements: Step 1: Start shift : The technician begins their workday and opens the mobile interface. Step 2: Mobile card views : Concise card views replace complex desktop forms with touch-friendly assignment cards. Offline data caching : When technicians work in shielded environments like the Cold Storage Room, the mobile app queues all transactions locally and syncs automatically upon returning to wireless network coverage. Pre-loaded job steps : Structured task execution provides single-tap step check-offs and straightforward failure code selection directly on the device. Streamlining the user experience ¤ Complex desktop screens designed for maintenance planners and database administrators create frustration when presented to field technicians wearing gloves or working on small screens. Switching from desktop forms to the Technician app ¤ The dedicated Technician role-based app presents a clean card layout tailored to field execution. Technicians see assigned work orders , view attached equipment manuals, record meter readings, and log labor hours with minimal taps. 💡 Tip: Keep required fields to an absolute minimum ¤ Audit the mandatory fields required to complete a work order . Every additional mandatory field increases the temptation for technicians to bypass the system or enter dummy placeholder data. Only enforce fields that directly drive regulatory compliance, failure tracking, or inventory reconciliation. Optimizing offline and mobile connectivity ¤ In facilities like the Ice Cream Main Plant, technicians frequently work in heavily insulated areas such as the Cold Storage Room where cellular and WiFi signals cannot penetrate. If the mobile app requires constant connectivity, technicians abandon the device. Configuring offline caching ensures technicians can view job instructions, complete inspection checklists, and record used parts without an active network connection. The device stores all transactions locally and synchronizes with the server once the technician re-enters network coverage. Configuring sync parameters in Mobile Properties ¤ Adjust synchronization settings in the desktop application to prevent timeout errors and ensure responsive background syncing. In the Find navigation item field, search for Mobile Properties and open it. In the Property Name filter, search for sync timeout and batch size properties. Select the property governing offline transaction batching, such as si.offline.download.batchsize . Update the Global Value to an appropriate batch limit, such as 50 records, to reduce synchronization latency over intermittent wireless connections. In the Select Action menu, click Save Properties . Click Live Refresh to apply the updated properties without restarting system services. Engaging technicians through better job preparation ¤ Technicians actively embrace the system when it helps them complete repairs faster rather than acting as a digital time clock. When a work order opens with exact safety procedures, equipment location details, and pre-staged parts lists, the software becomes an indispensable tool. Table 2: Elements of high-value work order preparation ¤ Preparation element Where configured Direct technician benefit Equipment location tags Location / Service Address Shows exact plant room and floor coordinates, eliminating wasted travel time Safety hazard warnings Job Plans Alerts the technician to lockout and tagout requirements before opening panels Pre-specified spare parts Job Plans Lists required replacement seals and gaskets with storeroom bin numbers Technical schematics Asset attachments Provides instant access to wiring diagrams and parts lists directly on mobile devices Technician adoption checklist ¤ Use this checklist to evaluate whether your software setup supports smooth field adoption. Table 3: Field adoption readiness checklist ¤ Check Item What to verify [ ] Role-based app deployment Technicians access assignments through the Technician app rather than desktop screens [ ] Offline sync readiness Devices reliably store and sync records when working in zero-signal zones like cold storage rooms [ ] Minimal required fields Only vital fields, such as actual hours and failure codes , are mandatory at work order completion [ ] Pre-loaded job plans Recurring preventive work orders contain numbered tasks and material lists [ ] Document attachments Equipment manuals and safety schematics are linked to asset records and visible on mobile devices [ ] Dashboard visibility Supervisors review active work queues daily to assist technicians with blocked jobs Related topics ¤ How do I simplify workflows?
